When he halted at Awtas, the people gathered around him, and Duraid said: (p-3095) "In what valley are you?" They said: "In Awtas." He said: "A fine place for horses; neither rugged rocky ground nor soft sand. Why do I hear the braying of camels, the bray of donkeys, the bleating of sheep and the crying of infants?" They said: "Malik has driven with the people their women, their wealth and their children, so that they may fight for them." He said: "A shepherd of sheep, by Allah! Can anything turn back the one who is defeated? If they are yours, they will benefit you only as a man with his weapon; and if they are against you, you will be disgraced regarding your family and your property!"

Then he said: "What did Ka'b and Kilab do?" They said: "None of them attended." He said: "The strength and the vigour are gone. Had it been a day of exaltation and high standing, Ka'b and Kilab would not have stayed away from them. I wish you had done what they did. Who among you attended it?" They said: "'Amr and 'Awf, the two sons of 'Amir." He said: "Those two are young camels that neither benefit nor harm." Then he objected to Malik's opinion on this and said to him: "You have done nothing by putting the egg of Hawazin before the necks of horses. Raise them to the stronghold of their lands and the highest of their people, then place the children on the backs of horses. If the victory is yours, those behind you will join you; and if it is for another, you will have secured your family and your property."

He said: "No, by Allah, I will not do that. You have grown old, and your reason has aged! By Allah, you will obey me, O assembly of Hawazin, or I will lean on this sword until it comes out through my back!" He disliked that Duraid ibn al-Simmah should have any mention or opinion in the matter. They said: "We obey you."

Duraid said: "This is a day I did not witness, and it has not escaped me." Then Malik said to the people: "When you see them, break the scabbards of your swords, then charge with the charge of one man."

He sent spies from his men, and they came to him while their limbs were trembling. He said: "Woe to you! What is the matter with you?" They said: "We saw men in white, on piebald horses. By Allah, we could not hold ourselves back from what has befallen us, as you see." By Allah, that did not turn him from his purpose; he went on as he intended.

When the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) heard of them, he sent 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Hadrad al-Aslami to seek news of them. He came and informed him of the clear facts, that they were heading toward him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) borrowed from Safwan ibn Umayyah one hundred coats of mail, and it was said four hundred. He went out with twelve thousand of the Muslims: ten thousand who had accompanied him from Madinah, and two thousand from the people who had accepted Islam at the conquest. He appointed 'Attab ibn Asid ibn Abi al-'Is ibn Umayyah over Makkah, and he set off in his direction. Among those who followed him were 'Abbas ibn Mirdas, and al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan (p-3096) al-Kilabi, and groups from 'Abs, Dhubyan, Muzaynah and Banu Asad."

On his way he passed by a green lote tree, which they had in the pre-Islamic period, and the Bedouins would circle around it, venerating it and calling it Dhat Anwat. They said: "O Messenger of Allah! Make for us a Dhat Anwat, as they have a Dhat Anwat." He said to them: "You have said what the people of Musa said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those who were before you."

Then he advanced until he came to the valley of Hunayn, one of the valleys of Tihamah, a narrow and rugged valley. They entered its middle at the dim light of dawn, while Hawazin had lain in ambush on both its sides. They charged upon the Muslims with the charge of one man, and the Muslims turned back, none looking back at anyone. He (ﷺ) called out to them, but they did not return. There remained with him Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, al-'Abbas, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and his son Ja'far, al-Fadl and Qutham, the two sons of al-'Abbas, and a group besides them. The Prophet (ﷺ) was on his white mule, Duldul, and al-'Abbas was holding its reins. He had a loud voice, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to call out to the Ansar and the companions of the tree (it is said: and to the Emigrants). They did not hear the voice and went to return, but the crowding of the people prevented them from turning their mounts. Then they stood firm, took up their swords and shields, and leapt down from their mounts, returning to the Prophet (ﷺ). About a hundred of them had gathered, and they confronted Hawazin while the people were arriving in succession. The fighting intensified and the battle grew hot.

When they surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he dismounted from his mule, then took a handful of dust from the earth, faced their faces with it and said: "Disfigured be the faces!" No one among them remained without being struck with it in his eyes and mouth. Then the Muslims charged against them sincerely, and Allah cast terror into the hearts of Hawazin.

They could not control themselves, so they turned away in defeat. The Muslims caught up with the last of the people. The captives of Hawazin were brought before him in chains, and the Muslims took their families and wealth as spoils. Slaughter was intense among Banu Malik of Thaqif, and seventy men of them were killed that day. Groups of Hawazin withdrew to Awtas, and a party of the horsemen of the Muslims who had set out from (Nakhlah) pursued them. They caught up with Duraid ibn al-Simmah among them and killed him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu 'Amir al-Ash'ari, the paternal uncle of Abu Musa, against those of Hawazin who had gathered at Awtas. He fought them, and was killed by an arrow shot at him by Salamah ibn Duraid ibn al-Simmah. Abu Musa took up the banner and charged at the killer of his uncle, and killed him. The polytheists were routed, and all the gatherings of Hawazin dispersed. Four of the Muslims were martyred that day. Then the captives and wealth of Hunayn were brought together to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he ordered them to be held at (al-Ji'ranah) under the supervision of Mas'ud ibn 'Amr al-Ghifari.

The Prophet (ﷺ) immediately marched to al-Ta'if, and besieged (Thaqif) there for fifteen nights. They fought from behind the fortresses. Those around them among the people accepted Islam, and their delegations came to him. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) withdrew from al-Ta'if and halted at al-Ji'ranah with those who were with him from the people. There came to him a delegation of Hawazin, Muslims seeking his favour. He gave them the choice between their families, their children and their wealth, and they chose their families and children. They spoke to the Muslims about this on the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) said: "What belongs to me and to the sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib is yours." The Emigrants and the Ansar said: "What is ours belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Whoever's soul was not content, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) compensated him for his share, and he returned to them all their women and children.

The number of the captives of Hawazin was six thousand, men and women; the camels were twenty-four thousand; the sheep were more than forty thousand; and four thousand ounces of silver. The Prophet (ﷺ) divided the wealth among the Muslims. He also gave a great many of the Tulaqa' (those whom the Prophet (ﷺ) freed on the day of the conquest of Makkah from captivity and the like, and whom he wished to win over to Islam) a hundred camels each. Among them was Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri, who, when he accepted Islam, said:

Never have I seen, nor heard of, anyone among all the people like Muhammad,
Faithful and generous when he is asked, and when he wills he informs you of what is in tomorrow.
And when the battalion flashes its fangs with spears and the striking of every Indian sword,
He is like a lion over his cubs, in the thicket, lying in wait in ambush.

**The second:** Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Zad al-Ma'ad) in a chapter in which he excelled:

An indication of some of the legal issues (fiqhi) and the wise points of judgement contained in this campaign, his words are:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had promised His Messenger, and He is truthful in promise, that when He conquered Makkah, people would enter His religion in multitudes, and all the Arabs would submit to him. When the clear conquest was complete for him, His wisdom required that He hold back the hearts of Hawazin and those who followed them from Islam, and that they gather and prepare to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims, so that the command of Allah might be manifest, and His honouring of His Messenger might be complete, and His support of His religion, and so that their spoils might be a thanksgiving for the people of the conquest, and so that Allah, glorified is He, might show His Messenger and His servants, and His subduing of this great might which the Muslims had never met the like of, so that after this no one among the Arabs would withstand them. And there are other brilliant wisdoms which appear to the reflective and show themselves to the discerning.

His wisdom, glorified is He, required that He first make the Muslims taste the bitterness of defeat and breakdown, despite their great numbers, their equipment and the strength of their might, so that He might humble heads that had been raised by the conquest, and so that they would not enter His land and His sanctuary as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered it, with his head lowered over his horse, such that his chin almost touched his saddle, out of humility before his Lord, submission to His majesty and humbling before His might. He made lawful for him His sanctuary and His land, which had not been made lawful for anyone before him or after him. And so that He, glorified is He, might show to the one who said: "We will not be defeated today because of few numbers" that victory is only from Him; whoever He helps, none can overcome, and whoever He forsakes, has no helper besides Him. He, glorified is He, is the One who undertook the support of His Messenger and His religion, not your multitude which pleased you, for it did not avail you anything, so you turned back in retreat. When their hearts were broken, the robes of consolation were sent to them with the messenger of victory, and Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down soldiers you did not see. His wisdom required that the robes and rewards of victory are poured out only upon people of brokenness: ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them inheritors﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], ﴿And to establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers what they were fearing from them﴾ [al-Qasas: 6].

(p-3099) Among them: when Allah, glorified is He, prevented the army from the spoils of Makkah, so they did not take from it gold, silver, goods, captives or land, as Abu Dawud reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "I asked Jabir: Did they take any spoils on the day of the conquest?" He said: "No!"

They had conquered it by pressing horses and camels, and they were ten thousand, and they had need of what an army needs of the causes of strength. So Allah, glorified is He, stirred the hearts of the polytheists to attack them, and cast into their hearts the bringing out of their wealth, their cattle and their sheep, and their captives with them, as a provision and hospitality and honour for His party and His army. He completed His decree, glorified is He, by making them hope for victory and showing them the beginnings of triumph, so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done.

After Allah had granted His victory to His Messenger and to his allies, the spoils were displayed before their owners, and the shares of Allah and His Messenger were applied to them, it was said: "We have no need of your blood, nor of your women and offspring." Then Allah, glorified is He, inspired their hearts with repentance (tawba) and turning back to Him (inaba), and they came as Muslims.

It was then said: "Indeed, among the thanks owed for your Islam and your coming is that we return to you your women, your sons and your captives."

And [Allah says]: ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you. Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Anfal: 70]

Among the lessons: Allah, glorified is He, began the military campaigns of the Arabs with the battle of Badr and concluded their warfare with the battle of Hunayn. For this reason the two campaigns are mentioned together, so it is said "Badr and Hunayn," even though seven years lay between them. The angels fought alongside the Muslims in both campaigns, and the Prophet ﷺ threw pebbles into the faces of the polytheists in both of them. Through these two campaigns the flame of the Arabs was extinguished by the raids of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims. The first frightened them and broke their edge, and the second drained their strength, exhausted their arrows and humbled their multitude, until they had no choice but to enter the religion of Allah.

Another lesson: Allah, glorified is He, consoled the people of Mecca through these events and gladdened them with what they gained of victory and booty. It served as a remedy for the defeat they had suffered, even though He had specified their consolation. He also made them aware of the completion of His blessing upon them by turning away from them the evil of Hawazin, for they had no strength against them; they were granted victory over them only through the Muslims. Had they been left alone, their enemy would have devoured them... and other wisdoms besides these, which none encompasses except Allah, the Exalted. End of quotation.

The third point: Some scholars said: The verse indicates that one must turn to Allah, the Exalted, alone and rely upon Him. What is related in the story also indicates the permissibility of what has been reported as commendable: the permissibility of conciliation (ta'lif) and of showing kindness to the believers, of throwing pebbles during battle, and of the cries by which the enemy is terrified. End of quotation.

Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zad al-Ma'ad, has excellent sections on the jurisprudence (fiqh) of this event, so let them be consulted.

The fourth point concerns His saying: ﴿وَيَوْمَ حُنَيْنٍ﴾ (and the day of Hunayn) [al-Tawba: 25]. It was said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb conjoined to (نَصَرَكم) (nasarakum, "He gave you victory"), meaning: "and He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn." Abu Mas'ud favoured its conjunction to the position (maHall) of ﴿فِي مَواطِنَ﴾ (in many battlefields) [al-Tawba: 25], with the omission of a governed noun (mudaf) in one of them, meaning: "and the battlefields of the day of Hunayn," or "in the days of many battlefields and the day of Hunayn."

Abu Mas'ud said: Perhaps the change in form is to hint at the lack of steadfastness that occurred at the beginning of the affair. End of quotation.

Al-Shihab (al-Alusi) said: Then the conjunction of (يَوْمَ حُنَيْنٍ) follows the pattern of (مَلائِكَتِهِ وجِبْرِيلَ) (angels and Gabriel), as if it were said: "Allah gave you victory at many times, and at the time when you were impressed by your numbers." The objection that the context does not support this is not valid, because it is not a case of preferring some events over others. He did not mention the battlefield as a preparation for the day of Hunayn, as with the angels, since the day of Hunayn is not superior to the day of Badr, which is the conquest of conquests, the lord of events, and through which they gained the highest portion and the lofty ranks. For the intention in such a case is that this particular event has a distinction that makes it different from its kind, since the distinction intended is not merely nobility and abundance of reward, so that one might suppose this; rather it includes the strangeness of its circumstances and what occurred in it being unusual: victory after despair, relief after hardship, and other excellences besides. End of quotation.

(p-٣١٠١) Then, may He be exalted, indicated that allying with the polytheists, since it does not yield the strengthening that brings about victory, harms by spreading the impurity of their inner hearts to the pure inner hearts of the believers. So He said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 28:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[28] ﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, those whose inner selves are purified by faith. ﴿Indeed the polytheists are unclean﴾, that is, possessors of uncleanness, because with them is polytheism, which is in the position of uncleanness. It is a metaphor for the impurity of the inner self and the corruption of belief, borrowed for this purpose. Or it is literal, because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ritual bathing, and do not avoid impurities, so uncleanness clings to them. Or they were treated as if they were uncleanness itself, as an exaggeration in describing them with it.

﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, that is, for Hajj or 'Umrah, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah. Al-Mahayimi said: because al-Masjid al-Haram is where those scattered across the earth gather, so that the clarity of hearts may flow from one to another, whereas here the spread of darkness into the general public is feared.

﴿after this, their year﴾, that is, after the Hajj of this year of theirs, which was the ninth year after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr was appointed over the season. It has already been mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them) after Abu Bakr, to proclaim among the polytheists: "That no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and that no naked person shall circumambulate the House." Allah then completed that, and decreed it by law and by decree.

﴿And if you fear poverty﴾, that is, destitution because of their being prevented from the Haram, due to the cutting off of the benefits that came to you from their arrival. ﴿Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾, that is, through the conquest of lands, the acquisition of spoils, the taking of the jizyah, and the coming of people from the corners of the earth.

Ibn Ishaq said: The people said: "The markets will be cut off from us, trade will perish, and the benefits we used to gain from them will be gone." So Allah, exalted is He, said: (p-3102) ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ up to His words:

﴿and they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], that is: this is the compensation for what you feared of the cutting off of those markets. Allah compensated them for what was cut off from them due to polytheism with what He gave them from the necks of the People of the Book in the form of jizyah. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing﴾, that is, of what sets you right; ﴿Wise﴾, that is, in what He commands and forbids.

Notes:

The first: The verse indicates the uncleanness of the polytheist. As in the authentic report: "The believer does not become unclean." As for the uncleanness of his body, the majority hold that he is not unclean in body and essence, because Allah, exalted is He, made the food of the People of the Book lawful.

Some of the Zahiriyyah held that their bodies are unclean. Ash'ath reported from al-Hasan: Whoever shakes hands with them should perform ablution. Narrated by Ibn Jarir, and transmitted by Ibn Kathir.

I say: The argument from Allah's making the food of the People of the Book lawful is not conclusive, because the discussion concerns the polytheists, and the principle of the noble revelation is the distinction between them and the People of the Book, so neither includes the other in this matter.

Some Yemeni exegetes said: The position of al-Qasim, al-Hadi and others is that the disbeliever is unclean in essence, taking the apparent meaning of the verse, because that is the literal sense. This is supported by the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, who said: He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We come to the land of the People of the Book and ask them for their vessels." He (ﷺ) said: "Wash them, then cook in them."

(p-3103) Zayd, al-Mu'ayyad billah, the Hanafiyyah and the Shafi'iyyah said: The polytheist is not unclean in essence, because the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ablution from the water-skin of a polytheist, borrowed armour from Safwan and did not wash it, the dishes used to pass between the houses of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the captives without being washed, and the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) cooked in the vessels of the polytheists without washing them. They interpreted the verse in the ways mentioned above, and each interpreter disputes what the other has argued from. End of quotation.

The second: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil, concerning His words ﴿so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year﴾, that the disbeliever is prevented from entering the Haram, and that he is not permitted to enter it, neither for trade nor for anything else, even if it were beneficial to us, because al-Masjid al-Haram, wherever it is mentioned absolutely in the Qur'an, is meant as the whole Haram, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata' and others.

Whoever permits his entry into the Haram other than the Masjid takes the apparent meaning of the verse, since it restricts the prohibition to it. Al-Shafi'i took the apparent meaning of the verse to mean that they are not prevented from entering all the mosques, because of His saying "al-Haram", and others analogized all mosques to it.

Abu Hanifah also took its apparent meaning to mean that the People of the Book are not prevented from entering, since it specifies the polytheist. End of quotation. This is the more evident view.

Al-Shihab said: Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, also followed the apparent meaning, for he restricted the prohibition on entering the Haram to Hajj and 'Umrah, based on His words ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾, for that only applies when they are prevented from entering the Haram, which is evident; that is, because the place of trade is not the mosque itself. The proclamation of 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, with the words: "Let no polytheist perform Hajj after this year of ours," is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) which specifies it, so it cannot be said that the explicit text of the verse contradicts it. End of quotation.

The third: al-Nasir said: Someone may argue from His words ﴿so let them not approach﴾ (the verse) that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Shari'ah, especially its prohibitions, since the apparent meaning of the verse is that the prohibition is directed at the polytheists. However, this is far-fetched, because it is known of the polytheists that they would not be deterred by this prohibition, and the aim is to purify al-Masjid al-Haram by keeping them away from it, which is achieved only by forbidding the Muslims from allowing them to approach it.

What indicates that the one addressed in reality is the Muslims is that the speech begins by addressing them in His words ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and that it explicitly includes their address in His words ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾. Often a prohibition is directed at one whose opposite is intended, and at what is intended to be its opposite, when there is a necessary connection, as in His saying: "I should not find you here," and ﴿and do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. End of quotation.

The fourth: "al-'Aylah" is a verbal noun from "'ala", meaning became poor. It was read as "'a'ilah", which is either a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ilah, or an active participle functioning as an adjective to an implied feminine noun, i.e., a state of being "'a'ilah", meaning impoverishing.

Ibn Jinni said: This is among the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'ilah, like al-'aqibah and al-'afiyah. From it is His saying ﴿you will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11], that is, lagw (idle talk). From it is also the expression "I passed by him especially" (khassah), that is, especially. As for His saying ﴿and you will not cease to observe treachery from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], it may be a verbal noun, that is, khiyanah, or it may be understood as "an act or a treacherous intention". Likewise here it may be understood as: "if you fear, in a state of being impoverished." End of quotation.

The fifth: If it is asked: What is the reason for conditioning with the will in His words ﴿if He wills﴾, when the context and the occasion of revelation, which is their fear of poverty, require removing it by a promise to enrich them without hesitation?

The answer: The condition is not mentioned to express doubt, but to show that it is by His will, with no cause other than it, so they should turn to Him alone and cut off their regard for anything else. It also alerts that He bestows it as a favour, not as an obligation upon Him, for if it were by obligation it would not be left to His will. It cannot be said that this does not need to be taken from the condition, together with His words "from His bounty", because His words "from His bounty" indicate that it is a gift and beneficence, whereas this indicates that it is without obligation, and the difference between the two is great. It has also been said that it is to alert that it is by His will, not by a person's effort and stratagem:

"Had wealth been gained by stratagems, you would have found me clinging to the stars of the horizons of the sky."

Thus in al-'Inayah.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 9, Verse 29 (Part 1 of 3)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[29] ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizya (poll tax) willingly, while they are humbled.﴾

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizya (poll tax) willingly, while they are humbled.﴾ Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the ruling concerning the polytheists, namely the declaration of disavowal of their covenant, the declaration of disavowal of them personally, the obligation to fight them, and their exclusion from the Sacred Mosque, and the absence of fear of the imagined poverty that might result from their cutting off, He next mentioned the ruling concerning the People of the Book, which is that they are to be fought until they submit or give the jizya. In the course of this, He alerted to some of the means of enrichment that had been promised in a general way, guiding the believers to pursue them seeking His bounty and seeking the fulfilment of His promise.

Mujahid said: The verse was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to fight the Romans, and after its revelation he undertook the expedition of Tabuk.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning Qurayza and al-Nadir among the Jews, and he (the Prophet) made a peace settlement with them. It was the first jizya that the people of Islam obtained, and the first humiliation that the People of the Book suffered at the hands of the Muslims. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the verse encompasses all of that without restriction.

Ibn Kathir said: This verse is the first command revealed to fight the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, and that was in the year nine (AH). For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prepared for fighting the Romans, called the people to it, made it public to them, and sent to the tribes of the Arabs around Medina, summoning them, and they came out in full force with him. About thirty thousand fighters gathered. Some of the people of Medina and those around it among the hypocrites and others stayed behind. That was in a year of drought and at a time of summer heat.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out intending Syria to fight the Romans, and he reached Tabuk and camped there for about twenty days. Then he sought Allah's guidance (istikhara) concerning returning, and he returned that year because of the hardship of the situation and the weakness of the people, as its explanation will come later, Allah willing. End of quotation.

The expression "the People of the Book" by the relative clause mentioned serves to indicate that what is within the relative clause is the cause for the command to fight. For they do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, as He, exalted is He, commanded, since they hold, regarding what is obligatory for Him, exalted is He, and regarding the Resurrection, the greatest misguidance and deviation. ﴿And do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾: meaning what has been established as forbidden in the Book and the Sunnah.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "His Messenger" is the Messenger whom they claim to follow. So the meaning is that they oppose the basic principle of their religion, which has been abrogated, in belief and practice, since they altered and changed it, following their own desires.

And His saying: (ha-ba) — so the intended meaning is: they do not follow our law nor their own law, and the combination of the two matters is a cause for fighting them. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the religion of truth﴾ is an idafa (construct phrase) of the qualified to the qualifier, or the intended meaning of "the truth" is Allah, exalted is He.

And His saying: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾: that is, what has been determined for them to give.

Ibn al-Athir said: The jizya is the wealth by which the Scripture-follower is granted dhimma (protected status). It is a form (fi'la) from "jaza" (recompense), as if it "compensated" for his killing.

Al-Raghib said: It was so named because it is sufficient (ijtiza') in place of sparing their blood.

Al-Shihab said: It has been said its derivation is from "al-jaza'" in the sense of "al-qada'" (judgment): one says "jizyatuhu bi-ma fa'ala" (I requited him for what he did), or "jaziytuhu" (I recompensed him). Or its root is the hamza from "al-juz'" and "al-tajzi'a" (division), because it is a portion of wealth given. It has also been said that it is an arabized word (mu'arrab), like zayt (oil), and it is the jizya in Persian. End of quotation.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿willingly (ʿan yad)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (yu'tu) "they give". And "yad" (hand) here may mean either submission and compliance, as one says: "This is my hand for you," meaning "I submitted to you and I yielded to you," and "he gave his hand," meaning he complied.

As it is said in its opposite: "he withdrew his hand from obedience," because whoever refuses and resists does not give his hand, unlike the obedient, compliant one.

Or it may mean payment in cash, that is: until they give it in cash, not on credit, and then it is like "yad" in his saying (ﷺ): "Do not sell gold for gold or silver for silver... up to his saying: 'hand to hand' (yadan bi-yad)."

Or it may mean the literal organ, and "ʿan" is in the sense of "bi" (by/with), meaning: they do not send it by the hand of anyone, but from the hand of the giver to the hand of the receiver.

Or it may mean: out of willingness of soul. Abu Ubayda said: Whoever submits to a conqueror and gives him something, without willing consent of heart and without being overpowered, from hand to hand, has given it ʿan yad. (Majaz al-Qur'an, vol. 1, p. 256.)

Or it may mean a group (jama'a). Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"He gave, and he gave me a hand (yad), and a house, and a courtyard, which he turned into an estate."
(al-Asas, vol. 2, p. 560, and al-Lisan, vol. 15, p. 425, Beirut.) From this is the hadith: "And they are one hand against whoever is other than them," meaning: they are united against their enemies, each assisting the other. This was said by Abu Ubayda. Or it may mean humiliation (dhull), which Ibn al-A'rabi related and cited as a possible sense in the verse.

This is if "yad" is intended as the giver's hand. If the receiver's hand is intended, then "yad" may mean strength, that is, "ʿan yad qahira mustawliya" (from a dominant, overpowering hand), and they say: "I have no yad for it," meaning "no strength." Or it may mean authority (sultan), and this is like the preceding. From it is the "yad" of the wind, its authority. Labid said:
"Dispersed clouds whose command is in the hand of the north wind."
When the wind was given control over the direction of the clouds, it was given authority over them.

Or it may mean blessing (ni'ma), that is, "ʿan inʿam ʿalayhim bi-dhalika" (as a favour bestowed upon them in this), because accepting the jizya and leaving them to themselves is a blessing upon them.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: This meaning is the most fruitful (amla bi-l-fa'ida).

Or it may mean wealth (ghina), related in al-ʿInaya, and al-Taj cited it among the meanings of "yad".

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they are humbled﴾: that is, abased (adhilla').

Notes:

First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ʿan yad﴾ may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (yu'tu), or from the jizya, meaning: accompanied by compliance, handed over by their hands, issuing from wealth, accompanied by abasement, and occurring as a favour upon them. Thus in al-ʿInaya.

Second: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: This verse is the foundation for accepting the jizya from the People of the Book.

Third: He also said: Whoever holds that the meaning of "yad" in what precedes is wealth has used it as evidence that it is obligatory upon the poor, and whoever holds that it is not sent by proxy uses it as evidence that a Muslim may not be appointed as an agent for it, nor may he guarantee it on their behalf, nor transfer it onto him.

Fourth: al-Suyuti also said: Whoever holds that it is collected with humiliation has used as evidence His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they are humbled﴾. They say the collector sits and the dhimmi stands, lowers his head, bends his back, places it in the scale, and the collector seizes his beard and strikes his jaw.

He said: This is refuted by al-Nawawi, who said: This is an evil and false practice. End of quotation.

I say: Al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, spoke truly, for it is an evil and ugly practice, which the generosity of the religion and its known gentleness reject. Had his purpose not been to refute the one who said it, the preface of the page would not have been disfigured by transmitting it.

Then I saw that Ibn al-Qayyim refuted it, saying: All of this has no evidence, nor is it what the verse implies, nor is it reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or from his Companions. He said: The correct understanding of the verse is that the humiliation (sagar) is their commitment to the application of Allah's rulings upon them and their giving of the jizya, for that is the humiliation. This is what al-Shafi'i said. End of quotation.

[p. 3109] Then al-Suyuti said: Whoever holds that the dhimmis are left in the land of the people of Islam has used the verse as evidence, since its implication is withholding from them upon their payment, and among withholding is that they are not expelled. And whoever holds that there is no minimum for it, and whoever holds that it is in exchange for sparing blood and not a rent for the dwelling, [has also reasoned from it]. End of quotation.

Fifth: Abu Ubayd related in the book al-Amwal from Ibn Shihab, who said: The first among the People of the Book to give the jizya were the people of Najran, and they were Christians.

Sixth: Abu Ubayd said: The jizya was established upon the Jews and Christians by the Book, and upon the Magians by the Sunnah.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: When the verse of the jizya was revealed, he (ﷺ) took it from three groups: from the Magians, the Jews, and the Christians, and he did not take it from idol-worshippers.

It was said: It is not permissible to take it from any unbeliever other than these, or whoever follows their religion, following his practice and his abstention. And it was said: Rather, it is taken from the People of the Book and from other unbelievers such as the idol-worshippers among the non-Arabs, but not among the Arabs. The first view is the view of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad (in one of his two narrations).

The second view is the view of Abu Hanifa, and Ahmad (in the other narration), may Allah have mercy on them both.

Proponents of the second view say: He only did not take it from the polytheist Arabs because its obligation was only revealed after the Arab lands had embraced Islam and no polytheist remained in them. For it was revealed after the conquest of Mecca and the entry of the Arabs into the religion of Allah in multitudes, so no polytheist remained in the land of the Arabs. For this reason, after the Conquest, he undertook the expedition of Tabuk, and they were Christians. Had there been polytheists in the land of the Arabs, they would have been nearest to him, and they would have been more deserving of raids than the more distant ones.

Whoever reflects on the biography (sira) and the days of Islam knows that the matter is as stated. The jizya was not taken from them because there was no one from whom it could be taken, not because they were not among its recipients. They said: He did take it from the Magians, and they are not People of the Book, and it is not correct that they had a scripture which was lifted; that is a hadith whose like is not established and whose chain is not sound.

There is no difference between fire-worshippers and idol-worshippers. Rather, idol-worshippers are closer in condition to fire-worshippers, and among them was adherence to the religion of Abraham which did not exist among the fire-worshippers. Rather, the fire-worshippers were the enemies of Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil). So if the jizya is taken from them, taking it from idol-worshippers is more fitting. The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indicates this, as established in Sahih Muslim that he said: "When you meet your enemy among the polytheists, invite them to one of three options. Whichever of them they answer you with, accept it from them, and hold back from them." Then he ordered him to invite them to Islam, or to the jizya, or to fight them.

And al-Mughira said to the agent of Kisra: "Our Prophet has commanded us to fight you until you worship Allah, or pay the jizya."

And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Quraysh: "Is there for you a word by which the Arabs would submit to you, and by which the non-Arabs would pay you the jizya?" They said: "What is it?" He said: "There is no god but Allah."

Then Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) made a peace settlement with the people of Najran for two thousand robes, half payable in Safar and the rest in Rajab, which they would pay to the Muslims, along with the lending of thirty coats of mail, thirty horses, thirty camels, and thirty of each kind of weapon, with which they would fight, and the Muslims would be responsible for them until they returned them, should there be treachery or deceit in Yemen. Also on condition that no church of theirs would be demolished, no priest would be expelled, and they would not be pressured in their religion, so long as they did not commit an offence or consume usury.

When he sent Mu'adh to Yemen, he commanded him to take from every adult male one dinar or its value in garments.

In this is evidence that the jizya is not fixed in its kind or its amount, but may be garments, gold, or robes, and it may increase or decrease according to the need of the Muslims, the capacity of the one from whom it is taken, and his condition in ease and the wealth he possesses.

[p. 3111]

The Prophet ﷺ and his successors did not distinguish between Arabs and non-Arabs (ʿajam) in the jizya. Rather, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it from the Christian Arabs, and he took it from the Magians (majus) of Hajar, who were Arabs. The Arabs, in origin, are a people that had no scripture, and each group among them followed the religion of the nations that bordered them. Thus the Arabs of Bahrain were Magians because of their proximity to Persia; Tanukh, Bahra, and the Banu Taghlib were Christians because of their proximity to the Romans; and some tribes of Yemen were Jews because of their proximity to the Jews of Yemen. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ applied the rulings of the jizya and did not consider their fathers, nor when they had entered the religion of the People of the Book: whether their entry had occurred before the abrogation (naskh) and alteration (tabdil) or after it, and how they could know that, how it could be ascertained, and what evidence indicates it? It is established in the biographies (siyar) and the campaigns (maghazi) that among the Ansar were those whose sons became Jews after the abrogation by the law of Jesus, and their fathers wished to compel them to Islam, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. And in his saying to Muʿadh: "Take from every adult male one dinar," there is evidence that it is not taken from a child or a woman.

Seventh: Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book (al-Kharaj):

There is no zakat on any of their property, men's or women's, except what they deal with in their trade; on that they owe half the tenth (nisf al-ʿushr). Nothing is taken from property until it reaches two hundred dirhams, or twenty mithqals of gold, or the value of that in goods for trade. No one among the People of the Dhimma is to be beaten in demanding the jizya from them, nor are they to be made to stand in the sun or anything else, nor is any form of hardship to be imposed on their bodies; rather, they are to be treated gently, and they are to be detained until they pay what they owe, and they are not to be released from detention until the jizya has been collected from them. It is not permissible for the governor to leave any of the Christians, Jews, Magians, Sabians, or Samaritans without the jizya being taken from them, nor to grant any of them a concession to abandon any part of it, nor to leave one and take from another, for that is not allowed, because their blood and property are protected only by the payment of the jizya, and the jizya is in the position of the kharaj revenue.

Then Abu Yusuf addressed Harun al-Rashid, saying:

It is fitting, O Commander of the Faithful, may Allah support you, that you proceed in showing gentleness to the People of the Dhimma of your Prophet and your cousin Muhammad ﷺ, and that you look after them, so that they are not wronged or harmed, nor burdened beyond their capacity, and nothing of their property is taken except by a right that is due from them. For it has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "Whoever wrongs a mu'ahid (covenanted non-Muslim), or burdens him beyond his capacity, then I will be his adversary (hajib)." Among the things ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said at his death was: "I charge the caliph after me with the dhimma of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he fulfil their covenant for them, that he fight on their behalf, and that they not be burdened beyond their capacity."

He said: Hisham ibn ʿUrwah narrated to us from his father, "that Saʿid ibn Zayd passed by a people who had been made to stand in the sun in some part of the land of Syria. He said, 'What is the matter with these people?' It was said to him, 'They have been made to stand in the sun over the jizya!' He disliked that, and entered upon their governor and said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever punishes people, Allah will punish him."'"

He said: Hisham ibn ʿUrwah narrated to us from his father, "that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab passed by the road to Syria, on his return journey from Syria, by a people who had been made to stand in the sun, with oil poured over their heads. He said: 'What is the matter with these?' It was said: 'The jizya is owed by them and they have not paid it, so they are being punished until they pay it!' ʿUmar said: 'What do they say, and what excuse do they give regarding the jizya?' They said: 'They say, "We do not have it."' He said: 'Leave them, and do not burden them with what they cannot bear; for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Do not punish people, for those who punish people in this world, Allah will punish them on the Day of Resurrection."' And he ordered them released, and they were released."

Then he said: Umayr ibn Nafiʿ narrated to me from Abu Bakr, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by the door of a people, and there was a beggar, an old man blind in sight, asking. ʿUmar struck his upper arm from behind and said: "Of which of the People of the Book are you?" He said: "A Jew." He said: "What has driven you to what I see?" He said: "I am asking for the jizya, and I have need and old age." ʿUmar took his hand and went with him to his house, and gave him something from the house, then he sent to the keeper of the treasury (bayt al-mal) and said: "Look after this man and his like. By Allah, we have not been fair to him if we eat of his youth and then abandon him in old age: ﴿The alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60]. The poor are Muslims, and this man is among the needy of the People of the Book." He remitted the jizya from him and from his companions. Abu Bakr said: I witnessed that from ʿUmar, and I saw that old man. End of quotation.

Eighth: On the purpose of the jizya and the compassion of the Muslims toward those they sheltered with their swords.

The Imam, Shaykh Muhammad ʿAbduh, Mufti of Egypt, said in his book "Islam and Christianity," under the discussion of the comparison between martial Islam and peaceful Christianity, the following, p. 74:

Martial Islam was content, in conquest, with bringing the conquered land under its authority, and then left the people with the religion they had, to discharge what was obligatory for them according to their belief as that belief dictated. It only imposed on them a jizya which they paid, to help secure their protection and the preservation of their safety in their homes; and after that they were free in their creeds, their places of worship and their customs, not harassed in any work, nor wronged in any dealing. The caliphs of the Muslims used to enjoin their commanders to respect the worshippers who withdrew from the common people into the monasteries and hermitages solely for worship, and they used to enjoin them to respect the lives of women, children, and everyone who did not aid in fighting.

The widely transmitted Sunnah came with the prohibition of harming the People of the Dhimma and with establishing their rights over the Muslims: they have what we have, and they have what is incumbent upon us, and whoever harms a dhimmi is not of us. The practice continued on this basis for as long as the power of Islam endured. I am not concerned if some Muslims deviated from these rulings when weakness began to afflict Islam and narrowness of heart, a trait of the weak, appeared; that is not attributable to its nature and is not mixed into its essence.

Peaceful Christianity held that it had the right to oversee every religion that came under its authority, monitoring the actions of its adherents and singling them out, apart from others, with kinds of treatment that no patience can endure, however great. Then, when it had the power to expel them, after failing to force them out of their religion or to baptize them, it drove them out of their homes and washed the lands clean of their traces, as has happened and still happens in every land that a Christian nation has conquered in genuine conquest, where nothing restrains a Christian from aggressing against non-Christians except the abundance of numbers or the strength of arm, as history witnesses and as its own writers attest.

Then he said: You see that Islam was content, from the nations and communities it overcame, with a sum of money less than what they used to pay before its domination over them, and with their living in peace, not disturbing the state's tranquility or upsetting the public order; then it leaves them, after that, free to choose in their private affairs, with no overseer over them in these except their own consciences. End of quotation.

And in the book "Famous Celebrities of Islam," in the discussion on the expulsion of the people of Najran, the following appears:

The basis of the call to Islam is proclamation, and there is no compulsion in religion. Whoever accepts it is among the Muslims; whoever refuses must submit to their authority and give them a portion of his wealth, with which they help protect his property, honor, and life, and he has the right to be fulfilled in the covenant he made with them. He (ﷺ) said: he shall not be turned from his religion, and he shall have the protection (dhimma) and the covenant wherever he is and wherever he is found in the lands of Islam, as long as he remains faithful to his covenant, pays his jizya, does not betray the Muslims, and does not collude with their enemy against them. The best evidence for this that we set before you in this section is the account of the people of Najran in Yemen, who were among the People of the Book, so that you may know how the People of the Dhimma were treated, and the extent to which the caliphs maintained their covenants with them, as long as they did not betray or deceive.

The account, precisely stated, is that a delegation of theirs came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he invited them to Islam, but they refused. They asked him for peace and that he accept a tribute from them, so he made peace with them for a specified amount, which they would pay to the Muslims each year, and he wrote them a document in which he granted them the dhimma and covenant of Allah, that they should not be turned from their religion or their ranks within it, that they should not be gathered for levy or tithed, and that they should be secured for their persons, their community, their land, their property, their absent and present members, their caravans, their messengers, and their images. Nothing that they had should be changed, and no right of theirs should be altered, and no army should trample their land; and whoever among them asks for a right, justice shall be done between them, neither wronging nor being wronged. For them, in this, is the protection of Allah and the dhimma of His Messenger forever, until the command of Allah comes, so long as they give sincere counsel and act righteously.

It was stipulated upon them that they should not consume usury (riba) nor deal in it.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, became caliph, he confirmed them in their situation and wrote them a document like the Messenger of Allah's document, although he feared them and wished to expel them, because of what was narrated: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Two religions shall not remain in the Arabian Peninsula."

When death came to Abu Bakr, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab enjoined their expulsion because they had violated the covenant by engaging in usury.

Observe how the Prophet ﷺ held that two religions should not coexist in the Arabian Peninsula, because the Arabs were a people newly come to Islam; he had endured much to gather their word and unify their direction, so it was dangerous that there should exist among them a people following a religion other than theirs, who would tempt those who neighbored them away from Islam, given the newness of their conversion and their not yet being firmly established in its sound foundations.

This is one aspect. In another aspect, the Najranis used to trade in usury, and the harm this does to those who neighbored them among the people of Yemen is not hidden; usury drains the spring of their wealth and heralds their poverty, without their awareness. Especially since Islamic law has forbidden it with a categorical prohibition, and there is no assurance that the Najranis, by continuing to engage in usury, would not lead some Muslim neighbors into committing sin by dealing with them in usury.

Despite these reasons which would necessitate compelling the Najranis to Islam, the Prophet ﷺ did not compel them, because his law did not permit compelling the People of the Book to Islam. Therefore he left them in their religion, after he had invited them to Islam in the best manner, and they refused; and he gave them the said document of covenant, except that he stipulated in it that they should not betray the Muslims and should not deal in usury, as you have seen.

When Abu Bakr became caliph he reaffirmed their first covenant, although he saw in their presence in the Arabian Peninsula the same danger that the Prophet ﷺ had seen; so he could do nothing regarding them except what the Messenger ﷺ had done. Until, when he learned that they had broken the covenant and dealt in usury, he ordered ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, while he was ill, to expel them from the Arabian Peninsula, without their being tempted in their religion.

When ʿUmar became caliph, the first expedition he dispatched was that of Abu ʿUbayd to Iraq and that of Yaʿla ibn Umayya to Yemen. He instructed him to expel the people of Najran, to treat them with gentleness, to buy their property from them, and to let them choose, concerning their land, any land within the lands of Islam they wished. He did not treat them as a strong victor treats a weak defeated people, as is the custom of every state before Islam and after it, even to this day, in dealing with peoples who differ from its creed and submit to the might of its rule. So they dispersed: some of them settled in al-Sham, and some settled in a district near Kufa, which came to be called after them (al-Najraniyya).

Care for them did not end with their expulsion, with preserving the covenant that they held, or with compensating them for the land and wealth they left behind. Rather, after that, they continued to receive every kind of consideration and kindness from the caliphs.

Among examples: when ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, became caliph, they complained to him once of the narrowness of their land and of the competition of the landowners (dahaqin) against them, and they asked him to lighten their jizya (poll tax, a tax on non-Muslim subjects in exchange for protection). He wrote to al-Walid ibn ʿUqba ibn Abi Muayt, his governor over Kufa, a letter enjoining care for them and ordering him to remove two hundred garments (hulla) from their jizya, for the sake of Allah, and as recompense for their land.

Al-Baladhuri narrated that when Muʿawiya, or Yazid ibn Muʿawiya, took power, they complained to him of their dispersion, of the deaths among them, and of the conversion to Islam of some of them. They presented to him the letter of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, in which he had remitted from them the garments, and they said: "We have only increased in loss and weakness." So he remitted two hundred garments more, completing four hundred garments.

When al-Hajjaj became governor of Iraq, and Ibn al-Ashʿath rebelled against him, he accused them and the landowners of supporting him, and he restored their jizya to what it had been.

When ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz became caliph, they complained to him of al-Hajjaj's oppression and the reduction of their numbers. He ordered that they be counted, and their total was found to be ten (?) of their former number. So he imposed upon them two hundred garments as jizya, on their heads only.

When Yusuf ibn ʿUmar became governor of Iraq, during the caliphate of al-Walid ibn Yazid al-Umawi, he restored them to what they had been under al-Hajjaj, out of partisanship for al-Hajjaj.

When the Umayyad dynasty ended and Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Saffah was made caliph, they brought their affair before him, along with what had been done by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and Yusuf ibn ʿUmar, and he restored them to the two hundred garments.

When Harun al-Rashid became caliph, they complained to him of the harshness of the officials toward them. He ordered that a letter be written for them confirming the two hundred garments, and he went to great lengths in gentleness toward them. He ordered that they be exempted from dealing with the officials, and that their payments be made to the public treasury (bayt al-mal) at the capital, so that no official could harass them.

This is what the historians have related concerning these People of the Book whom ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, expelled from the Arabian Peninsula.

From what has preceded, I have seen the extent of ʿUmar's care for them, since he found no alternative to their expulsion for the reasons that have been mentioned.

It would have been easy to compel them to Islam and to have them enter it, just as those multitudes of the idolaters of Arabia and the general population of the Arabian Peninsula entered it, willingly or unwillingly.

Rather, it is the Islamic law that forbade compelling anyone other than the idolaters of Arabia to embrace Islam, just as it forbade breaking a covenant and violating a protected status (dhimma), except for a lawful cause.

Therefore, when the Najranis broke their covenant by dealing in usury (riba), although they had pledged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would not deal in it in the Peninsula, it became lawful for the Commander of the Faithful to expel them to another land, after compensating them for their property and land with its equivalent.

The caliphs after him continued—out of exceeding gentleness toward the People of the Book, in fulfilling the duty of just sovereignty, and in fidelity to the covenant of Allah and His Messenger—to treat the Najranis with the best treatment accorded to the general body of Muslim subjects, and to repel from them the harm of injustice and oppression, as you have seen.

Three matters result from this story:

The first matter: the Najranis were not compelled to Islam, even though their presence in the Arabian Peninsula posed a clear danger, because the people there were recent converts to Islam. This is because non-compulsion is one of the foundations of the Islamic Shariʿa. The jihad which the enemies of the Muslims magnify was legislated only to protect the call (to Islam), not for compulsion—except for the jihad against the idolaters of Arabia in that era, which was legislated to subdue them into Islam, for wise reasons not hidden from the discerning, the most important of which was purifying the souls of that great nation from the evils of idolatry, and uprooting ignorance and savagery from the Arabian Peninsula. That peninsula was the middle ground between the lands of the East and the West, of Asia, Africa, and Europe; indeed, it was the point of political and commercial connection between those lands. Therefore, the spread of the lights of civilization and religion there necessarily entailed their spread, by the nature of proximity and adjacency to those lands as well, as is well known.

The second matter: the caliphs did not deviate from the Lawgiver's command regarding fulfilling covenants, and they reaffirmed the covenant of the Najranis, one after another, despite these people's weakness and small numbers and the strength and dominion of the Islamic caliphate. This was not out of dread or desire, but out of pure adherence to the covenant and justice among the peoples subject to the authority of the caliphate and the sovereignty of Islam, of every community and religion.

The third matter: the zeal of the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, for the principle of protecting the dhimmi in his person and property, by compensating the Najranis for their land and property with the equivalent from the land and property of the Muslims, when necessity required their expulsion from their land to other lands of the Muslims.

It is mentioned in the biography of Abu Bakr, concerning ʿUmar, may Allah be [p. 3119] pleased with both of them, what he did in this manner with the people of ʿArabsus, one of the frontier fortresses of the Byzantines (Rum). When he ordered their expulsion from their land, because they had betrayed the protection of the Muslims and broken the covenant of security and truthfulness, he ordered that they be compensated for their property, real estate, and livestock at double the value.

In the days of the great conquests and after them, the caliphs continued to safeguard the right of settled residence and ancient dominion for the peoples defeated by the Muslims and subject to their rule, whether they were Christians or others. Nothing is reported of anyone among them who expelled a people from their land or seized it from them without right or compensation.

The occasional injustice of some officials, whose appetites overcame their virtue so that they deviated from the path of the Shariʿa, carries no weight in this matter. Indeed, the Muslims themselves are more often afflicted by the injustice of such people than others are. This does not detract from the principles of Islamic rule, which rejects injustice and calls to gentleness and justice. This is the stance of Islam in preserving the rights of defeated nations.

It has been seen from what preceded that the Muslims were not granted the rights of conquest that victors claim in every age, except what extreme necessity calls for and the preservation of the realm and religion requires—not what the desires of dominion and the appetites of the victorious nation call for.

The Muslims and their caliphs knew this well, and that the dhimmis have their rights and their obligations. So they went to great lengths in gentleness toward their neighbors and those who entered their protection from the adherents of other faiths. They left them freedom of ownership and of religion, and did not contend with them over any right of citizenship and neighborhood. Rather, they regarded them as a part of the state and a member of their society, indispensable to share in its labor and to partake of the causes of civil happiness and national life.

This is confirmed by the reliance of the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs on People of the Book, Jews and Christians, in organizing the registers of land tax (kharaj) and in translating the sciences of the Greeks, and in drawing near to those among them who excelled in geometry and medicine, and in relying on them for the cure of their ailments. Indeed, the Muslims went so far as to regard the People of the Book as a limb of the body of their social order, one that may not be severed under any circumstances. [An example: when the Tatar armies swept through the lands of Islam from the borders of China to al-Sham, (p. 3120) and some Muslims and Christians fell into their captivity, then the Muslims broke the power of the Tatars in al-Sham, and their kings embraced Islam, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, the foremost scholar of his age, addressed the Tatar commander Qatlushah, asking him to release the captives. He agreed to release the Muslims but refused to release the dhimmis. Shaykh al-Islam said to him: "You must release all who are with you of the Jews and Christians, who are our dhimmis, and we shall not leave a single captive, neither of the (Muslim) community nor of the dhimmis." So he released them for him.] End.

From this it is known the position of the Islamic rule regarding the dhimmis, and the extent of the care the caliphs and scholars showed for them. And His, the Exalted's, saying:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[30] ﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their saying with their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾

﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"﴾ is a new sentence, brought to affirm what has passed concerning the lack of faith in Allah, Glorified is He, on the part of the People of the Two Scriptures, and their being classed by this with the polytheists.

"Ezra" (ʿUzayr) has been read with tanwin, according to the original form, and its omission, due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, is an irregular lightening. It is a subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). There are other possibilities for its grammatical analysis (i'rab), but the one we have mentioned is the preferred one.

Know that what prompted both groups to their statements is extremism in glorification. As for the belief of the Christians, it is well known and famous, and the Noble Revelation has undertaken to mention it repeatedly and to refute its doubts.

As for the Jews concerning ʿUzayr, their extremists and ignorant ones utter this hideous word, whereas the rest of them regard him in the position of Moses, always honouring his mention, and believe that Allah, Exalted is He, raised him up to gather the scattered Torah and to renew the Mosaic religion, returning it to its former state and repairing what had decayed of its norms and customs, by inspiration. (p-3121) For the original copy of the Torah and the rest of their books were lost when the people of Babylon, the army of Nebuchadnezzar, raided Jerusalem, destroyed it, and took its people captive to their kingdom of Babylon, where they remained for seventy years. Then, when ʿUzayr arose among them and became famous, and entreated one of their kings for their release, the king granted him permission, so he returned from Babylon with those of the Jews who remained to Jerusalem, and renewed what had been obliterated of the Mosaic law.

One of the Scripture people said in a dictionary of his: The Jews claim that their leaders held an assembly in the time of ʿIzra (Ezra) and gathered the Hebrew books into a canon customary among them today, and they added to it what had not existed before the exile of Babylon.

In their book "al-Dhakhira" there is the following text: The people agreed that ʿIzra, who was expert in the traces of his homeland and its antiquity, skilled in knowledge of Jewish rites, and accomplished in the sacred sciences, was the first to establish this canon and to fix its various parts, after the Babylonian captivity, around the year 542 BC. When the Torah was scattered at the time of the exile, ʿIzra arose, gathered what was found of the scattered copies, and compiled from them a copy which he corrected and refined as far as he could, and changed the names of places that had ceased to be used there with other names more famous in their usage, and arranged the whole in a firm order. And all agreed that in all the books he replaced the letters of the Hebrew script with Chaldean letters, which the Jews had grown accustomed to using during their captivity, which lasted seventy years. End.

Because of this important work, they called him "son" (ibn). There is in this such boldness against the Lordly station as there is. Even if they claim that they intend a metaphorical sense in this, there is no escape for them from being charged with disbelief, for it is obligatory to take precaution in declaring Him far above everything, even with chastity of the tongue, from uttering what suggests a deficiency on His part; so one must disassociate oneself from such a word absolutely and from everything resembling it.

It has been said that the one who said this was some of their predecessors, and it has been said that some people of Madinah in the time of the Prophet ﷺ said it. There is no indication in the verse specifically of either of these. And attributing a disgraceful thing that is said by some of a people to the whole of them is something commonly known.

(p-3122) A subtle point:

ʿUzayr has been read with tanwin according to the original form, because it is diptote-free (munsarif). It has also been read without it, due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, as an irregular form, not because it is a non-Arabic name that is not declinable on account of being a proper noun and being foreign, as has been said, because that would only be valid if it were in its original wording, which is (ʿUzrāʾ) or (ʿUzriyā), two Hebrew words, the first of which has a definite meaning and the second of which means "Allah is my helper." But since the Arabs have inflected it by diminutive formation, this is not the case.

It is evident that most ancient names, because of their transfer from one nation to another and their frequent circulation, have had some admixture of distortion, addition and omission, which has altered their original form to some extent. When the Arabs used Hebrew names and similar ones, adopting into their language what they adopted, whether shaped from the ancient ones or distorted from them, they became, by convention, among the Arabic proper nouns, except for those that remain in their original form.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what proceeded from them of the two monstrous sayings, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the great degree of the thing referred to in heinousness and enormity. Said by Abu al-Su'ud.

﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, every saying is uttered with the mouth, so what is the meaning of "with their mouths"? I say there are two aspects to it:

One of them: that it is meant that it is a saying not supported by any proof, so it is merely a word they utter, empty of any meaning beneath it, like meaningless words which are jingles and tones, which indicate no meanings.

For a saying that signifies a meaning has a wording uttered by the mouth, and its meaning affects the heart, whereas what has no meaning is merely uttered by the mouth and nothing more.

The second: that by "saying" is meant the doctrine, as in their saying: "the saying of Abu Hanifa," meaning his doctrine and what he holds to. It is as if it were said: that is their doctrine and their religion with their mouths, not with their hearts, because there is no argument with it nor any doubt, such that it might affect the hearts.

For when they acknowledge that He has no consort, there remains no doubt regarding the negation of offspring. End.

There is also a third aspect, common in such cases, which is emphasis on the attribution of this saying to them, together with amazement at their declaring that corrupt doctrine.

Some have said: a saying may be attributed to mouths and to tongues, and the first is more eloquent.

﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them﴾, i.e., their saying resembles the saying of those who disbelieved before them among the nations, who went astray just as those went astray.

It has been said: what is meant by "those who disbelieved" is the polytheists of Makkah, who said that the angels are daughters of Allah. This is complete if what is meant by "the Jews and the Christians" in the verse are the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, which is an aspect in the verse as previously mentioned, for they preceded the people of Makkah in disbelief in him ﷺ.

It has been said: what is meant by them are their ancestors, meaning that whoever was among them in his time ﷺ, their saying resembles the saying of their ancestors, and what is meant is the deep-rootedness of their disbelief, i.e., that it is an ancient disbelief among them, not newly invented.

Abu al-Su'ud said: In this there is that there is no multiplicity in the saying, such that the comparison could be made, and making it between the sayings of the two groups, while the uttered content is one, has no added distinction in it.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to the Christians, i.e., their saying "The Messiah is the son of Allah" resembles the saying of the Jews "Ezra" etc., because they are older than them.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This too, as you see, for it requires that the refutation and nullification in His words, Exalted is He, "That is their saying with their mouths," be specific to the saying of the Christians. End.

Al-Mudahah means resemblance. It is said: ḍāhaytu and ḍāha'tu, as al-Jawhari said. The recitation of the general readers is (yuḍāhūna), with a dammed ha' followed by a waw.

ʿĀṣim recited it with a kasra on the ha' followed by a dammed hamza, and both have the same meaning from al-Mudahaʾa, which is resemblance, and they are two dialects.

It has been said: the yaʾ is a derivative of the hamza, as they said: qaraytu, tawaḍḍaytu and akhṭaytu.

﴿May Allah destroy them﴾, i.e., may He curse them, or kill them, or be hostile to them, or be amazed at the monstrosity of their saying.

﴿How are they deluded?﴾, i.e., how are they turned away from the truth toward falsehood?

His words, Exalted is He:

(p-3124) The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[31] ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary. And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary. And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ is an additional affirmation of their disbelief in Allah, the Exalted, mentioned earlier, and in it they are described with another kind of shirk.

Al-Ahbar (sing. hibr) are the scholars of the Jews. The word hibr is pronounced with either a kasra or a fatha on the ha'. It means the one who is learned in embellishing speech (tahbir al-kalam wa tahsinih), as the lexicographers have mentioned. Some have said: "The hibr is the greatest of the nobles among the Israelites. He is a means of drawing near to Allah for them, and his rank is hereditary within the family of Aaron, the eldest of those in it being the one who holds it." End of quote.

Al-Ruhban (sing. rahib) means the one who worships with humility and asceticism. The root of tarahhub, which is taken from the Christians, is withdrawal from worldly occupations, abandoning its pleasures, renouncing it, and isolating oneself from its people.

In a hadith: "There is no monasticism in Islam." As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿lords besides Allah﴾, al-Razi said: Most of the commentators (p-3125) said: the meaning of "lords" is not that they believed these men to be the gods of the universe; rather, the meaning is that they obeyed them in their commands and prohibitions. This is supported by what al-Tirmidhi related from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "I came to the Prophet ﷺ with a golden cross around my neck, and he said: 'O Adi, cast away from you this idol.' I heard him reciting in Surah Bara'a: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾, and he said: 'As for them, they did not worship them; but when they declared something lawful for them, they considered it lawful, and when they declared something forbidden to them, they forbade it.'"

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir related through several chains, from Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the call of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reached him, he fled to Syria. He had been a Christian in the Jahiliyya. His sister and a group of his people were taken captive. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bestowed favour upon his sister and gave her gifts, and she returned to her brother and encouraged him to embrace Islam and to come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So Adi came to Medina. He was a chief among his people, Tayy, and his father was Hatim al-Ta'i, famous for generosity. People talked about his arrival, and he entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a silver cross around his neck, reciting this verse: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾. He said: I said: "They did not worship them." He said: "Yes indeed, they declared lawful for them what was forbidden, and declared forbidden for them what was lawful, and they followed them; that is their worship of them."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Adi, what do you say? Does it harm you that it be said, 'Allah is greatest'? Do you know of anything greater than Allah? Does it harm you that it be said, 'There is no deity except Allah'? Do you know of any deity other than Allah?" Then he invited him to Islam, and he embraced Islam and bore witness to the truth.

(p-3126) He said: "I saw his face light up with joy." Then he said: "Indeed, the Jews are those who earned anger, and the Christians are those who went astray."

Ibn Kathir said: Likewise said Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Ibn Abbas and others in the interpretation of this verse, that they followed them in what they made lawful and unlawful.

Al-Suddi said: They sought counsel from men and cast the Book of Allah behind their backs.

Some commentators mentioned another interpretation of their taking them as lords: that they obeyed them by prostrating to them.

Al-Shihab said: The first is the interpretation of the Prophet ﷺ, so it is fitting to limit oneself to it, because when Adi ibn Hatim came to him while he was reciting it, he said to him: "We did not worship them." He said: "Did you not follow them in what they made lawful and unlawful? That is worship." People say, "So-and-so worships so-and-so" when he greatly exceeds in obeying him; it is a metaphor by likening obedience to worship, or an unrestricted metonymy by applying the general term "worship" to a specific kind of obedience. The first is more eloquent. End of quote.

Al-Razi said: al-Rabi' said: I said to Abu al-Aliyya: "What was that lordship among the Children of Israel?" He said: "They would often find in the Book of Allah what contradicted the statements of the rabbis and monks, yet they would take their statements, and they would not accept the ruling of the Book of Allah, exalted is He."

Al-Razi said: Our teacher and master, the seal of the verifiers and the mujtahids, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have witnessed a group of blind followers of jurists. I recited to them many verses of the Book of Allah, exalted is He, on certain matters, and their schools of thought were contrary to those verses. They did not accept those verses nor pay them any attention, and they remained looking at me as one astonished, meaning: how is it possible to act upon the apparent meanings of these verses when the transmitted reports from our predecessors are contrary to them? If you reflect with full reflection, you will find this disease spreading through the veins of most of the people of Medina." End of quote.
