﴿Those who believe in Allah do not ask your permission﴾, i.e., because their belief in Him prevents them from disobeying Him while they are able to comply. ﴿And the Last Day﴾: their belief in it prevents them from forsaking the reward and the eternal life in exchange, if they are commanded. ﴿to strive with their wealth and their lives﴾, i.e., because they love striving with them as an act of drawing near (to Allah), so they spend them in His way. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious﴾, i.e., He will give them of the reward what is appropriate to their piety.

In this there is a testimony for them of being included among the company of the God-fearing, and a promise to them of the most generous reward.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 45:

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿Only those seek your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt.﴾

﴿Only they seek your permission﴾, that is, to abstain from jihad with their wealth and their selves. ﴿Those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, since they do not hope for His reward or for life thereafter, and they are the hypocrites. For this reason He said: ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾, that is, about what you call them to, meaning that doubt has taken firm root in them. ﴿So they waver in their doubt﴾, that is, they have no firm footing in anything. They are a bewildered, doomed people, belonging neither to these nor to those.

Remarks:

The first: Know that in His opening the address with the good news of pardon, rather than with something that suggests reproach, there is a consideration for his side (peace and blessings be upon him), and a care to conduct the discussion graciously and to return to the matter gently, which is not hidden from people of understanding.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "Look at this gentleness: He began with the pardon before mentioning the one who is pardoned."

Makki said: "﴿May Allah pardon you﴾ [al-Tawba: 43] is an opening of speech like (may Allah set you right and honour you)." Al-Dawudi said: "It is an honour."

I say: This is supported by the words of Ali ibn al-Jahm addressing al-Mutawakkil when he had ordered his banishment:

"May Allah pardon you. Is there no sanctity that will protect me by your pardon from being sent away?
Have you not seen a servant who transgressed his bounds, and a master who pardoned and a rightly guided one who guided?
Release me, for He who never ceases to protect you and to turn away from you misfortune will release you."

What is well known, that pardon occurs only for a sin, is not correct. It is necessary to interpret it in every context according to what suits it.

Al-Shihab said: It is used where there is no sin, as you say to one whom you honour: "May Allah pardon you, what did you do regarding my affair?" And in a hadith: "I was amazed at Joseph and his patience and his generosity, and Allah forgives him."

Al-Sakhawandi said: It is a teaching to honour him (peace and blessings be upon him), and had the pardon not been in the address, the reproach would not have stood with its force.

Al-Qadi 'Iyad said in (al-Shifa): As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawba: 43], it is a matter for which Allah had not previously forbidden the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), so it is not counted as disobedience, and Allah did not count it as disobedience against him. Rather, the scholars regard it as a rebuke, and they considered those who went to that view to be mistaken.

Niftaweyh said: Allah has surely protected him from that. Rather, he was given the choice between two matters.

They said: He had the right to do what he wished in matters on which no revelation had come down to him. And how could it not be so, when Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So give permission to whom you wish of them﴾ [al-Nur: 62]? When he gave them permission, Allah informed him, by what He did not reveal to him of their secret, that had he not given them permission they would have stayed behind because of their hypocrisy, and that there is no blame on him for what he did. And ﴿pardon﴾ here does not mean forgiveness. Rather, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Allah has pardoned you regarding the charity of horses and slaves." It had never been obligatory upon them, meaning it was not binding upon them.

Al-Qushayri said something similar: "Only one who does not know the language of the Arabs says that pardon occurs only for a sin." He said: The meaning of ﴿May Allah pardon you﴾ [al-Tawba: 43] is that He did not hold you to account for a sin. End of quotation.

What occurred in al-Kashshaf here has been counted among its gravest slips.

The scholar Abu Mas'ud had a debate with him on this, which he cited because it reaches the peak of eloquence. He said, may Allah have mercy on him:

"He erred, and violated good manners, and how wretched was what he did in what he said and wrote, claiming that the speech is a metaphor for the offence, and that its meaning is 'you erred and how wretched was what you did.' Suppose it is a metaphor. Is it not that choosing it over stating the offence explicitly is for gentleness in the address and lightness in the reproach? And suppose that pardon entails that it is of such ugliness and draws blame, to the degree that it justifies this level of speaking evil face to face, or permits the making of a declaration of disapproval with the phrase 'how wretched was,' which indicates that the ugliness has reached a degree at which one wonders? It is not hidden that there was in their going out no benefit for the religion, nor any advantage for the Muslims. Rather there was in it corruption and ruin, as His saying, mighty and majestic is He, has stated: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added to you nothing but corruption﴾ [al-Tawba: 47], and so on. He, glorified is He, disliked it, as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿But Allah disliked their going forth﴾ [al-Tawba: 46], and so on. Yes, it would have been better to delay the permission until their lie became clear, which is the most eloquent of eloquence, and until they were exposed before the eyes of all, and were unable to enjoy life in security and ease, and were unable to rejoice among themselves in having deceived him (peace and blessings be upon him) and pleased him with falsehoods.

Moreover, life was not pleasant for them, nor were their eyes comforted, since they were not in security and tranquillity. Rather they were in fear of their affair being revealed, and it was revealed." End of quotation.

Al-Khafaji said: Some have tried to interpret the words of al-Kashshaf by saying that its intent is that the original wording was of that kind, and that he replaced it with pardon to magnify his status. For this reason he put the pardon before what entails the offence, so there is no error in it.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Had he and the one who offered this interpretation avoided the places of suspicion, it would have been better and more appropriate. End of quotation.

The second: The verse has been cited as evidence that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) sometimes judged by ijtihad (independent reasoning, the exertion of personal judgement within the sources of law), as Al-Razi expounded.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): Those who said that his ijtihad may err, but that he is alerted to it quickly, cited it as evidence.

The third: Al-Razi said: The verse indicates the obligation to beware of haste, the obligation of verification and deliberation, and abandoning being deceived by outward appearances, and exerting oneself greatly in investigation, until one can treat each group according to what it deserves of closeness or distance.

The fourth: Abu al-Su'ud said: The change of style, in that He expressed the first group by the relative clause whose predicate is a verb indicating occurrence, and the second group by the active participle indicating continuity, is to signify that what appeared from the first group is a truthfulness that occurred in a particular matter, which does not qualify them to be listed among the truthful, and that what proceeded from the others, although it is a lie that occurred concerning a particular matter, is a matter that follows their constant habit, arising from their being firmly rooted in falsehood. He, may Allah have mercy on him, examined in detail other subtle points, so let one refer to him.

The fifth: It has been said: The verb in the future tense indicating continuity, in His saying, ﴿They do not seek your permission﴾ [al-Tawba: 44], when negated, denotes the negation of continuity. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement: "It is not the habit of the believers," that is, that they seek permission.

Al-Nihrir said: It is not far-fetched to take it as the continuity of negation, as in most instances, that is, their habit is not to seek permission.

Al-Nasir said: This courtesy must be followed in every case. It is not fitting for a person to seek his brother's permission to do him a kindness, nor for a host to seek his guest's permission to offer him food, for seeking permission in such situations is a sign of constraint and reluctance. And the blessings of Allah be upon His friend (Abraham) and His peace. He reached such a degree of generosity and courtesy with his guests that he would not undertake any of the preparations for hospitality in their sight. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, praised him through His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) for this lovely trait and noble courtesy, and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Then he went quietly to his family and brought a fat calf﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 26], that is, he went away secretly from them so that they would not perceive it. The one who attends to his guest's affairs in plain sight may be regarded as one who has asked permission to host him. So this is among the courtesies that people of manliness and strength ought to hold fast to.

And more severe than seeking permission to go out for jihad and the support of the religion, and being slow to hasten to it after being urged and called to it, is the worst state of one who is slow when people have been called to the raid: that he holds fast to a branch of hypocrisy. We seek refuge in Allah from exposing ourselves to His wrath.

(Then) He, exalted is He, made clear the true state of those hypocrites who sought permission, that they did not truly intend to go out for jihad, and for this reason He forsook them. So He, glorified is He, said:

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[46] ﴿Had they intended to set out, they would surely have made preparation for it, but God disliked their being sent forth, so He held them back, and it was said, "Sit with those who sit."﴾

﴿They would surely have made preparation for it﴾ (*'uddah*, with a *damma* on the *'ayn* and a *shaddah* on the *dal*), meaning strength in the form of money, weapons, provisions and the like. ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth﴾, meaning their rising up to go out. ﴿So He held them back﴾, meaning He made them lazy and weakened their desire. ﴿And it was said, "Sit with those who sit"﴾, meaning among the women and children.

**Remarks:**

**First:** The words ﴿they would surely have made preparation for it﴾ indicate that the preparation for war, including mounts, weapons, and everything used to gain strength against the enemy, is part of *jihad* (struggle in the way of God).

Whatever is spent on the fighters is spent on this. This is clear regarding what one protects oneself with, such as weapons. As for what produces intimidation, such as banners, drums and the like, by which the enemy's heart is weakened, this too falls under *jihad*. God Almighty has said in Surat al-Anfal (the Chapter of the Spoils, *surah*): ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of strength and of steeds of war, to terrify thereby the enemy of God and your enemy﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]. This is like wearing silk during war. This is clear, so long as it does not lead to extravagance.

**Second:** An act is made good or bad by its intention, even if the two acts are the same in outward form. Going forth is obligatory with the intention of giving victory, and is reprehensible with the intention of achieving something reprehensible. This is because God Almighty informed us that He disliked their rising up, due to what would result from it, namely their intention to plot against the Muslims.

**Third:** It is permissible for the *imam* (ruler or leader) to prevent anyone who is suspected of harming the Muslims from going out to *jihad*. He may therefore expel the spy, the one who spreads demoralizing rumours, and the one who discourages others. Some of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah (a Shi'i school) mentioned all of this.

**Fourth:** They mentioned that God Almighty's words ﴿and it was said, "Sit with those who sit"﴾ are an image of God casting into their hearts the aversion to going out. That is, He made the creation of the motive to remain seated in them take the place of a command and a demanding speech, as in His words: ﴿So God said to them, "Die," then He brought them back to life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243], meaning He caused them to die. Or it is an image of Satan's whispering, commanding them to sit. Or it is a report of some of them saying to others. Or it is the permission of the Messenger (ﷺ) for them to sit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the meaning of His words ﴿with those who sit﴾?" I answer: it is a rebuke of them and a declaration of their incapacity, and an association of them with the women, the children, and the disabled, whose nature is to sit and crouch in their houses. They are the ones who remain seated and the ones who stay behind (*khalifun*, *khawalif*). This is clarified by His words: ﴿They were content to be with those who stay behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87].

Al-Nasir said: This is one of his fine observations. We expand upon it, saying:

If it were said, "Sit," restricted to this alone, it would convey nothing beyond ordering them to sit. Likewise, "Be with those who sit."

This benefit cannot be obtained by associating them with these categories of people, who are known among people for lagging behind and remaining idle, and who are marked with this characteristic, except through the expression of the verse. May God curse Pharaoh! He exaggerated in threatening Musa (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 29], and he did not say, "I will surely make you imprisoned." This is because of such a subtle point of eloquence.

Then God Almighty explained the secret of His aversion to their going forth, in His words:

(p-3169)The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[47] ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have increased you only in corruption, and they would have rushed about among you, seeking to cause you trouble. And among you are those who listen to them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have increased you only in corruption﴾ i.e., in mischief and evil. ﴿And they would have rushed about among you﴾ i.e., they would have hastened their pace and movement among you with corruption.

Al-Shihab said: al-īḍāʿ (rushing) is the quickening of the pace of camels. It is said: "The she-camel hastened (waḍaʿat al-nāqa, taḍaʿu) when she quickened, and I made her hasten (awḍa'tuhā)."

The intended meaning is hastening with tale-bearing (namāʾim), because the rider is faster than the one on foot. It is said: the object is implied, namely the tale-bearings (al-namāʾim), and tale-bearing is likened to riding-camels in their running and their movement, and the rushing is attributed to them. Thus there is a fanciful (takhyīliyya) and an implicit (makniyya) metaphor in it.

It is also said that it is an extended metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya): their swiftness in sowing discord between people is likened to the swift pace of riding-camels, then the term al-īḍāʿ, which belongs to camels, is borrowed for it.

And khilāl is the plural of khalal, which is a gap, used as an adverb meaning "between" (bayn).

Know that His words ﴿wa-la-awḍaʿū﴾ are written in the Imam (the standard codex) with two alifs, because the fatḥa used to be written as an alif before the Arabic script was invented; the Arabic script was invented shortly before the revelation of the Qur'an. A trace of that alif remained in the habits of scribes, so they wrote the hamza in the form of an alif and its fatḥa as another alif. Similar is: ﴿aw la-adhbahannahu﴾ [al-Naml: 21].

﴿They seek to cause you trouble﴾ i.e., they seek for you what would put you to trial, by provoking disagreement among you, casting terror into your hearts, and corrupting your intentions. ﴿And among you are those who listen to them﴾ i.e., those who submit to their words and find their speech agreeable, even if they do not know their true state, because of the weakness of their minds, so they imagine from them counsel and assistance, while they intend discouragement and sedition. This leads to the occurrence of evil among the believers and great corruption.

Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jarir said: i.e., among you are spies who listen to them for news and carry it to them.

(p-3170) Ibn Kathir said: This does not remain specific to their going out with them; rather this is general in all circumstances. The first meaning is more apparent in its fit with the context, and this is the view taken by Qatada and other exegetes.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Those of noble standing among them had, as far as I have been told, sought permission, among them ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and al-Jadd ibn Qays, and they were nobles among their people. So Allah discouraged them, knowing that if they went out they would corrupt his army against him.

Among his army were people who loved them and obeyed them, and to whom they called on his behalf, because of their nobility among them. So He said: ﴿And among you are those who listen to them.﴾ End of quotation.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: nothing of their affair is hidden from Him, and this includes both groups: those who stayed behind and those who listened.

Then, exalted is He, demonstrated their seeking of sedition on every occasion with His words:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[48] ﴿They had already sought to cause dissension before, and had upset affairs for you until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed, while they were averse.﴾

﴿They had already sought to cause dissension before﴾ meaning: they sought harm by scattering your company and separating your companions from you, before the expedition of Tabuk, as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul did when he turned away with his companions from the Muslims on the day of Uhud. ﴿And had upset affairs for you﴾ meaning: they devised for you stratagems and schemes and turned over opinions in order to nullify your affair.

Al-Shihab said: What is meant by ﴿al-umur﴾ [al-Anfal: 44] is the schemes, so "turning them over" is a metaphor for arranging them; or [it means] "opinions" (al-ara'), so "turning them over" is examining and reversing them.

﴿Until the truth came﴾, and it is Your support, Your victory and Your triumph. ﴿And the command of Allah prevailed﴾, meaning: His religion became exalted. ﴿While they were averse﴾, meaning: in spite of them.

Ibn Kathir said: When the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, the Arabs shot at him from one bow, and the Jews of Medina and its hypocrites waged war against him. Then, when Allah gave him victory on the day of Badr and exalted His word, Ibn Ubayy and his companions said: "This is a matter that has taken its course" (i.e., it has come about), and they entered Islam outwardly. Then, whenever Allah strengthened Islam and its people, that enraged them and grieved them.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[49] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave and do not put me to trial." Surely, they have fallen into trial already. And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾

﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave"﴾ — i.e., to remain behind (from the expedition). ﴿And do not put me to trial"﴾ — i.e., do not cast me into temptation.

It is related from Mujahid and Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays, brother of Banu Salama, and this is according to what Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated: that the Prophet ﷺ said to him one day while he was in his equipment, "Would you like to go out to fight the Banu al-Asfar?" He said, "O Messenger of Allah! Will you grant me leave and not put me to trial? By Allah, my people know that there is no man more prone to infatuation with women than me, and I fear that if I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I will not be able to restrain myself from them." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and said, "I have granted you leave!"

Al-Shihab said: it means that he fears infatuation with them, or having intercourse with them unlawfully.

Banat al-Asfar: refers to the Romans, as do Banu al-Asfar. Various reasons have been given for the name: among them, that some Abyssinians ruled over them, so women and children with golden complexions were born among them. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: this al-Jadd ibn Qays was among the most noble of Banu Salama.

In the Sahih it is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them, "Who is your chief, O Banu Salama?" They said, "al-Jadd ibn Qays, though we consider him stingy." 

He said, "And what disease is more grievous than stinginess? Rather, your chief is the young man with curly hair and white complexion, Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur."

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Surely, they have fallen into trial already﴾, Abu al-Su'ud said: i.e., in its very essence and self. Its most complete instance is the one free from description by perfection, deserving that the generic noun be exclusively applied to it. ﴿They have fallen,﴾ not into something other than it, let alone a refuge and a deliverance from it. That is due to what they did of resolve to stay behind, boldness in asking leave in this shameful manner, remaining behind with the leave built upon it, and offering false excuses. It has been read with the verb in the singular, in observance of the wording of (min) ["whoever"]. The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting, together with the fronting of the adverbial phrase, signifies that they fell into it while supposing it to be a refuge from trial, claiming that trial is nothing but staying behind without permission. In expressing "being tried" as "falling into trial," it is presented as a deadly abyss, revealing their plunging into the depths of ruin, to the lowest of the low. End of quotation.

﴿And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ — i.e., it will encompass them on the Day of Resurrection, so there will be no escape from it and no refuge. This is a warning to them for what they did.

Then He clarified their enmity, adding to the exposure of their evils, with His words, glorified is He:

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[50] ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; and if a misfortune strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before," and they turn away rejoicing.﴾

﴿If good befalls you﴾, i.e., a conquest, victory, or spoils of war, ﴿it distresses them﴾, i.e., it brings them grief because of the intensity of their enmity. ﴿And if a misfortune strikes you﴾, i.e., some kind of hardship, ﴿they say, "We had already taken our precaution"﴾, i.e., by exercising prudence in staying behind, ﴿before﴾, i.e., before the misfortune struck, so they boast of what they did, praising (p-3173) their own opinions. ﴿And they turn away﴾, i.e., from their gathering in which they displayed their joy at their own opinion, ﴿rejoicing﴾, i.e., at their opinion, at what befell you, and at their own safety.

Then Exalted God guided [the Prophet] to answer them by refuting the basis upon which they built their delight, with His words, glory be to Him:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[51] ﴿Say: "Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our Protector (mawlana), and upon Allah let the believers rely."﴾

﴿Say: "Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has decreed for us"﴾, i.e., what He has ordained for our worldly or otherworldly benefit. So there is no reason for this rejoicing, since we are content with His decree concerning that calamity. Thus it does not truly grieve us, how so?

Nor did He prescribe it upon us in order to harm us by it, since ﴿He is our Protector﴾, i.e., He manages our affairs. Rather, He prescribed it upon us in order to grant us success in patience and contentment with it, and so He gives us a reward better than it. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, i.e., because there is no helper and no one who takes charge of their affairs besides Him.

The commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[52] ﴿Say: "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him, or at our hands. So wait; indeed we are waiting with you."﴾

﴿Say: "Do you await"﴾ i.e., do you wait and expect ﴿for us anything but one of the two best outcomes﴾, i.e., the two outcomes, each of which is the best of outcomes (ḥusnā al-ʿawāqib), and they are victory and martyrdom. ﴿And we await for you﴾ i.e., one of the two evil outcomes, either: ﴿that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him﴾, i.e., as He afflicted the nations before you, ﴿or﴾ with a punishment ﴿at our hands﴾, and it is killing for disbelief.

﴿So wait﴾ i.e., for us, for what has been mentioned of our outcomes, ﴿indeed we are waiting with you﴾ i.e., expecting what is your outcome (p-3174), for it is inevitable that each of us will meet what he awaits, and it will not pass him by. So you will witness only what gladdens us, and we will witness only what grieves you.

And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 53:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you. Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾

﴿Say, "Spend"﴾ means your wealth in the way of Allah and in the avenues of righteousness. ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ are two verbal nouns (masadir) that stand in the position of the subject (fa'il), meaning: willing, out of your own selves, or unwilling, for fear of being killed. ﴿it will never be accepted from you﴾ means: that spending. Then He explained the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people﴾, meaning: transgressing, rebellious.

Subtleties (lata'if):

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How did He command them to spend and then say, ﴿it will never be accepted from you﴾?" I say: It is a command in the sense of a report, like His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension"﴾ [Maryam: 75], and its meaning is: it will never be accepted from you whether you spend willingly or unwillingly. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 80].

And his saying:

*"Be harmful to us or be good to us, you will not be blamed"*

meaning: Allah will never forgive them, whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and we will not blame you, whether you have wronged us or done good to us.

(p-3175) If you ask: When is this permissible? I say: When the speech indicates it, just as its reverse is permissible in your saying: "May Allah have mercy on Zayd and forgive him."

If you ask: Why did he do that? I say: For a point in it, which is that Kuthayyir, as if he is saying to Izza: "Test the gentleness of my position with you, the strength of my love for you, and deal with me by harm and by good, and see whether my state with you varies, whether you are harmful or good!" And in its meaning is the saying of the poet:

*"Your brother is the one who, if you rise with the sword intending to strike him, will not deceive you in friendship."*

Likewise the meaning is: Spend and see whether it is accepted from you; and ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and look whether you see any difference between the state of asking forgiveness and leaving it?

If you ask: What is the purpose in negating acceptance? Is it that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not accept it from them and returns to them what they offer, or is it that it is not accepted by Allah, the Exalted, going to waste as dust with no reward for it? I say: It admits both meanings together.

It has been narrated that the verse is a continuation of the answer of al-Jadd ibn Qays, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "This is my wealth; I will help you with it, so leave me and do not tempt me." And Allah knows best.

(p-٣١٧٦) The discussion on the ta'wil (interpretation) of His saying, exalted is He:

[54] ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while lazy, and they do not spend except while unwilling.﴾

When Exalted is He had explained the ugly deeds of the hypocrites (munafiqun), the painful punishment they will have in the Hereafter, and the non-acceptance of their expenditures, He followed this with an explanation that what they suppose to be worldly benefits is in reality a cause of their punishment and affliction. Thus it becomes fully clear that hypocrisy (nifaq) is a pit of ruin, for it brings upon its people the calamities of this world and the Hereafter. So He, glorified is He, said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 55:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you﴾ meaning: because that is a gradual drawing-on (istidraj) for them, as He said: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world﴾, meaning: because of what they undergo in gathering and preserving them of hardships, and what they see in them of severe trials and calamities. As for His saying: ﴿to punish them﴾, it was said: the lam (la, "in order to") is extra (za'ida, redundant).

It was also said: the object (maf'ul) is omitted, and this lam is causal (ta'lília, expressing purpose or reason), meaning: He intends to give them in order to punish them. ﴿And that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers﴾, meaning: so that they die as disbelievers, heedless, occupied with enjoyment and distracted from considering the outcome, and so that becomes a gradual drawing-on for them.

The root of (zahuq, "departure") is the going out with difficulty, as stated by al-Qadi (al-Baydawi).

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[56] ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are fearful.﴾

﴿And they swear by Allah﴾ means the hypocrites. ﴿That they are surely of you﴾ in religion, so that by means of the oath they may ward off the indications of hypocrisy. ﴿But they are not of you﴾ in that, meaning they are liars. ﴿Rather, they are a people who are fearful﴾, i.e., they fear being killed and what is done to the polytheists, so they display Islam out of dissimulation (taqiyyah), and they support it with false oaths.

Then he pointed to the cause of the fear, which is their being compelled to [leave] their dwellings together with their weakness, through His words, may He be exalted:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[57] ﴿If they could find a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter, they would turn to it while they rushed headlong.﴾

﴿If they could find a refuge﴾, meaning: a fortress to which they could take refuge. ﴿Or caves﴾, meaning: hollows in the mountains, each one of them dwelling in a cave. ﴿Or a place to enter﴾, meaning: a place of entry they could enter, and the (burrow/tunnel) (sirb) in the earth. ﴿They would turn to it﴾, meaning: they would hasten towards it. ﴿While they rushed headlong﴾, meaning: they would hurry with great speed, nothing turning them back, like the unbridled horse (al-faras al-jamuh), that is, the one that bolts and which no bridle can restrain. That is: if they found any of these places from which they flee and which they find repugnant, they would surely come to them out of their intense fear, their hatred for the Muslims, and their grief at the might of Islam and the victory of its people.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[58] ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are pleased; but if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry.﴾

﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾, i.e., who criticize you, ﴿concerning the charities﴾, i.e., concerning their distribution.

Then He explained the corruption of their fault-finding, and that it has no source other than their greed for the goods of this world, by His saying: ﴿If they are given from them﴾, i.e., an amount they desire, ﴿they are pleased﴾, and so they consider it just. ﴿But if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry﴾, and so they consider it unjust.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 59:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[59] ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them, and had said, "Sufficient for us is Allah; Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we are turning in hope."﴾

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them, and had said, "Sufficient for us is Allah"﴾ meaning: His bounty suffices us, and what He has apportioned for us.

﴿Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger﴾ meaning: after this, according to what we hope for and aspire to.

﴿Indeed, to Allah we are turning in hope﴾ meaning: that He will grant us spoils and bestow upon us His bounty.

The answer (al-jawab) is omitted, its meaning being evident. That is: it would have been better for them.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was distributing booty (fai'), Dhu al-Khuwaysira came to him, a man from the Banu Tamim, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, be just!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to you! Who will be just if I am not just?' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'Permit me to strike off his neck!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, for he has companions, such that one of you will belittle his prayer in comparison with their prayer, and his fasting in comparison with their fasting. They recite the Qur'an, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass through the religion as an arrow passes through the game.'"

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

(p-3179) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
[60] ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect them, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing captives and debtors, and for the cause of Allah, and for the wayfarer; an obligation from Allah. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned their (the hypocrites') faultfinding regarding the alms, He followed it with a statement of the rightness of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did in the distribution, since he did not exceed in it the lawful categories allowed to him. This is the very essence of justice. That is because He, exalted is He, prescribed its distribution to these people and did not entrust it to anyone other than Himself, and he (ﷺ) did not take anything from it for himself. So what is the basis for faultfinding against its distributor, may the blessings of Allah be upon him?

Al-Bukhari narrated from Mu'awiyah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whomever Allah wants good for, He gives him understanding of the religion. I am only a distributor, and Allah is the Giver."

Abu Dawud narrated from Ziyad ibn al-Harith, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and pledged allegiance to him. Then a man came and said: 'Give me from the alms.' He said to him: 'Allah, exalted is He, has not been pleased with the judgment of a prophet or anyone else concerning the alms until He Himself judged regarding them, and He divided them into eight portions. So if you are among those portions, I will give you your due.'"

So the verse is a rebuttal to the claims of those faultfinders and a cutting off of their greed, by stating that they are far from being entitled to it. It also informs that giving to whom He gave is justice, and withholding from them is injustice.

(p-3180) "Al-fuqara'" (the poor) is the plural of faqir, a form (fa'il) in the sense of the active participle (fa'il). It is said: faqira yafqaru, from the pattern ta'iba, meaning: his wealth became little.

"Al-masakin" (the needy) is the plural of miskin, from (sakana sukunan), its movement having ceased, because of its stillness toward people. It is with a fatha on the mim in the dialect of the Banu Asad, and with a kasra according to others.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: The miskin is the one who has nothing, and the faqir is the one who has a means of livelihood. Yunus said the same, and the faqir was considered to be in a better condition than the miskin.

He said: I asked a Bedouin: "Are you a faqir?" He said: "No, by Allah, rather a miskin." Al-Asma'i said: The miskin is in a better condition than the faqir, and this is the more correct view, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to needy people (masakin)﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], and it was worth a whole sum. And He said concerning the poor (fuqara'): ﴿They cannot move about in the land; the ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their restraint﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273]. Ibn al-A'rabi said: The miskin is the faqir, and he is the one who has nothing, so he made them equal. Thus (it is stated) in al-Misbah.

Al-Badr al-Qarafi said: When the two are combined they are distinguished, as when a bequest is made to "the poor and the needy", it is necessary to give to both categories. And if they are distinguished they are combined, as when a bequest is made to one of the two categories, it is permissible to give to the other.

Al-Mahayimi said: Then He, exalted is He, mentioned those whom the needy need, the recipients of alms, and said: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾, that is: those who strive in collecting them: the collector, the weigher, the measurer, and the scribe, and they are given their wages from them.

Then He mentioned those whom the Imam needs, and said: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾, and they are a people whose intention in Islam is weak, so the Imam needs to reconcile their hearts with gifts, to strengthen their Islam, lest their weakness spread to others; or they are nobles whose Islam is hoped for through giving to them, which would bring about the Islam of their counterparts.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned those who are helped with it in removing slavery, by His words: ﴿and for captives﴾, that is: and for assistance in freeing captives, so the mukatabun (slaves contracted for manumission) are given from it what they use to (p-3181) pay the installments of the contract of manumission (nujum al-kitabah), even if they are earning. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Layth. Or: and for spending on the freeing of captives, by purchasing captives from it and freeing them.

Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: There is no harm in freeing a slave from zakat (the obligatory alms), and this is the position of Malik, Ahmad, and Ishaq.

It is not hidden that (al-riqab, "captives") includes both aspects, and numerous hadiths have come regarding the reward of manumission and freeing a slave.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned those whose obligations are relieved of debts, by His words: ﴿and debtors﴾.

They are those whom debts have burdened on account of themselves, in a matter other than disobedience, and they did not find the means to repay, or (they incurred debts) for the reconciliation of people even if they are wealthy.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned assistance for jihad, by His words: ﴿and for the cause of Allah﴾.

So it is spent on volunteers in jihad, and horses and weapons are purchased for them.

Al-Razi said: His words ﴿and for the cause of Allah﴾ do not necessitate restricting it to fighters. For this reason al-Qaffal reported in his Tafsir from some jurists the permissibility of spending the alms on all the aspects of good, such as shrouding the dead, building fortresses, and maintaining mosques, because His words ﴿and for the cause of Allah﴾ are general in all of these. End of quote.

For this reason al-Hasan, Ahmad, and Ishaq held that Hajj is among "the cause of Allah", so it is spent on pilgrims from it.

In al-Iqna' and its commentary it is said: Hajj is among "the cause of Allah" by explicit text, reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, because of what Abu Dawud narrated: that a man dedicated a she-camel to the cause of Allah, and then his wife wanted to perform Hajj. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "Ride it, for Hajj is among the cause of Allah." So he takes from zakat, if he is poor, what he uses to fulfil the obligatory Hajj or Umrah, or what he uses to be assisted in it. The same applies to their voluntary forms, because each of them is among the cause of Allah. End of quote.

Ibn al-Athir said: "The cause of Allah" is general, applying to every pure deed by which the path of drawing near to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, is taken, by performing obligatory and voluntary acts and various kinds of voluntary acts. When it is used absolutely, it mostly refers to jihad, until it became, through frequent usage, as if it were restricted to it. End of quote.

And in al-Taj it is said: Every path by which Allah, mighty and majestic is He, is intended, and which is righteous, is included in the cause of Allah.

(p-3182) Then He, exalted is He, mentioned assistance for the sons of the road by His words:
﴿and for the wayfarer﴾, so he gives to the traveller passing through a town what he uses to reach his own town.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾, its governing verb is implied, that is: Allah has prescribed this as an obligation. His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾, that is: of the conditions of people and the ranks of their entitlement. His words: ﴿Wise﴾, that is: He does nothing except what wisdom requires, among the good matters, of which is directing rights to their rightful recipients.

Notes:

The first: The apparent meaning of the verse requires distribution among the eight categories. Two things support this:
The first: what the linguistic wording requires, if we say that the conjunction (waw) is for joining and combining.
The second: what Abu Dawud recorded in his Sunan from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has not been pleased with the judgment of a prophet or anyone else concerning the alms until He Himself judged regarding them, and divided them into eight portions," the hadith.

This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ikrimah, and al-Zuhri, except that if one of them becomes self-sufficient, it is given to the others, without disagreement.

Groups went to the permissibility of spending on one category of them, among them Umar, Ibn Abbas, Hudhayfah, Ata', Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Hadi, al-Qasim, Asbat, and Zayd. In (al-Tahdhib) it is said: They departed from the apparent meaning of the mentioned verse and the report, in several ways:
The first: that Allah, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿If you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], which shows that the mention of the number here is to specify the type of those who deserve it.
The second: the report, which is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Mu'adh: "Inform them that Allah has made it obligatory upon them to give alms from their wealth, which is taken from their rich and returned to their poor."
The third: the hadith of Salamah ibn Sakhr, for the Prophet (ﷺ) assigned to him the alms of Banu Zurayq.
The fourth: that no disagreement appeared regarding this from the Companions, so it was treated as if it were consensus.
The fifth: the opposition (p-3183) of the wording to the meaning, for the intended aim is to fill the need.

The author of (al-Nihayah) said: This is closer to the meaning, and the first is closer to the wording. What supports that they are entitled by meaning and not by name is that if we said they are entitled by name, it would follow that whoever is poor, a warrior, a debtor, and a traveller, would be entitled to shares for all these causes together. Thus (it is stated) in the commentary of some Zaydis.

Al-Nasir said in (al-Intisaf): The view that it is obligatory to spend them on all the categories, so that it is not permissible to leave out a single category of them, taking it from the indication of the particle (lam) of ownership, as al-Shafi'i held, is not supported by the context. The verse begins with the word of restriction, which indicates limiting the kind of alms to the enumerated categories, and that they are specific to them, and that others have no right to a share in them, as if it were said: they are only for them and not for others. This is the purpose for which the verse was revealed, so there is no implication in it for anything else. End of quote.

The second: Some said: The word (alms) in its generality includes obligatory and voluntary alms. Then obligatory alms are of various kinds, among them the zakat (obligatory alms) which is a tenth, or half a tenth, or a quarter of a tenth, and the zakat on livestock and the zakat al-fitr, and expiations, such as the expiation for an oath, for zihar, and for fasting. Likewise the sacrificial animal in Hajj. And among them is what is taken from the wealth and heads of the unbelievers. For this reason Allah called the spoils of war alms, regarding the occasion of the revelation of the verse, which was the distribution of the spoils of Hunayn. So when the word includes what has been mentioned, is the verse to be taken in its generality regarding its distribution to what has been mentioned, or is some of it specified?

Then he said: The scholars divided the alms and made their recipients different. The expiation is not reported to be spent on the eight categories.
Allah's words have come: ﴿Then its expiation is feeding sixty needy people (miskin)﴾, and in the hadith: "Feed a needy person for each day," and regarding the zakat al-fitr it came: "Enrich them on this day."
Have the evidences come specifying the general wording of "alms"? For the zakat is agreed upon as to its recipients being the eight categories. Or how does the verse fit the principles of jurisprudence? End of his words.

(p-3184) It is not hidden that it specifies the general wording of "alms", because the specific governs the general, with the meaning that its purpose is restricting them to these categories. So everything that has been mentioned has not gone outside of them, since they include it. And Allah knows best.

The third: The ruling regarding "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" remains in force, because the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to those whose hearts were to be reconciled from among the Muslims and the polytheists, so they are given when there is need.
As for Umar, Uthman, and Ali not giving them, this is interpreted as there being no need to give them during their caliphates, not that their share had lapsed. For the verse is among the last to be revealed, and Abu Bakr gave to Adi ibn Hatim and al-Zibriqan ibn Badr.
And denying the existence of need over the passage of time, and the differences in the strength and weakness of souls, its corruption is not hidden. Thus (it is stated) in (al-Iqna') and its commentary.

Those whose hearts are to be reconciled, as in (al-Iqna'), are the leaders of their people: either an unbeliever whose Islam is hoped for, or whose evil is restrained; or a Muslim whose faith is hoped to be strengthened by his gift, or whose counterpart's Islam is hoped for, or whose counsel in jihad or in defending the Muslims is hoped for, or whose evil is restrained, such as the Kharijites and others like them; or one who has strength to collect zakat from those who do not give it. End of quote.

The fourth: In (al-Iklil) it is said: Those who permit giving to a capable poor man who is able to earn have used the general wording of the verse as evidence. (It is also permitted to give) to a dhimmi (non-Muslim subject), to one whose maintenance is obligatory for him among all relatives, to a spouse, and to the family of the Prophet (ﷺ), since they were deprived of their share of the one-fifth, and to their clients, and to one who permits transferring it.

Ibn al-Faras said: From His words, exalted is He, ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾ is derived the permissibility of taking a wage for everyone who occupies himself with any of the works for the Muslims.

He said: Abu Ubayd has used it as evidence for the permissibility of a judge receiving provision. He said: Allah has ordained for those employed to collect the alms, and made for them a right from it by their standing in it and their striving. Likewise, judges may take a wage for their work, and likewise anyone occupied with any of the works of the Muslims.

The Fifth: al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did he shift from the preposition *al-lam* (ل, "for") to *fi* (في, "in") in the last four categories? I say: to signal that they are more firmly deserving of charity than those mentioned earlier. *Fi* denotes a container, so he indicates that they are worthy of having alms placed within them and becoming their target and destination. This applies to freeing slaves (*fakk al-riqab*), which includes the *mukatabah* (a slave contracted to buy his freedom), enslavement, or captivity, and to freeing debtors (*al-gharimin*) from debt, which means rescuing and delivering them.

(p. 3185) And the poor warrior or the one cut off from his means on the pilgrimage combines poverty with worship. Likewise, the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabil*) combines poverty with being far from his family and wealth. The repetition of *fi* in His words, ﴿and in the way of Allah and the wayfarer﴾, gives these two preference over the slaves and the debtors. End.

Al-Nasir said: There is another secret that is more evident and closer, which is that the first four categories are owners of what may be given to them, and they take it as property. Therefore, the entry of *al-lam* suits them. As for the last four, they do not own what is spent on them; rather, it is not even spent into their hands. Instead, it is spent on interests that concern them.

So the wealth spent on slaves is actually received by the masters, the contracting parties and the sellers. Their share is not delivered into their hands, so it would not be expressed with *al-lam*, which indicates their ownership of what is spent toward them. Rather, they are the locus (*mahall*) for this expenditure and for the interest connected to it.

Likewise the debtors: their share is spent on the creditors of their debts, to free their obligations, not for them. As for ﴿the way of Allah﴾, it is clear that this applies to it.

As for the wayfarer, it is as if he was included within the way of Allah, but he was singled out for mention to draw attention to his particularity. Although he is free of both particles, his coordination with the noun governed by *al-lam* is possible, but its coordination with what is closest to it is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

Then he said: My grandfather, Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Faris al-Faqih, derived from the difference between the two particles mentioned an argument for Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, that the purpose is to specify the recipients, and that *al-lam* here is the *lam* of ownership. He says: the complement of the preposition that serves as the predicate for the alms (*al-sadaqat*) is omitted, so its estimated form must be determined. Either the estimate is: "Alms are only spent upon (*masrufah*) the poor," as Malik said, or: "Alms are owned (*mamlukah*) by the poor," as al-Shafi'i said. But the first is definite, because it is an estimate that suffices for both particles together: *al-lam* and *fi* can both attach to it. So we can say, "This thing is spent on such-and-such, and for such-and-such." In contrast, estimating it as "owned" fits only with *al-lam*, and when it reaches *fi* it needs the estimate "spent" to fit.

Thus its estimate from *al-lam* is of general attachment, encompassing validity, and is definite. And Allah is the Granter of success. End.

The Sixth: al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did this verse come to be among the mentions of the hypocrites and their schemes?

I say: By the fact that these categories are the exclusive recipients of alms, to the exclusion of others, it indicates that the hypocrites are not among them, as a means of cutting off their greed and signalling that they deserve deprivation, and that they are far from it and from its recipients. So what have they to do with it? And what empowered them to speak about it and to slander its divider, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him? End.

Its explanation was also mentioned earlier.

And His words, may He be exalted:

The discussion of the words of God Most High:

[61] ﴿And among them are those who abuse the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and he believes the believers, and he is a mercy to those of you who believe. And those who abuse the Messenger of Allah—for them is a painful punishment."﴾

﴿And among them﴾ i.e., among those who swear by Allah that they are surely of you, and [among them are] those who are more severe than the one who finds fault in the charities, since they are ﴿those who abuse the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear"﴾ i.e., he hears everything that is said to him and believes it. They mean that he is not deep in discernment, but quick to be deceived by everything he hears.

Abu al-Su'ud said: They only said this because he (may the blessings of Allah be upon him) would not confront them with the evil of what they did, and would overlook it out of forbearance and generosity. So they took him to be of sound heart, and said what they said.

The linguists said: (al-udhun) is a man who listens and accepts whatever is said to him. It is applied to the singular and the plural, so one says: "a man who is udhun" and "men who are udhun," and it is not made dual or plural. They named him by the name of the organ to magnify and denounce him, so it is a metonymy (majaz mursal), in which the part is used for the whole in hyperbole, by making his entire being, because of his excessive listening, an instrument of hearing—just as a spy is called "eye" for this reason. And similar to it is the saying:

"When Layla appears, I am wholly eyes; and if they speak of her, I am wholly ears."

Some of them considered it a simile (tashbih): likened to "the ear" in that there is nothing in it beyond listening, with no distinguishing of truth from falsehood.

Al-Shihab said: This is not worth relying on. It was also said that it is by way of an omitted modifier, i.e., "one who possesses an ear."

Al-Shihab said: This spoils its brilliance. It was said: it is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) from (adhina ilayhi wa lahu), like fariha, meaning "he listened." 'Amr ibn al-Ahyam said:

"When we travelled together a little, they inclined their ears to the talk, so they were like images."

And Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib said:

"If they hear a suspicion, they fly with it joyfully, from me; and what they hear of good, they bury.
Deaf when they hear good spoken of me; but if I am mentioned with evil among them, they are all ears."

And in a hadith: "Allah has never given ear to anything as He gives ear to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an beautifully."

Abu 'Ubayd said: He means that Allah has never listened to anything as He listens to one who recites it aloud.

And the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And it hearkens to its Lord and is obliged﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 2], i.e., it listens. Thus in the Taj al-'Arus.

On this basis, (udhun) is an adjective meaning "listener," and there is no figurative usage in it; so there are four aspects to it.

The clause "and they say" is an explanatory conjunction, since it is the abuse itself.

The words of God Most High: ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you"﴾ are an idafa of the qualified to the qualifier for emphasis, like "a man of truth," intending hyperbole in goodness and righteousness, as if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what a fine ear!" Or its idafa is in the sense of (fi), i.e., he is an ear in good and truth, and in what must be heard and accepted, and he is not an ear (p-3188) in anything other than that.

This is indicated by the reading of Hamza, "wa rahmatin" in the genitive, conjoined to it, i.e., he is an ear of good for you and of mercy, hearing nothing but these two and not accepting anything else.

Then He explained his being an ear of good by His words: ﴿He believes in Allah﴾. Al-Qashani said: This is a statement of his gentleness (ﷺ) and receptivity, for faith does not exist except with soundness of heart, refinement of soul and its softness. ﴿And he believes the believers﴾ i.e., he affirms their words concerning good deeds, hears their speech on them and accepts it. ﴿And a mercy﴾ i.e., he is a mercy ﴿to those of you who believe﴾ i.e., he is kind to them, tender toward them, and saves them from punishment through purification and teaching, and sets right the affairs of their livelihood and their hereafter, through righteousness and kinship, and the teaching of morals—forbearance, compassion, and enjoining good—by their following him in them, and by laying down the laws that bring order to their affairs in both abodes, and by urging them to the gates of righteousness by word and deed, and so on. Thus said al-Qashani.

Others said: i.e., he is a mercy to those among you who showed faith, the company of hypocrites, in that he accepts it—not because he believes you, but out of kindness to you and compassion for you, and he does not expose your secrets, nor disgrace you, nor do to you what is done to the polytheists, in consideration of what the Exalted saw of wisdom in sparing you.

Al-Shihab said: The meaning is: he is an ear of good that hears the signs and proofs of Allah and believes them, and listens to the believers, so he accepts what they say and affirms them; and this is an allusion that the hypocrites are an ear of evil, who hear the signs of Allah and do not trust them, and hear the words of the believers and do not accept them. And he (ﷺ) only listens to their words out of compassion for them, not because he accepts them for lack of discernment, as they claimed.

Al-Qashani said in his tafsir: They used to abuse him, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, and backbite him, with the soundness of his heart and his quickness to accept and affirm what he heard. So he affirmed them in that and submitted, and said: "He is so, but in relation to good." For the proud soul, the coarse and harsh, the rigid and stiff which hardens in matters and is not affected, is not prepared for perfection, since human perfection is only through acceptance and being affected. Thus, the more gentle of disposition, the sounder of heart, and the easier to accept a soul is, the more receptive it is to perfection and the more ready for it.

This gentleness is not of the kind of weakness and foolishness that requires being moved by everything it hears, even the impossible, and being affected by everything that reaches it and that it sees, even falsehood, evils and misguidance; rather it is of the kind of refinement and quickness to accept what suits it of good and truth. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "An ear of good"﴾, for the purity of readiness and the subtlety of soul require the acceptance of what suits it of goodness, not what contradicts it of evil, for the readiness for good does not accept evil, nor is it affected by it, nor does it take its impression, because of its opposition to it and its distance from it. End.

Subtleties:

The first: In His words: ﴿Say, "An ear of good"﴾ is the most eloquent method of reply to them, for He affirmed their claim that he is an ear, but explained it with what is praise of him and commendation of him.

An-Nasir said: Nothing is more eloquent than replying to them in this way, for at the beginning there is an enticement to them with agreement, then He turned on their hope with decisive cut, and followed their disparagement with despair of it.

Similar to this among the usages of the jurists is "the qawl bil-mujib" (accepting the implication), for at its beginning there is enticement to the opponent with concession, then a swift cutting off of hope; and nothing is sharper than enticement followed by despair that comes after and follows it. And Allah is the Granter of success.

The second: The lam in His words "lil-mu'minin" is added to distinguish between faith in the common sense, which is acknowledgment, and faith in the sense of submission and affirmation—so said Abu al-Su'ud, following al-Qadi.

Al-Shihab said: He means that faith in Allah in the sense of acknowledgment and affirmation takes the preposition bi, which is why He said "bi-Allah," while faith "lil-mu'minin" in the sense of granting them security from denial by affirming them, given what is known of their sincerity, is transitive by itself, so the lam in it is added for emphasis.

The third: Abu al-Su'ud said: The attribution of faith to them by the verbal form, after its attribution to the believers by the active participle which indicates firmness and continuity, is to signal that their faith is a matter that is newly arising and has no stability.

And His words: ﴿And those who abuse the Messenger of Allah﴾ i.e., by what was reported of their saying: ﴿He is an ear﴾ and the like, ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾ i.e., because of their audacity in harming him.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is a parenthetical statement sent down by Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in the manner of a warning, not included within the address.

And His mention of him (ﷺ) by the title of Messenger, attributed to the Exalted Name, for the utmost magnification, is to alert that harming him returns to His own sacred presence, requiring complete wrath and anger. End.

And His words, Exalted:

The commentary on His words, may He be exalted:

[62] ﴿They swear by Allah to you, to please you; but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾

﴿They swear by Allah to you, to please you; but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to the Muslims. The hypocrites used to speak with slander, or hold back from jihad, and then they would come to them and make excuses to them, confirming their excuses with oaths so that they would excuse them and be pleased with them. So it was said to them: If you are believers as you claim, then the one most entitled that you please is Allah and His Messenger, with obedience and agreement. End of quotation.

Since the apparent form after the conjunction with "waw" should be the dual, and yet it has been given in the singular, they gave it these interpretations:

Because pleasing the Messenger is pleasing Allah, by the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 80]. Because of their inseparability, the two were treated as one thing, so the singular pronoun returned to both of them. And "ahaqq" (more entitled), on this view, is a predicate about both of them without any elision.

Or, the pronoun refers to Allah, may He be exalted, and "ahaqq" is its predicate, because it comes first.

The sentence consists of two clauses, with the predicate of the second clause omitted because the first indicates it, meaning: "And Allah is more entitled that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise."

Sibawayh made it refer to the second, because it is closer, with the safety from separating the subject and predicate, as in his saying:

"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, and opinions differ."

Or, the pronoun refers to both of them by way of interpreting what was mentioned, or each of them separately; and it was not made dual out of courtesy, lest Allah be joined with another in a dual pronoun, which has been prohibited, though there is discussion on this point.

Or, the discussion concerns harming the Messenger ﷺ and pleasing him, so the mention of Allah is an honouring of him and a preparation; for this reason the predicate was not stated about Allah, and the predicate was given specifically to the Messenger. Al-Shihab said: In this there is room for reflection. End of quotation.

The saying of this kind is familiar from them in many verses. The answer to the condition is implied, indicated by what precedes it. The reading with the "ta" (of the second person, tuhibbuna-type address) is by way of iltifat (shift of address), for rebuke.

And His, may He be exalted, saying:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[63] ﴿Did they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein? That is the great disgrace.﴾

﴿Did they not know﴾ i.e., those hypocrites.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The interrogative is for reproach regarding what they undertook of the great offense, while knowing the evil of its consequence.

It was also read with the letter "ta'" (tā', i.e., "Did you not know"), as an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), for the increase of rebuke and reproach. That is: Did they not know, from what they heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, of the various kinds of thunderous warnings and admonitions, ﴿that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein﴾, i.e., whoever contravenes Allah and His Messenger.

Al-Layth said: "Hadadtuhu" means "I opposed him." Al-muhadadah is like al-mujanabah, al-mu'adah and al-mukhalafah. Its derivation is from "al-hadd" (the limit, boundary) in the sense of a direction or side, just as al-mushaqqah is from "al-shiqq" (the side) in its meaning as well, for each of the two who oppose and enmity-bear one another is on one limit and one side, other than that on which his companion stands.

So the meaning of ﴿yuhadid Allah﴾ is that he becomes on a limit other than the limit of the friends of Allah, through opposition.

Abu Muslim said: al-muhaddah is derived from "al-hadid" (iron), the iron of weapons.

His Exalted saying ﴿That is the great disgrace﴾ means: the humiliation and the lasting degradation. And His Exalted saying:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[64] ﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on! Indeed Allah will bring forth what you are wary of."﴾

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down against them﴾, meaning: concerning them, for whatever is revealed regarding them is revealed upon them. ﴿Informing them of what is in their hearts﴾, meaning: of the hidden secrets, in addition to what they used to openly say among themselves of statements of disbelief and hypocrisy.

As for the meaning of its informing them of what is in their hearts, although they already know it, and what they feared was that the believers would learn of their secrets, not that they themselves would be informed of them: the surah would disclose what they had been concealing of their secrets, so they would spread among the people and be heard from men's mouths as something broadcast, as if it were informing them of these things.

The intended meaning of "informing" is an exaggeration in the surah's containing their secrets, as if it knew of their inner states what they themselves did not know, so it informs them of these and censures their ugly deeds.

It has been said: the meaning of "yahdharu" (is wary) is "liyahdhara" (so that he may be wary). It has also been said: the first two pronouns refer to the believers and the third to the hypocrites, and there is no objection to this shift of reference when the matter is clear, since the meaning returns to it. That is, the hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down upon the believers informing them of what is in the hearts of the hypocrites. This was related by Abu al-Su'ud.

If you say: the hypocrite is a disbeliever, so how could he be wary of the revelation descending upon the Messenger? I answer: although these people disbelieved in the Messenger's religion, they had witnessed that he ﷺ used to inform them of what they concealed, and because of this experience, wariness and fear entered their hearts.

(p-3193) Al-Asamm said: They knew that he was a truthful messenger from Allah, but they disbelieved in him out of envy and obstinacy.

Al-Qadi criticized this, saying: it is far-fetched that one who knows Allah, His Messenger, and the soundness of his religion should be opposed to them. However, al-Razi said: it is not far-fetched, because when envy grows strong in the heart, it reaches the point of disputing even what is perceptible. End of quote.

Abu Muslim said: This is a wariness that the hypocrites displayed in a mocking manner when they saw the Messenger ﷺ mentioning everything and claiming that it came from revelation, while the hypocrites used to deny this among themselves. So Allah informed His Messenger of this and commanded him to inform them that He would expose the secret they were wary of having exposed. Therefore He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Mock on!"﴾, meaning: at Allah, His signs, and His Messenger; or, "Carry out the mockery," which is a command of threat. ﴿Indeed Allah will bring forth what you are wary of﴾, meaning: He will reveal through revelation what you are wary of being brought out by the sending down of the surah, and of your blemishes and disgraces lying hidden in your hearts, which will expose you, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their rancor?﴾ [Muhammad: 29] up to His saying: ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. For this reason Qatadah said: this surah used to be called "the Exposer" (al-Fadihah), exposing the hypocrites.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[65] ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Is it Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾

﴿And if you ask them﴾ i.e., about their committing those abominations that involve mocking what was mentioned. ﴿They will surely say﴾ i.e., in their excuse, that it did not come from the heart so as to be hypocrisy and disbelief, but rather: ﴿We were only conversing﴾ i.e., we were entering into this speech for the relaxation of the soul ﴿and playing﴾ i.e., joking. ﴿Say, "Is it Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ i.e., in your relaxation and your jesting, and you found no other speech for these.

(p-3194) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[66] ﴿Do not make excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾

﴿Do not make excuses﴾ means: do not occupy yourselves with your false excuses. The prohibition is against engaging in them and persisting in them, since they have already occurred. ﴿You have disbelieved﴾ means: you have manifested disbelief by harming the Messenger (ﷺ), slandering him, and mocking his words. ﴿After your belief﴾ means: after you had displayed belief.

Note:

Al-Kiya al-Harrasi (in "al-Iklil") said: "In this there is evidence that the one who jests and the one who is serious in uttering a word of disbelief are equal, and that mocking the signs of Allah is disbelief." End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: "Because mockery indicates belittling, whereas the foremost essential of faith is the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, to the utmost possible degree, and combining the two is impossible."

Imam Ibn Hazm said in "al-Milal": "Everything that contains disbelief in the Creator, exalted is He, or belittling of Him, or of one of His prophets, or of one of His angels, or of one of His signs, mighty and majestic is He, it is not permissible to listen to it, nor to utter it, nor is it permissible to sit where it is spoken." Then he cited the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾ means: for their repentance and sincerity, or their refraining from harming and mocking. ﴿We will punish another group, because they were criminals﴾ means: those who persisted in hypocrisy, or who proceeded to harm and mock.

Note:

Various narrations have been reported concerning the manner of the hypocrites' mockery. Ibn Ishaq said: A group of the hypocrites, among them Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, brother of Banu Amr ibn (p-3195) Awf, and a man from Ashja' who was an ally of Banu Salamah called Mukhashshin ibn Humayyir (it is also said Makhshi), were pointing at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was setting out for Tabuk. Some of them said to others: "Do you think that the fighting of the Banu al-Asfar (the Byzantines) is like the fighting of the Arabs against one another? By Allah, it is as if we see you tomorrow bound together in ropes!" – spreading alarm and intimidating the believers. Mukhashshin ibn Humayyir said: "By Allah, I would love to be judged such that each of us is struck a hundred lashes, and that we be spared a Qur'an being revealed about us for this saying of yours." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as it reached me, said to Ammar ibn Yasir: "Go to the people, for they have been burned. Ask them what they said, and if they deny it, say: 'Yes, you said such and such.'" So Ammar set out to them and said that to them, and they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) making excuses to him. Wadi'ah ibn Thabit said – while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was standing on his she-camel: "O Messenger of Allah! We were only conversing and playing." So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say, "We were only conversing and playing."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65].

Mukhashshin ibn Humayyir said: "O Messenger of Allah! My name and my father's name have held me back." The one pardoned in this verse was Mukhashshin, so he named himself Abd al-Rahman, and asked Allah, exalted is He, to kill him as a martyr whose place is unknown; and he was killed on the day of Yamama, and no trace of him was found. End of quotation.

Ikrimah said: Among those whom Allah, if He wills, pardoned, was one who would say: "O Allah, I hear a verse that concerns me; the skins shiver from it and the hearts tremble from it. O Allah, make my death a killing in Your way, such that no one says: 'I washed him, I shrouded him, I buried him.'"

He said: So he was struck down on the day of Yamama, and there was not a single Muslim who did not find someone other than him (among the dead).

Among what is reported of their mockery: "A man from among the hypocrites said: 'I have never seen the likes of these reciters of ours: greater in appetite for food, more lying in tongue, and more cowardly at the encounter.' This was reported to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he came to the Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, when he had already set off and mounted his she-camel, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! We were only conversing and playing.' He said: ﴿Was it at Allah and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] – the verse – while he was clinging to the Messenger's saddle, and the Messenger (ﷺ) did not turn to him."

Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Ta'ifah" (the group) in the language originally means a company, because it is the quantity that can surround a thing; then it is permissible to call an individual a "ta'ifah." End of quotation.

Applying a plural form to a single individual is well known in the speech of the Arabs.

And His saying, exalted is He:

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[67] ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another. They enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right, and they withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ means they are alike in hypocrisy and in distance from faith, like the parts of a single thing that resemble one another. What is intended is unity in reality and attribute. Here *min* is *ittisaliyya* (the *min* of connection).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is intended to deny that they are among the believers, and to refute their claim when they say, "And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you," and to affirm His saying, "And they are not of you." Then He described them with what shows the opposition of their state to the state of the believers, by His saying: ﴿They enjoin what is wrong﴾, such as disbelief and acts of disobedience, ﴿and forbid what is right﴾, such as faith and acts of obedience. ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, that is, out of stinginess with good deeds and with spending in the way of Allah. Withholding the hand is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for miserliness and avarice, just as extending the hand is a *kinaya* for generosity, because whoever gives extends his hand, unlike whoever withholds. ﴿They have forgotten Allah﴾, that is, they neglected His remembrance and obedience, so He abandoned them from His mercy and bounty.

Al-Shihab said: The meaning of "they forgot Allah" is that they do not remember Him and do not obey Him, because remembering Him necessarily entails obeying Him. So forgetting was made a *majaz* (metaphor) for abandonment, and it is a *kinaya* for abandoning obedience. Allah's forgetting of them means withholding His kindness and bounty from them.

(p-3197) Al-Nihrir said: Forgetting was made a *majaz* because its literal sense is impossible for Him, Exalted is He, and because it is not possible to hold humans accountable for forgetting.

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, those who are complete in *fisq* (defiant disobedience), which is persistent rebellion in disbelief and total withdrawal from every good.

It suffices the Muslim as a deterrent that he should commit what earns this foul name with which Allah described the hypocrites when He went to great lengths in censuring them.
