And if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked for a Muslim to say, "I am lazy (kasilt)," because the hypocrites were described with laziness in His saying, "lazily (kusala)," then what do you think of defiant disobedience? This was conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[68] "Allah has promised the hypocritical men and hypocritical women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, wherein they will abide eternally. It is sufficient for them. And Allah has cursed them, and for them is an enduring punishment."

"Allah has promised the hypocritical men and hypocritical women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, wherein they will abide eternally. It is sufficient for them" — i.e., as a recompense and a requital. "And Allah has cursed them, and for them is an enduring punishment" — i.e., one that does not cease.

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[69] ﴿As those before you were, they were stronger than you in might and more abundant in wealth and children, and they enjoyed their share, so you have enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share. And you have plunged in as they plunged. Those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾

﴿As those before you﴾ means: you are like those, or you have done as they did, namely among those who were blessed (p-3198) and then punished. The shift (al-iltifat, a change from the third person to the second person) is for emphasis. ﴿They were stronger than you in might﴾ means in their own persons. ﴿And more abundant in wealth﴾ means that it brought them greater strength and many benefits. ﴿And children﴾ means that it brought them greater strength that does not cease when wealth is lost, and other benefits. ﴿They enjoyed their share﴾ means they profited from their portion. Then He gave you, O hypocrites, less than He gave them. ﴿So you have enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share. And you have plunged in as those who plunged﴾ means you entered into falsehood, like the plunging in which they plunged, or like the group that plunged. ﴿Those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ means they did not deserve any reward for them in either abode. As for the Hereafter, this is evident. As for this world, they have what they have of humiliation and disgrace and other things. ﴿And those are the losers﴾ means those who lost both abodes.

Ibn Jurayj narrated from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you, span by span, cubit by cubit, and fathom by fathom, to the extent that if they had entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it too." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they? The People of the Book?" He said: "Then who else?" In another narration, Abu Hurairah said: "Recite, if you wish, the Qur'an": ﴿As those before you﴾ up to the end of the verse. Abu Hurairah said: "Al-khalaq means the religion." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, as Persia and the Romans did?" He said: "And who are the people other than they?" This hadith has a witness in the Sahih, as Ibn Kathir reported.

**A subtle point:**

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and they enjoyed their share﴾, when His saying ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾ suffices in place of it, just as His saying ﴿as those who plunged﴾ suffices in place of saying "and they plunged, so you plunged as those who plunged"? I say: its benefit is to censure the earlier ones for enjoying what they were given of the portions of this world, and for their contentment with it, and for their being distracted by their perishable desires from considering the outcome and seeking success in the Hereafter. It also degrades the matter of enjoyment and disparages the one who is content with it. Then He compares the condition of those addressed with their condition, just as you would want to warn some oppressor about the wickedness of his act, so you say: "You are like Pharaoh, who used to kill without a crime, and torture and oppress, and you do the same as he did." As for ﴿and you have plunged in as they plunged﴾, it is coordinated with what precedes it, depending on it, and by its dependence on it, it is independent of that introduction.

Then Allah the Exalted admonished the hypocrites by saying:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[70] ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. It was not Allah who wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

﴿Has there not come to them﴾, i.e., by way of tawatur (mass-transmitted report), ﴿the news﴾, i.e., the report of ﴿those before them﴾, and it is their destruction after they had been given comfort because of their disbelief: ﴿the people of Noah﴾, upon whom He bestowed favors, among them the lengthening of their lifespans, and then they were destroyed by the flood; ﴿and ʿAd﴾, the people of Hud, upon whom He bestowed favors, among them an increase in their strength, and then they were destroyed by the wind; ﴿and Thamud﴾, the people of Salih, upon whom He bestowed favors, among them palaces, and then they were destroyed by the earthquake; ﴿and the people of Abraham﴾, who were destroyed by collapse. Thus it is in (al-Tanwir).

Al-Mahayimi said: He bestowed favors upon them, among them the greatness of kingship, then He destroyed their king, Nimrod, by a gnat that entered his nose. ﴿And the companions of Madyan﴾, the people of Shuʿayb, upon whom He bestowed favors, among them trade, then He destroyed them by pouring fire upon them. ﴿And the overturned cities﴾, the villages of the people of Lot, which were overturned with their inhabitants, i.e., they were turned upside down, so that their upper part became their lower part, and they were rained upon with stones of sijjil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ is a resumed statement explaining their news: that the messengers came to them with the signs indicating their prophethood. ﴿It was not Allah who wronged them﴾, i.e., by destroying them, because He established the proof against them by sending the messengers and removing excuses.

The fa' is for coordination with an implied element to which the speech refers and which the context requires, i.e., "so they denied them, and Allah the Exalted destroyed them, and He did not wrong them thereby." ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, i.e., through disbelief and denial, and abandoning thanking Him, and turning His favors, which He gave them for a purpose, to other than that purpose; so they deserved that punishment.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[71] ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, establish prayer, give zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those — Allah will have mercy on them. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ is in contrast to His saying about the hypocrites: ﴿They are of one another﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67]. ﴿They enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and establish prayer﴾, meaning they never cease to remember Him, exalted is He. This corresponds to what preceded in His saying: ﴿They forgot Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67].

﴿And give zakah﴾ corresponds to His saying: ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67]. ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning in every command and prohibition. This corresponds to the description of the hypocrites, with their complete wickedness and departure from obedience: ﴿Those — Allah will have mercy on them. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

(p-3201) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[72] ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence (ʿAdn). And approval from Allah is greater. That is the great achievement.﴾

﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ That is: from beneath their trees and dwellings flow rivers of wine, water, honey and milk. ﴿abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings﴾ That is: good residences that souls find pleasant, or in which life is pleasant. ﴿in gardens of perpetual residence﴾ That is: a dwelling and stability. It is also said that ʿAdn is a proper name for a specific place in Paradise, because of the traces (āthār) in it. Since ﴿pleasant dwellings﴾ is conjoined to "gardens," it has been said: the two conjoined items either differ in essence, so that they were promised two things, namely the gardens in the sense of orchards and pleasant dwellings in Paradise, so that each person has a garden and a dwelling; or the gardens intended are other than ʿAdn, and these are for the general body of believers, while ʿAdn is for the prophets, peace be upon them, the martyrs and the truthful (ṣiddīqūn). Or they may be one in essence but differ in attribute, so the second difference is treated as the first and conjoined to it; each of them is general, but the first is by reference to its containing rivers and orchards, and the second by reference to the mansions and abodes.

Al-Qadi said: It is as if He first described the promised reward as being of the kind of the most splendid places they know, so that their natures would incline toward it at the first striking of their ears; then He described it as surrounded by pleasant living, free from the impurities of turbidity of which the places of this world are never wholly free, and in it is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in.

Then He described it as an abode of residence and stability in the neighborhood of the ʿIlliyyūn, where neither decay nor change befalls them. Then He promised them something greater than that, saying: ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾, for upon it revolves the attainment of every good and happiness, and upon it depends the gaining of every honor and lordship. Perhaps its not being placed in the string of the promise, despite its greatness in itself, is because it is realized within every promised thing, and because it is continuous in both abodes. Abu al-Suʿud reported this.

The preference for the approval of Allah over what was mentioned indicates that a small portion of it is better than all of that.

Imam Malik and the two Shaykhs [al-Bukhari and Muslim] narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' They say: 'Here we are, our Lord, at Your service and pleasure, and all good is in Your hands.' He says: 'Are you content?' They say: 'And why should we not be content, O Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He says: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say: 'O Lord, and what could be better than that?' He says: 'I shall cause My approval to descend upon you, so that I shall never be displeased with you after it, ever.'"

Al-Mahamili and al-Bazzar narrated from Jabir, traced to the Prophet: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Do you desire anything that I may increase for you?' They say: 'Our Lord! What could be better than what You have given us?' He says: 'My approval is greater.'"

﴿That is the great achievement﴾ That is: not what people regard as success from the portions of this world.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[73] ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their abode is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ It has been said: the striving against the hypocrites is by argument, not by the sword.

In al-'Inayah it says: The apparent meaning of the verse requires fighting the hypocrites, although they do not openly display disbelief, and we are commanded to follow what is apparent. Therefore, the early generations (al-Salaf) interpreted the verse in a way that averts this, on the basis that jihad (striving) is the exertion of effort in repelling what is not pleasing (to Allah), whether by fighting or by other means. If it is taken literally, this is clear. Otherwise, it is understood in its broader figurative sense: the striving against the disbelievers is by the sword, and the striving against the hypocrites is by imposing proofs upon them, removing doubts and the like, or by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them when they commit what necessitates them, as was narrated from al-Hasan regarding the verse.

It has been objected to this that establishing the prescribed punishments is obligatory upon others as well. It is answered that these punishments were most frequently carried out against them during the Prophet's ﷺ time. End of quote.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a claim without evidence. The one who disobeys is not a hypocrite; rather, the hypocrite is one whose hypocrisy is hidden in his heart, not one who is apparently afflicted with sins in his limbs. And the narrations about those who were subjected to the prescribed punishments, their context shows that they were not hypocrites.

Ibn Kathir said: It was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent with four swords: a sword for the polytheists: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]; a sword for the disbelievers among the People of the Book: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], and so on; a sword for the hypocrites: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾; and a sword for the rebels: ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], and so on. This indicates that they are to be struggled against with swords when they openly display hypocrisy. This is the view preferred by Ibn Jarir. End of quote.

In al-Iklil, it says: Whoever held that the hypocrites should be killed used this verse as evidence. End of quote.

﴿And be harsh with them﴾ That is: be severe toward both groups, in speech and in action. ﴿Their abode is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

(p-٣٢٠٤) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing, but they had certainly uttered the word of disbelief and reverted to disbelief after their Islam and planned what they did not attain. And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty. So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will not have in the earth any protector or helper.﴾

﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾ i.e., nothing about you that would displease you. ﴿But they had certainly uttered the word of disbelief and reverted to disbelief after their Islam﴾. Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, when two men fought, one a man of Juhayna and the other an Ansari. The Juhanni overcame the Ansari, so ʿAbd Allah said to the Ansar: "Will you not help your brother? By Allah, our likeness and the likeness of Muhammad is only as the one who said: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.'" And he said: "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." A man among the Muslims reported this to the Prophet ﷺ, and he sent for him and questioned him, and he began swearing by Allah that he had not said it. So Allah revealed this verse concerning him.

Al-Umawi related in his "Maghazi" from Ibn Ishaq that al-Jullas ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit, who was among the hypocrites who had stayed behind, when he heard what was being revealed concerning them, said: "By Allah, if this man is truthful in what he says, then we are worse than donkeys." ʿUmayr ibn Saʿd heard it, and he was in his care, so he said: "By Allah, O Jullas, you are the dearest of people to me, the best of them in my estimation, and the most dear to me that some harm should reach him that he dislikes. You have said a statement; if I mention it, it will disgrace me, and if I conceal it, it will destroy me, and one of the two is easier for me than the other."

So he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him what al-Jullas had said. When this reached al-Jullas, he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and swore by Allah that he had not said it. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning him: ﴿They swear by Allah﴾ to the end of the verse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then confronted him with it. It is said that al-Jullas repented, his repentance was good, and he withdrew and withdrew well.

These two reports and others narrated here all indicate a variety of statements and words that were disbelieving and of this kind, although it is not possible for us to specify any of them in this verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they planned what they did not attain﴾. Ibn Kathir said: it was said that it was revealed concerning al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, for he planned to kill ʿUmayr, the son of his wife, when he conveyed his earlier statement to the Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him.

It is also reported that a group of hypocrites planned to assassinate the Prophet ﷺ while he was on the expedition to Tabuk, on some of those nights during the journey, and they were some ten men or more. al-Dahhak said: concerning them this verse was revealed.

Imam Ahmad said in his Musnad: Yazid related to us, al-Walid ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Jumayʿ informed us, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from the expedition to Tabuk, he commanded a caller who called out that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had taken the ʿAqabah, so none should take it.

While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was being led by Huzayfah, and ʿAmmar was driving him, a group of men wrapped in face-coverings approached on their mounts and surrounded ʿAmmar while he was driving the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ʿAmmar, may Allah be pleased with him, came striking the faces of the mounts, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Huzayfah: "Qad, qad" (enough, enough), until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ descended.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ descended he dismounted, and ʿAmmar returned. He said: "O ʿAmmar! Did you recognise the people?" He said: "I recognised most of the mounts, and the people were wrapped up." He said: "Do you know what they intended?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "They intended to startle the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and throw him down." Then ʿAmmar whispered to a man from among the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "I adjure you by Allah, how many do you know were the companions of the ʿAqabah?" He said: "Fourteen men." He said: "If you were among them, then they were fifteen."

He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then named three of them, and they said: "By Allah, we did not hear the caller of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and we did not know what the people intended."

ʿAmmar said: "I testify that the remaining twelve are at war with Allah and His Messenger in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand."

﴿And they did not resent﴾ i.e., they did not disapprove of or find fault with, ﴿except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty﴾. For before his ﷺ coming to Madinah they were in a state of want of livelihood, then they became rich through the spoils, and a client of al-Jullas was killed, so the Prophet ﷺ ordered that his blood-money be paid to him, and he became wealthy.

The meaning is that the hypocrites acted contrary to what was obligatory, so that what they plotted was made the place of the Prophet's ﷺ gratitude; and there is no fault in them except that he favoured them. This is in the sense of the saying: "I have no fault with you except that I have been good to you," and the words of Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"They resent of the people of Umayyah nothing except that they bear when they are angry."

And the words of al-Nabigha:

"And there is no fault in them except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions."

It is said: "nagama min fulan al-ihsan" (like ʿalima), when he regards it as leading to ingratitude for the blessing, as in al-Taj.

Then He, exalted is He, called them to repentance by His saying: ﴿So if they repent﴾, i.e., from disbelief and hypocrisy, ﴿it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world﴾, i.e., by killing, distress and grief, ﴿and the Hereafter﴾, i.e., with the Fire and other things, ﴿and they will not have in the earth any protector﴾, i.e., one who intercedes for them to avert the punishment.

﴿Nor any helper﴾, i.e., who would repel it by his strength.

(p-٣٢٠٧) Then He, exalted is He, explains some of those who resented, despite Allah's enriching them with what He gave them of His bounty, from among those who broke their oath and turned away from repentance, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[75] ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God, saying: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous."﴾

﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God﴾, meaning: swore, ﴿"If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous"﴾, meaning: by giving every person with a right his right.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted, saying:

[76] ﴿So when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾

﴿So when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿—⁠﻿﻿ i.e., from the covenant⁠﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿—⁠﻿﻿ ﴿while they were refusing﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 77:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿So He caused them to follow up hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they will meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they had promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾

﴿So He caused them to follow up﴾, i.e., Allah made the consequence of their act that, or ﴿He caused them to inherit﴾ stinginess, ﴿hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they will meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they had promised Him﴾, i.e., of giving charity and righteousness, ﴿and because they used to lie﴾ regarding the covenant.

(p. 3208) Commentary on His words, may He be exalted:

[78] ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private talk, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret﴾: that is, what they conceal of hypocrisy and of their resolve to break what they promised Him, and what they confer about among themselves of reproaches against the religion. ﴿And that Allah is the Knower of the unseen﴾: that is, what is hidden from the servants.

(p. 3208) Observations:

First: al-Suyuti said in *Lubab al-Nuqul* (The Core of the Narrations): Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated, with a weak chain, from Abu Umamah, that Tha'labah ibn Hatib said: "O Messenger of Allah! Pray to Allah that He grant me wealth." He said: "Woe to you, O Tha'labah! A little that you can render thanks for is better than a great deal that you cannot bear." He said: "By Allah, if Allah gives me wealth, I will surely give everyone who has a right his right." So he prayed for him, and he acquired sheep, and they multiplied until the alleys of Medina became too narrow for them, so he moved them out. He would attend the prayer and then go out to them. Then they multiplied until the pastures of Medina were unavailable to him, so he moved them out. He would attend the prayer and then go out to them. Then they multiplied until the pastures of Medina were unavailable to him, so he moved them out. He would attend Friday prayer and then go out to them. Then they multiplied, and he moved them out, and he abandoned Friday prayer and the congregational prayers. Then Allah revealed to His Messenger: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So he appointed two men over the charities and wrote them a letter. They went to Tha'labah and read him the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "Go to the people, and when you have finished, pass by me." They did so, and he said: "This is nothing but a sister of the jizyah (poll tax)." So they departed, and Allah revealed: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 75] until His words: ﴿they used to lie﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77]. The hadith.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, through al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, something similar, and in it: "Afterward he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity, and he said: 'Allah has forbidden me to accept it from you.' So he placed dust on his head. He said: 'This is your deed; I commanded you, but you did not obey me.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away, and he came with it to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), but he did not accept it; likewise Umar and Uthman. Then he died in the days of Uthman."

Al-Shihab said: Tha'labah's coming and throwing dust was not for repentance from his hypocrisy, but out of shame at the non-acceptance of his zakat along with the Muslims. And his saying (ﷺ), "This is your deed," means the recompense of your deed, which is his not giving to the collectors, together with his repulsive statement.

(p. 3209) Al-Hakim said: If it is asked: how was his charity not accepted when he was obligated to give charity? I answer: It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, commanded that so that people would not dare to break the covenant, to oppose the command of Allah, exalted is He, and to reject the collectors of the Prophet (ﷺ). And it would be a means of grace (lutf) in abandoning miserliness and hypocrisy.

Second: Some exegetes of the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i school) said: The fruits of the verse and the cause of its revelation are rulings, among them:

That fulfilling a promise is obligatory when the covenant is bound to an obligatory matter. If the covenant is taken as an oath by Allah, that is clear; and if it is taken as a vow (nadhr), then it is an affirmation of what Allah has made obligatory.

And among them: that the imam may do the like for the sake of a public interest, i.e., he may refrain from taking an obligatory due when there arises a reason similar to the reason that arose in the story of Tha'labah. End of quotation.

Third: al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil* (The Crown): In it is that breaking promises and lying are among the traits of hypocrisy, so fulfilling and truthfulness are among the branches of faith.

And in it is punishment for a sin with something more severe than it, due to His words: ﴿so He caused them hypocrisy to follow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77]. Some used this as evidence that whoever swears, "If I do such-and-such, then it is incumbent upon me by Allah to do such-and-such," it becomes binding upon him. Others used it as evidence that the one who withholds zakat is punished by the withdrawal of its collection from him, as was done to the one about whom the verse was revealed. End of quotation.

Fourth: al-Razi said: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that breaking a covenant and breaking a promise produce hypocrisy, so the Muslim must be extremely careful to avoid it. When he makes a covenant with Allah in a matter, he should strive to fulfill it.

The position of al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) is that it necessarily produces hypocrisy, and he held to this verse and to the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Three qualities whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he prays and fasts and claims he is a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays."

(p. 3210) Fifth: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], indicate that this covenant-maker died a hypocrite.

Al-Razi said: This report, its informant's account corresponded to it, for it was narrated that Tha'labah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity, and he said: "Allah, exalted is He, has forbidden me to accept your charity." He remained in that state, and none of the caliphs (may Allah be pleased with them all) accepted his charity until he died. So this was a report of the unseen, and therefore it was a miracle.

Sixth: The pronoun in (yulqunahu) refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah), and what is meant by (the Day) is the Day of Resurrection, and it has many parallels in the Revelation.

Some exegetes gave a grammatical analysis, saying: The pronoun in (yalqawnahu) either refers to Allah, and what is meant by the Day is the time of death; or it refers to miserliness, and what is meant is the Day of Resurrection, with an omitted genitive, which is the recompense. End of quotation.

Meeting (liqa'), when attributed to the disbelievers, is a meeting suited to their condition, of standing for the reckoning while being veiled from Him, exalted is He, since they are not worthy of seeing Him, may His name be sanctified.

When it is attributed to the believers, as in His words: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44], it is a meeting suited to their station of seeing Him, exalted is He. This is in accordance with what other verses have made clear about the condition of both groups, of which the like is applied to them.

Whoever stops at a word in some verses and begins to derive rulings from it, without regard to whom it is used for and applied to, that is rigidity and partisanship, not taking hold of the hand of truth.

We say this in response to al-Jubba'i's statement that meeting in this verse does not indicate seeing Him, exalted is He, by consensus (ijma') that the disbelievers do not see Him, exalted is He; so it does not indicate it either in His words: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44].

Al-Razi has a debate with him from another angle. What we have mentioned is firmer. And Allah knows best.

Seventh: al-Razi said: (al-sirr) is what their hearts conceal, and (al-najwa) is what they discuss among themselves in private. It is derived from al-Nujuww, which is secret speech, as if the two confidants prevented others from joining them and kept away from others.

Then Allah, exalted is He, showed another kind of the bad qualities of the hypocrites, which is their defaming of those who give charity, by His saying, glorified is He:

(p-3211) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[79] ﴿Those who slander the volunteers among the believers regarding charity, and those who find nothing to give except their effort, so they mock them—Allah will mock them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Those who slander﴾, i.e., who find fault with, ﴿the volunteers﴾, i.e., those who give voluntarily, ﴿among the believers regarding charity﴾, claiming that they give charity only for show (riya'). ﴿And those who﴾, i.e., and they slander those who ﴿find nothing except their effort﴾, i.e., they find nothing to give in charity except a little, which is the measure of their capacity.

﴿So they mock them﴾, i.e., they ridicule them, saying that Allah is free of need of their charity. ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, i.e., He requites them for their mockery. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from Abu Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: When the verse on charity was revealed, we used to carry loads (for hire). A man came and gave a large amount in charity, and they said, "He is showing off." Another man came and gave a sa' (of dates), and they said, "Indeed Allah is free of need of this man's charity." So the verse was revealed: ﴿Those who slander﴾ to the end of the verse. Muslim also narrated it.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu al-Salil, from a man who related to him from his father or his paternal uncle, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Who will give a charity for which I will bear witness for him on the Day of Resurrection?" A man came, whom I had never seen blacker, shorter or more wheat-colored than him, with a she-camel more beautiful than any I had seen, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, take this she-camel." Then a man slandered him, saying: "This man gives charity with this? By Allah, it is better than him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard it and said: "You have lied! Rather, he is better than you and better than it," three times. Then he said: "Woe to your companions, except for one who speaks about wealth like this and like this," and he gathered his two hands to his right and left.

Ibn Ishaq said: Among the believers who were volunteers in charity were 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and 'Asim ibn 'Adi, brother of the Banu 'Ajlan. That was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encouraged charity and urged it, so 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf stood and gave four thousand, and 'Asim ibn 'Adi stood and gave a hundred wasq of dates. They slandered them and said: "This is nothing but show."

The one who gave according to his effort was Abu 'Uqayl, brother of the Banu Unayf, who brought a sa' of dates and poured it into the charity. They mocked him and said: "Indeed Allah is free of need of Abu 'Uqayl's sa'."

Al-Hafiz al-Bazzar narrated in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give charity, for I intend to send out an army." 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have four thousand: two thousand I lend to my Lord, and two thousand for my dependents." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah bless you in what you gave and bless you in what you kept."

A man from the Ansar spent the night and obtained two sa' of dates. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I obtained two sa' of dates: one sa' I lend to my Lord, and one sa' for my dependents." They said, so the hypocrites slandered him and said: "What 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf gave was only for show. Did Allah and His Messenger not have need of this sa'?" So Allah revealed the verse.

His words (ﷺ) "I intend to send out an army" mean: to fight the Romans, and that was at the Battle of Tabuk.

Notes:

First: al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): This verse prohibits slandering and mocking the believers. End of quote.

Second: Regarding ﴿Those who slander﴾ there are several grammatical possibilities (i'rab): it is the predicate of a subject understood as (they are "those who"), or an object of an implied verb (a'ni, "I mean"), or (adhummu, "I condemn") those who; or it is a genitive substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (sirrahum). It is also permitted that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, and it was said that the predicate is ﴿so they mock﴾, with the (fa') entering because of the resemblance of (alladhina, "those who") to a conditional. As for (those who find nothing...) and so on, it was said that it is conjoined to ﴿Those who slander﴾, and it was said that it is conjoined to (the believers), but the best view is that it is conjoined to ﴿the volunteers﴾.

Al-Hafiz (in al-Fath) said: This is conjoining the specific to the general, and the point of it is to draw attention to the specific, because mockery of the poor is generally more severe than mockery of the wealthy.

Third: Al-Hafiz (in al-Fath) said: The reading of the majority is ﴿al-muttawi'in﴾ with a doubled ta' and waw. Its origin is al-mutatawwi'in, and the ta' was assimilated into the ta'. End of quote.

That is, because the points of articulation are close. Tatawwu' (voluntary acts) is supererogatory devotion, namely obedience to Allah Exalted with what is not obligatory.

As for (al-juhd), al-Layth said: it is a small amount on which the poor person lives. The majority read it with a dammah on the jim, while Ibn Hurmuz and a group read it with a fathah. It was said: they are two dialects with one meaning. It was also said: the fathah means hardship, and the dammah means capacity. It was also said: the dammah is a little on which one subsists, and the fathah is labor. The preferred view is that both have the same meaning, namely capacity and what one's strength can reach. Al-Farra' said: the dammah is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the fathah is for others. Al-huzu' and al-sukhriyyah have the same meaning.

And His Exalted words:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them. If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them. That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾

﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ means: for these hypocrites. ﴿Or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ means: for in their case both are equal.

Then He explained the impossibility of their forgiveness, even if seeking forgiveness is exaggerated, with His saying: ﴿If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them﴾, meaning, their non-forgiveness, ﴿because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, meaning, those who go beyond His limits.

Remarks (tanbihat):

First: The sentence ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ and what follows is imperative in wording but informative in meaning.

The intended sense is the equality between seeking forgiveness for them and abandoning it, with regard to the impossibility of forgiveness.

Its expression in the form of a command is for emphasis in clarifying their equality, as if the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him had been commanded to test the situation, by asking forgiveness at one time and leaving it at another, so that the clear matter would become evident to him. This is like what passed in His saying: ﴿Say: "Spend willingly or unwillingly"﴾ [al-Tawba: 53]. It has come in the form of a report in Surat al-Munafiqun, in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5]. ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will not forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6].

Second: al-Zamakhshari said: "Seventy" functions in their speech like a proverb, for the sake of multiplicity. Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said:

"I will surely leave the son of al-As and the son of al-As
Seventy thousand, with their forelocks bound."

That is, its mention is for emphasis in cutting off the matter of seeking forgiveness for them, following the Arabs' methods of using it for emphasis rather than for exact limitation, such that whatever exceeds it would be the opposite of it.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The use of seven, seventy and seven hundred has become common for general multiplicity, since seven includes all the divisions of number, so it is as if it were the whole number.

It was also said: It is the most complete of numbers, because it combines their meanings, and because six is the first perfect number, since its whole parts are equal: its half is three, its third is two, its sixth is one, and their sum is six; and with the one it is seven. So it is complete, for there is no rank beyond completion except perfection. Then seventy is the ultimate of perfection, since units reach their ultimate in tens, and seven hundred is the ultimate of ultimates. End of quotation.

Third: al-Bukhari and others narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he wanted to prevent him from praying over Abd Allah ibn Ubayy: "Allah only gave me a choice when He said: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them…﴾ (the verse), and I will add to it beyond the seventy."

The apparent meaning of this is that "or" is for choice, and that the seventy has a limit whose ruling differs from what lies beyond it, and this is a matter of considerable difficulty.

For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how was this hidden from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he was the most eloquent of the Arabs and the most knowledgeable of their methods of speech and figures of expression? What is understood from this number is the abundance of seeking forgiveness. How can this be, when it is followed by His saying: ﴿That is because they disbelieved…﴾ (the verse), which clarifies the obstacle to their forgiveness, until he said: "My Lord has granted me leave, so I will add beyond the seventy"?

Then al-Zamakhshari answered with his saying: I say, this was not hidden from him, but he imagined by what he said the manifestation of the utmost of his mercy and compassion towards those he was sent to, like the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿And whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

In the Prophet's ﷺ display of compassion and mercy is kindness to his community, and an invitation for them to show mercy to one another. End of quotation.

The commentators said: He means that he gave the listener the impression that he understood a specific number and not mere abundance, so he permitted the reply with an increase, aiming to show compassion and mercy, just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made the recompense for "whoever disobeys me", that is, who does not comply with the command to abandon the worship of idols, ﴿indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ rather than saying "severe in punishment". So it was imagined that He would have mercy on them and forgive them out of compassion for them, and as an encouragement to follow.

Understanding the literal meaning from a word whose figurative use has become well known does not contradict his eloquence or his knowledge of the language, for there is no error in it, nor is it far-fetched, since it is the original meaning. His eagerness for their guidance, his compassion for them, and his concern for those other than them, made this preferable to him.

Al-Nasir said: The judge, may Allah be pleased with him, rejected the hadith about seeking forgiveness and did not authenticate it, while a group went to excess in accepting it, to the extent that they adopted it as a foundation for the implication of the opposite (mafhum al-mukhalafa), and built upon it the claim that the Prophet, peace be upon him, understood from the limitation of the negation of forgiveness to seventy the establishment of forgiveness for what exceeds it. This was the reason for the judge's rejection of them.

It was also said: When Allah made seeking forgiveness and not seeking it equal, and made non-acceptance follow from it, and did not forbid it, it was understood that it was good and permitted. This is what he, ﷺ, meant, and not that choice was understood from "or", such that it would contradict the equality between them, which entails non-forgiveness. This was to console their hearts and to show that he had spared no effort in showing compassion to them.

Al-Shihab said: The verification is that the intended meaning is equality in the absence of benefit, and this does not contradict choice. If choice is established, it is by way of implication, since it occurs between two opposites neither of which may be left or done. So one of them must be chosen. It may be in affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqara: 6], since he is commanded to convey the message. It may be in negation, as here, and in His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6]. So it requires explanation, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "It has been permitted for me." Perhaps He permitted him to do so regarding Ibn Ubayy for a wisdom, even though it did not entail the benefit of acceptance. End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani said in al-Fath: Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them. If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them﴾, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I will surely add beyond the seventy.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6]."

Then he said: It is possible that both verses were revealed together concerning this matter. End of quotation.

Then Allah, exalted is He, pointed to another kind of the evil conduct of the hypocrites, which is their making joy in place of sorrow and aversion in place of contentment, by His saying, glorified is He:

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[81] ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting [at home], against the Messenger of God, and they disliked striving with their wealth and their selves in the way of God, and they said: "Do not go forth in the heat." Say: "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they understood."﴾

﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting [at home], against the Messenger of God, and they disliked striving with their wealth and their selves in the way of God.﴾ *Al-mukhallafūn* (those who were left behind) are the hypocrites who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission, and he permitted them to stay behind, as we have said. Or it is because he (ﷺ) left them behind in Madinah during the expedition of Tabuk.

The form *al-mukhallafūn* is preferred over *al-mutakhallifūn*, because he (ﷺ) prevented some of them from going out, and so the term applied to the others as well. Or the intended meaning is that their "being left behind" refers to their laziness or their hypocrisy. Or it is because Satan incited them to this and drove them to it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿bi-maq'adihim﴾ (in their sitting [at home]), is connected to *faraḥa* (rejoiced), meaning: in their remaining behind from the expedition of Tabuk. On this reading, *maq'ad* is a *maṣdar mīmī* (a noun of place or action formed with the prefix *mīm*), or it is a noun of place, and the intended place is Madinah.

His saying, ﴿khilāfa rasūli Allāh﴾ (against the Messenger of God), means: behind him, after his departure, since he went out and they did not go out.

So *khilāf* is an adverb of place (*ẓarf*) meaning *khalfa* (behind) and *ba'da* (after).

It is said: "So-and-so stayed behind *khilāf* the tribe", meaning after them, when they departed and he did not depart. This is supported by the reading of one who recited *khalfa rasūli Allāh*, where its accusative case is that of an adverb of place governing *maq'adihim*, since there is no benefit in restricting their rejoicing to this (otherwise).

Al-Shihab said: The use of *khilāf* in the sense of *khalf* is because the direction of behind is opposite to the front. It is also permissible that *al-khilāf* means *al-mukhālafa* (opposition), so it is a *maṣdar* of *khālafa*, like *al-qitāl*. This is strengthened by the reading of one who recited *khulfa rasūli Allāh* with a *ḍamma* on the *kha'*. In its accusative case there are two possibilities:

The first: it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*), and the governing word is either *faraḥa*, meaning: they rejoiced for the sake of opposing him (ﷺ) by sitting [at home]; or *maq'adahum*, for the sake of opposing him (ﷺ). So it is a cause either for the rejoicing or for the sitting.

(p-٣٢١٨) The second: it is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), and the governing word is one of the two mentioned, meaning: they rejoiced, opposing him (ﷺ), by sitting [at home], or they rejoiced at sitting [at home], opposing him.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-karihū﴾ (and they disliked), etc., means: because of the sickness of hypocrisy in their hearts.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The noble composition was preferred over saying "and they disliked going forth to the expedition", to indicate that striving in the way of God, despite being among the most noble desires and the most exalted aims, which the competitors should vie for, they disliked, just as they rejoiced at the most vile of vileness, which is sitting [at home] against the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His saying, ﴿and they disliked striving with their wealth and their selves﴾: it is an allusion (*ta'rīḍ*) to the believers, to their bearing great hardships for the countenance of God, exalted is He, and to what they did of spending their wealth and their lives in the way of God, exalted is He, and their preferring that over ease and comfort, that is, "rest and indulgence in food and drink". The hypocrites disliked this, and how could they not dislike it? They do not have what the believers have of the impulse of faith and the call of certainty.

Al-Shihab said: The point of the allusion is clear, because the intended meaning is that they disliked it, unlike the believers who loved it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they said: "Do not go forth in the heat"﴾, means: they said to their brothers, "Do not go forth to the striving in the heat, for its intensity cannot be endured."

This is because the departure for the expedition of Tabuk took place in the intense heat, at the time when shade and fruit were pleasant. They said this to strengthen them in staying behind and to counsel one another in evil and corruption. Or they said to the believers to discourage them from striving, to forbid what is right, and to display some of the pretexts that impelled them to what they rejoiced in, namely sitting [at home], and disliking striving, and forbidding others from it. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say﴾, means: in reply to them and to show their ignorance: ﴿The Fire of Hell﴾, that is, which you will enter (p-٣٢١٩) because of what you have done: ﴿is more intense in heat﴾, that is, than the familiar heat that you fear and warn people about. So why do you not fear it, and expose yourselves to it by preferring sitting [at home] over going forth?

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if only they understood﴾, is a concluding remark (*i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī*) from Him, exalted is He, not included within the statement that was commanded, and it emphasizes its meaning.

The answer to *law* (if) is either implied, meaning: if they understood that it is so, or what it is like, or that their ultimate fate is toward it, they would not have done what they did; or they would have been affected by this compelling argument. Or it is not intended, with *law* being merely for wishing, which indicates the impossibility of the realization of what follows it, meaning: if they were among the people of understanding and perceptiveness, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth, though signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe."﴾ [Yunus: 101].

Thus it is in Abu al-Su'ud.

**Two notes:**

The first: Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: The Fire of Hell﴾, etc., is a rebuke to them, because whoever guards himself from the hardship of an hour, and as a result of that guarding falls into the hardship of eternity, is more ignorant than every ignorant person. One of them said:

*The joy of ages, after which you encounter*
*the sorrow of a day whose taste is like bitter aloe.*

*So how is it with one who casts away the joy of an hour*
*whose passing leaves behind the sorrow of ages?*

— End quote.

(p-٣٢٢٠) That is: they are as the other said:

*Like one seeking refuge from the scorching sand in the fire.*

Another said:

*You spent your life in zeal,*
*out of fear of the cold and the heat.*

*It would have been better for you to guard yourself*
*from sins, out of fear of the Fire.*

The second: Imam Malik and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The fire of the children of Adam, with which they kindle, is one part of seventy parts." Imam Ahmad added: "of the Fire of Hell."

The two Shaykhs related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the least punished of the people of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection is one who has two sandals and two straps of fire, from which his brain boils like a cauldron. He does not think that anyone among the people of the Fire is punished more severely than he, while in fact he is the least punished of them."

Then He, exalted is He, informed about their immediate and ultimate state, of little laughter and long weeping, which their evil deeds bring about, of which the rejoicing mentioned is part, with His saying, glorified is He:

(p-3221) The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[82] ﴿So let them laugh a little, and let them weep much, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾

﴿So let them laugh a little﴾ means: laughter that is little, or a little time, its limit being the duration of their lives. ﴿And let them weep much﴾ means: weeping, or a long time, after death, forever and ever. ﴿As recompense for what they used to earn﴾ means: for their joy at opposing Allah and His Messenger, and for the enormous sins of disbelief and disobedience.

Subtle points (lata'if):

The first: the reason their worldly and otherworldly states are expressed in the form of a command (amr), which indicates that what is reported is certain to occur. A command from one whose orders are obeyed is such that the one commanded almost never fails to carry it out. If it is said: they have mentioned that a command is sometimes expressed as a report for emphasis, since a report implies that the thing commanded has been realized, so the report is stronger. Why then is it reversed here?

The answer: there is no contradiction between the two, because every context has its own manner of speech, and rhetorical purposes do not conflict. When a command is expressed as a report, the aim is to convey that the one commanded, because of the intensity of his compliance, is as if he had already done it and it had come to pass before the command, which is more eloquent. When a report is expressed as a command, the aim appears to be conveying that it is binding and obligatory, so it is as if it were something commanded. This conveys emphasis from another angle.

The second: the combination of the two forms, the past and the present, in His saying (بِما كانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ) ("what they used to earn") indicates continuous renewal, for as long as they remain in this world.

The third: (جَزاءً) ("as recompense") is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for the second verb, meaning: "let them weep as recompense." Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) whose governing verb has been omitted, meaning: "they will be recompensed with the much weeping mentioned."

When He, glorified be He, had made clear what He made clear of their affair, He followed it with His saying:

(p-3222) The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[83] ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, then say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me. Indeed, you were satisfied with sitting [at home] the first time, so sit [now] with those who remain behind."﴾

﴿So if Allah returns you﴾, that is, brings you back from the expedition of Tabuk, ﴿to a group of them﴾, that is, of the hypocrites who stayed behind in Medina, ﴿and they ask your permission to go out﴾ with you on another expedition after Tabuk, seeking to ward off the shame that preceded, ﴿then say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me. Indeed, you were satisfied with sitting [at home] the first time"﴾, that is: Allah has forsaken you, you have fallen from His regard, and rather He is angry with you and has made shame cling to you.

﴿So sit with those who remain behind﴾, that is: among the women and the children, always.

Subtleties (lata'if):

His saying, ﴿You will never go out with me, ever﴾, is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, for emphasis. He mentioned fighting because it is the purpose of going out. Had He limited the prohibition to one of them, it would have sufficed as a removal of them from the station of companionship and the station of jihad, or from the register of the warriors and the register of the mujahidin, and as a display of His dislike for their company and the lack of need to count them among the soldiers. Or He mentioned the second for emphasis, since it is clearer in meaning, while the first corresponds to their request, as in the verse:

"I say to him: depart, do not stay among us."

So it is more indicative of their being disliked. This was stated by al-Shihab (al-Khafaji).

Abu al-Su'ud said: Thus the erasing of their names from the register of the mujahidin and their being joined to the group of those who stay behind is a punishment for them, of the most severe kind.

Then he said: The masculine form of the superlative (ism al-tafdil) when attached to a feminine noun is the most common and is what circulates on people's tongues, for you hardly ever hear a speaker say: "she is the greatest of women," or "the first time."

**Commentary on His saying, exalted is He:**

[84] ﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they died while they were defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever﴾: al-Mahayimi said, "Because it is an intercession (*shafa'ah*), and there is no intercession on their behalf." ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾, i.e., do not stand at it for burial or for visitation and supplication.

Al-Shihab said: "*Al-qabr* (the grave) is the place where the dead is placed, and it may mean burial (*dafn*). It is permitted to read it that way here."

﴿Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ during life, inwardly. ﴿And they died while they were defiantly disobedient﴾, i.e., they had departed from outward faith, which they had held, so that they were judged as believers.

**Notes:**

**First:** Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, his son Abdullah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to give him his shirt in which to shroud his father. He gave it to him. Then he asked him to pray over him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose to pray over him. Umar rose, took hold of the garment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Will you pray over him when your Lord has forbidden you to pray over him?'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Allah only gave me the choice when He said: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], and I will increase it beyond seventy.' He said, 'He is a hypocrite.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him, and Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed the verse: ﴿And do not pray over any of them...﴾ until the end."

Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz said: "It occurred in a narration in Umar's words: 'Will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you to pray over the hypocrites?' It did not specify the object of the prohibition. Its specification occurred in the narration of Abu Damra from al-Umari, and its wording is: 'Allah has forbidden you to ask forgiveness for them.'" End of quote.

That is, in His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. This verse was revealed concerning the story of Abu Talib, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will certainly ask forgiveness for you, as long as I am not forbidden from you." Abu Talib died in Makkah before the Hijrah, by agreement, while the death of Abdullah ibn Ubayy was in Dhu al-Qa'dah, in the ninth year, after the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk. Thus it is reported in *Fath al-Bari*.

What was mentioned above of Umar's hadith also occurs in the *Musnad* of Imam Ahmad, in Umar's own words:

Umar said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to him, and he stood over him. When he stood over him intending to pray over him, I moved until I stood in front of his chest, and I said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Over the enemy of Allah, Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who said on such-and-such a day such-and-such?' He enumerated his days. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was smiling, until when I had said too much, he said: 'Step back from me, O Umar. I was given a choice and chose. It has been said to me: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], to the end of the verse. If I knew that if I added beyond seventy he would be forgiven, I would add.'"

He said: "Then he prayed over him, walked with him, and stood at his grave until he finished with it. I was amazed at my boldness toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah and His Messenger know best."

He said: "By Allah! It was not long before these two verses were revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever﴾ until the end of the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not pray over any hypocrite after him, nor stand at his grave, until Allah, mighty and majestic, took him."

Al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Jabir, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, his son came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! If you do not come to him, we will continue to be shamed by him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) came to him and found that he had been placed in his grave. He said: 'Why not before you placed him in it?' So he was taken out of his grave, and the Prophet (ﷺ) spat on him from his saliva from his head to his foot, and dressed him in his shirt." An-Nasa'i narrated it. Al-Bukhari and al-Bazzar in his *Musnad* narrated something similar and added: "Then Allah revealed the verse."

Ibn Ishaq added in *al-Maghazi*, with his chain: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not pray over any hypocrite after him until Allah took him, nor did he stand at his grave."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Qatadah, who said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to a funeral, he would ask about the deceased. If good was said of him, he would stand and pray over him. If it was otherwise, he would say to his family: 'Deal with him as you wish,' and he would not pray over him."

**Second:** The Prophet (ﷺ) was prevented from praying over any of them when they died, because the prayer over the dead is supplication, asking forgiveness, and seeking intercession for him, and the disbeliever is not fit for that.

**Third:** Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: In His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾ to the end of the verse, there is a prohibition of praying over the disbeliever and standing at his grave, and that his burial is permissible. Its implication is that praying over a Muslim and burying him is obligatory, and that it is prescribed to stand at his grave, to supplicate for him, and to ask forgiveness for him. End of quote.

Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished burying the deceased, he would stand over him and say: 'Ask forgiveness for your brother, and ask that he be made firm, for he is now being questioned.'" Abu Dawud alone narrated it.

**Fourth:** Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: The apparent meaning of the verse is that it was revealed concerning all the hypocrites. However, there is a report indicating that it was revealed concerning a specific number of them.

Al-Waqidi said: Ma'mar informed us from al-Zuhri, who said: Hudhayfah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'I will confide a secret to you, so do not mention it to anyone. I have been forbidden to pray over so-and-so, a group of hypocrites of a considerable number.'"

He said: Therefore, whenever Umar intended to pray over someone, he would ask Hudhayfah to accompany him. If Hudhayfah walked with him, he would pray over him; otherwise he would not pray over him.

From another route, from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, they were twelve men.

Hudhayfah also said once: "Only one man of them remains." Perhaps the wisdom in specifying those mentioned is that Allah knew they would die in disbelief, unlike others, who repented. End of quote.

Then He, exalted, explained that the continuance of His anger upon them does not contradict His giving them wealth and children, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[85] ﴿And let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the worldly life and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

﴿And let not their wealth or their children impress you﴾: that is, because Allah did not intend by them to bestow favor upon them, which would indicate His approval of them, but rather to take vengeance upon them. He said: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the worldly life﴾, that is, by the hardship in acquiring and preserving them and the grief over them, ﴿and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers﴾, that is, they die as disbelievers, heedless of reflection upon the outcomes.

This verse has already occurred in this surah, with a difference in its wording.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿And let not... impress you﴾ is repeated because the recurrence of the revelation concerning it has a bearing on establishing and emphasizing what it was revealed for, and in wishing that it be in the mind of the addressee, so that he does not forget it or neglect it, and that he believes that acting upon it is important and requires special attention to it, especially when the interval between the two revelations is long, so it resembles the matter that its owner considers important, so he returns to it in the course of his speech and reverts to it. This meaning was repeated only for its strength regarding what one loves to warn against. End of quotation.

Al-Farisi said: It is not for emphasis, because that one is about one people and this one is about others. Their pronunciation differs: here it is "wa la" (ولا) with the waw, due to the suitability of conjoining a prohibition to a prohibition before it in His saying: ﴿And do not pray...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84], etc., so the waw is appropriate; there it is with the fa' (فلا) due to the suitability of sequence following His saying before it: ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], that is, for spending. So they are impressed by the abundance of wealth and children, so He forbade the impressedness that follows it. Here it is: "wa awladuhum" without (lā) before it, because He forbade being impressed by the two together, whereas there it is with the addition of lā, because He forbade each one individually; so the totality of the two verses indicates the prohibition of being impressed by the two together and separately. Here: ﴿that He punish them﴾ (an yu'adhdhibahum); there: (li-yu'adhdhabahum) with the lam of causation and the omission of the object, meaning: Allah only intends to test them with wealth and children; here the intended meaning is punishment, so the object of the intention differs apparently in them. There: ﴿in the life of this world﴾ [al-Tawbah: 55]; here: ﴿in the worldly life﴾ as an alert that their life is as no life in it, and mentioning it after death is fitting, as though they are dead forever. End of quotation.

And His saying, may He be exalted:

(p-3228) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[86-87] ﴿When a surah is sent down, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," the people of wealth among them ask your permission and say, "Leave us; we will be with those who sit back." They were content to be with the women left behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87].

His words, exalted is He:

﴿When a surah is sent down, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," the people of wealth among them ask your permission and say, "Leave us; we will be with those who sit back." They were content to be with the women left behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87] This is a rebuke and a censure of those who stayed behind from jihad and shrank from it, despite having ample means, which is abundance and wealth. It also informs of the evil of their conduct, for they were content with shame and sitting with the *khawalif* (those left behind, i.e., women), who guard the homes. This was because they preferred love of wealth over love of Allah. Because of this, ﴿a seal was set upon their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87], meaning it was sealed over, ﴿so they do not understand﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87], meaning they did not grasp the success and happiness in loving Allah and drawing near to Him through jihad, nor the misery and ruin in staying behind.

Points of benefit:

First: al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by "a surah" in His words ﴿when a surah is sent down﴾ is meant the whole surah, and it is permissible that it means part of it, just as "the Qur'an" and "the Book" apply to the whole and to a part of it. 

It was also said: it is [surat] Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), because it contains the command to believe and to strive. End of quote.

It was also said: what is meant is every surah in which belief and jihad are mentioned.

Al-Shihab said: This is more apt and more beneficial, because their request for permission at the revelation of the verses of Bara'ah is known from what has already passed. It has also been said that *idhā* (when) indicates repetition by the context of the situation, not by its lexical form, and there is an extended discussion of this in its proper place.

(p-3229) Second: He specified "those of means" because they are the ones being blamed, namely those who have financial capacity; and by analogy, physical capacity is understood from this as well.

Third: *al-khawalif* is the plural of *khalifah*, who is a woman left behind from the work of men. The intent is to censure them and to associate them with women, as the poet said:

"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us, and for the women trailing their skirts."

*Khalifah* can also mean one who has no good in him, the *tā'* in it being for transfer to the nominal form. If it is intended here, the meaning is one who has no benefit for jihad.

It takes the plural pattern *fawā'il* in both senses. As for the first, it is obvious. As for the second, it is because its wording is feminine, since *fā'il* is not pluralized as *fawā'il* for male rational beings except anomalously, as in *nawākis*. This was noted by al-Shihab.

Then the Exalted explained what the believers have of good praise and the excellent reward, the opposite of those, with His words, glory be to Him:

(p-3228) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[86-87] ﴿When a surah is sent down, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," the people of wealth among them ask your permission and say, "Leave us; we will be with those who sit back." They were content to be with the women left behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87].

"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us, and for the women trailing their skirts."

Then the Exalted explained what the believers have of good praise and the excellent reward, the opposite of those, with His words, glory be to Him:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[88] ﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives. And those—for them are the good things, and those are the successful.﴾

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives﴾ That is, in the way of Allah, because the love of Allah prevailed over them above their love of wealth and lives. ﴿And those—for them are the good things﴾ That is, the benefits of both abodes: victory and spoils in this world, and Paradise and honor in the Hereafter. ﴿And those are the successful﴾ That is, those who attain what they sought.

(p-3230) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[89] ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾

﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾ That is, the achievement beyond which there is no achievement.

Then, after mentioning the hypocrites of Madinah, He, glorified is He, explained the condition of the hypocrites among the Bedouins by His saying:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[90] ﴿And those with excuses among the Bedouins came to be given leave, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. Those of them who disbelieve will be afflicted with a painful punishment.﴾

﴿And those with excuses among the Bedouins came to be given leave﴾ meaning: to be excused from jihad. They were some of the Bedouin tribes around Madinah. The word ﴿al-mu'adhdhirun (those with excuses)﴾ has two recitations (qira'at), the doubled (tashdid) and the single (takhfif). The doubled form has two interpretations:

The first: from ('adhdhara fi al-amr), meaning he fell short in it, was negligent and did not exert himself, so he fabricated an excuse. Thus his excuse is false.

The second: from (i'tadhara), meaning to offer an excuse. This may be either false or true, and its original form covers both: (mu'tadhirun). The fatha of the ta' was transferred to the 'ayn, the ta' was changed into a dhal, and it was assimilated into it (idgham).

As for the single form, it is from (a'dhara), meaning one who has a valid excuse. In this sense, they are truthful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾ meaning: in their claim of faith. They are the hypocrites among the Bedouins who neither came nor offered an excuse, but sat back out of their indifference toward Allah and His Messenger.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, threatened them with His saying: ﴿Those of them who disbelieve will be afflicted with a painful punishment.﴾ The pronoun in (minhum, of them) either refers to the Bedouins in general, so that "those who disbelieved" are their hypocrites, or it refers to a wider group. Or it refers to those with excuses, since (p-3231) among them are those who offered excuses due to laziness, not disbelief. It is also permitted that the meaning of "those who disbelieve among them" is those who persist in disbelief.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, explained the excuses for which there is no blame on one who stays behind from fighting. He mentioned among them what is inherent in a person and never separates from him, and what is incidental and occurs to him due to an illness that prevented him from going out in the way of Allah, or due to his inability to prepare for war. He began with the first, saying, glorified is He:

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[91] ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the ill, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blame against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾: these are those who are unable, despite being healthy, to fight the enemy and bear hardships, such as the old man, the child, the woman, and the frail. ﴿Nor upon the ill﴾: that is, those who are incapacitated by a condition that befalls them, such as blindness, lameness, and chronic illness. ﴿Nor upon those who find nothing to spend﴾: that is, nor upon the able-bodied and healthy poor, and those unable to spend on the journey and on weapons. ﴿Blame﴾: that is, sin in staying behind. The root meaning of ḥaraj (blame) is constriction, and then it was used for sin, which is what is intended here. ﴿When they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, they perfect their faith and righteous deeds, so they do not spread fear, do not stir up strife, convey goods to the fighters, and attend to the welfare of their households.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no cause for blame against the good-doers﴾ is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) affirming the content of what preceded it. That is: there is no sin upon them, and there is no path to rebuking them. The word min (from) here is extra, for emphasis. The expression "the good-doers" (al-muḥsinīn) is used in place of a pronoun, to indicate that by their sincerity to Allah and His Messenger they are included among the good-doers. Alternatively, it is a reason given for the negation of blame from them: that is, there is no path (blame) against the category of good-doers, and they are among them. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

Al-Shihab said: "There is no path against a good-doer" is a statement functioning as a proverb. It is either general, including those mentioned, or specific to them. Thus ihsān (good-doing) is sincerity to Allah and His Messenger, and the sin negated is the sin of staying behind. It becomes an emphasis of what came before it in the most eloquent manner and most refined composition, and it is from eloquent speech, because its meaning is that there is no path for a rebuker against him, that is, the rebuker does not pass by him, and he may pass through his land, so how far is rebuke from him! So reflect on the eloquence of the Qur'an, as it has been said:

*Blessings upon our past days, when the blamer did not pass through my land.*

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) confirming the content of what was mentioned, pointing out that they still have need of forgiveness, even if their staying behind was due to an excuse. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated.

That is: because a person is never free from some shortcoming, so it cannot be said that He negated sin from them first, so what is the need for forgiveness, which implies sin? This is what al-Shihab stated.

The discussion of the word of Allah Most High:

[92] ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who, when they came to you that you might provide them with mounts, you said: "I cannot find anything to mount you upon." They turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears out of grief that they could not find what they might spend.﴾

﴿Nor is there blame upon those who, when they came to you that you might provide them with mounts⦆ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "the doers of good" (al-muḥsinīn), or with "the weak" (al-ḍuʿafāʾ), meaning: that you might give them a mount (ẓahr) to ride to the jihad with you. ﴿You said﴾, i.e. to them: ﴿"I cannot find anything to mount you upon"﴾, i.e. for the jihad.

The words of Allah Most High, ﴿They turned back﴾, are the response (jawāb) of "when" (idhā), i.e. they left from your presence, ﴿while their eyes overflowed with tears out of grief that they could not find what they might spend﴾, i.e. for the mounts. Those people, although they had the capacity to bear hardships, there is likewise no way (sabīl) against them.

Remarks (tanbīhāt):
