The first: al-Suyuṭī said in (al-Iklīl): regarding the words of Allah Most High, ﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾ [al-Tawba: 91], etc., the lifting of jihad from the weak and the sick, and from one who does not find expenses, nor equipment for jihad, nor a mount. End of quote.

And some of the Zaydīs said: this noble verse establishes the negation of hardship, which is sin, for abandoning jihad due to these excuses, on condition of sincere counsel (naṣīḥah) to Allah and His Messenger, i.e. that one wishes for them what one wishes for oneself.

- from Abū Muslim.

The second: al-Ḥākim said: in the verse there is evidence that sincere counsel in religion is obligatory, and that this includes enjoining good and forbidding evil, testimonies, judgments, legal opinions (fatāwā), and the explanation of proofs.

The third: Ibn al-Faras said: it is inferred from the words of Allah Most High, ﴿There is no way (sabīl) against the doers of good﴾ [al-Tawba: 91], that the slayer of an aggressive beast is not liable for it.

And some of the Zaydīs said: it indicates that the depositary, the guardian (waṣī), and the one who picks up a lost item are not liable for it provided there is no negligence, and that they are not obliged to return it, unlike the borrower (mustaʿīr).

The fourth: the words of Allah Most High, ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who﴾, etc., indicate that one who lacks the means of expense and seeks assistance, if it is not obtained for him, then there is no blame upon him. And there is in it an allusion: if assistance is provided to him by the imam, he is obliged to go out.

The fifth: the verse indicates the permissibility of weeping and of showing grief over missing an act of obedience, even if one is excused.

The sixth: the words of Allah Most High, ﴿their eyes overflowed with tears (tafīḍu min al-damʿ)﴾ are more eloquent than "her tears overflow" (yafīḍu damʿuhā), because the eye is made as though all of it were overflowing tears, and "min" is for specification (bayān), like your saying: "I ransom you from a man." The place of the prepositional phrase is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) — related by al-Zamakhsharī.

The seventh: Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Zayd ibn Thābit who said: "I was writing (Barāʾah), and I had placed the pen behind my ear when He commanded us to fight. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ began looking at what was being revealed to him, when a blind man came and said: 'What about me, O Messenger of Allah, since I am blind?' Then there was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾ [al-Tawba: 91], the verse."

Al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning this verse: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the people to set out fighting with him, and a group of his companions came to him, among them ʿAbd Allah ibn Mughaffal ibn Muqarrin al-Muzanī, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Carry us.' He said to them: 'By Allah! I cannot find anything to carry you upon.' So they turned back weeping, and it grieved them that they should sit out from jihad while not finding expenses or a mount. When Allah saw their eagerness for His love and the love of His Messenger, He revealed their excuse in His Book, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾ [al-Tawba: 91]."

Imam Aḥmad narrated from Jābir who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, there are men whom you left behind in Madinah; you did not cross a valley nor traverse a path except that they shared with you in the reward; sickness held them back." Related also by Muslim.

Then Allah Most High rebuked those who asked permission to remain behind while they were wealthy, with His words:

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[93] ﴿The blame lies only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich. They are content to be with those who stay behind; and Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know.﴾

﴿The blame lies only﴾, that is, with reproach and punishment, ﴿upon those who ask your permission while they are rich﴾, that is, those who are able to obtain the equipment (for jihad). ﴿They are content to be with those who stay behind﴾, that is, with women, children and the rest of the categories of the incapable: they were content with lowliness, baseness, and being counted among those who stay behind.

Al-Mahayimi said: This contentment, just as it is the cause of reproach, is also the cause of punishment, because when it stemmed from their little concern for Allah, Allah became angry with them. ﴿And Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know﴾, that is, what follows from it of religious and worldly calamities; or, they do not know the command of Allah, so they do not believe.

A subtle point:

Al-Shihab said: Know that their saying "lā sabīla ʿalayhi" (there is no way against him) means: there is no blame or reproach, and it has the sense of "no one reproaches him, let alone blames him." When it is followed by (ilā, "to"), as in his saying:

*Alā layta shiʿrī hal ilā Umm Sālim sabīlun? Fa-ammā al-ṣabru ʿanhā fa-lā ṣabru*
(Would that I knew whether there is any way to Umm Salim? As for patience regarding her, there is no patience.)

then it means reaching, as he said:

*Hal min sabīlin ilā khamrin fa-ashrabahā* ∗∗∗ *Am min sabīlin ilā Naṣr ibn Ḥajjāj?*
(Is there any way to wine so that I may drink it, or any way to Naṣr ibn Ḥajjāj?)

and similar. So be attentive to the places where it is used, for it is among the essentials of eloquence. End of quote.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed of what they would confront upon the return from that expedition, by His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 94:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[94] ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say, "Do not make excuses; we will not believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will observe your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

﴿They will make excuses to you when you return﴾ i.e., as a way of blocking the path of blame against them for staying behind. ﴿Say, "Do not make excuses"﴾ i.e., because your lying is evident, since neither poverty nor sickness prevented you, and excuses will not benefit you. ﴿We will not believe you﴾ i.e., we will not accept your words as true.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has already informed us of your news﴾ (p-3236) is a reason for the denial of belief, i.e., He has informed us through revelation of your secrets, your hypocrisy, and your corruption, which contradict belief. ﴿And Allah will observe your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger﴾ i.e., [whether you turn back from disbelief or remain steadfast in it], with a knowledge upon which the recompense depends. ﴿Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ i.e., for recompense for what has appeared from you of deeds. The placement of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun serves to intensify the threat and to show that He, exalted is He, is aware of their secrets and their open affairs, and nothing of their inner thoughts and deeds escapes His knowledge, so He will recompense them according to that.

Al-Nibras says: "By the unseen is meant what is hidden from the servants, or what the servants do not know, or what will be; and by the witnessed is meant what the servants know, or what has been."

﴿He will inform you﴾ i.e., He will tell you ﴿of what you used to do﴾ i.e., in the world, before they are informed of it.

He mentioned it to them as a rebuke.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning of "informing" here is recompense for it, and this word is preferred over the other out of regard for what preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has already informed us﴾ etc., since what is informed of are the reports related to their deeds. It also indicates that they were not knowing in the world the reality of their deeds, and that they only come to know them at that time.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed of what they will use to reinforce their excuses, namely their wicked oaths, by His saying, glorified is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[95] ﴿They will swear to you by Allah, when you return to them, that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed, they are impure (rijs), and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾

﴿They will swear to you by Allah, when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ means: so do not rebuke them or reproach them.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ means: give them what they seek (their request). ﴿Indeed, they are impure (rijs)﴾ is a justification for leaving off reproaching them, meaning that reproach does not benefit them or set them right. Only the hide that has a skin is reproached, whereas the believer is rebuked for a lapse that escapes from him so that the rebuke may purify him by driving him to repentance and seeking forgiveness. But as for these, they are impurities (arjas) for whom there is no path to purifying them. (Conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.)

Al-Shihab said: It means that they are left alone and shunned, as impurity is shunned. They asked for the turning away of forgiveness, so they were given the turning away of abhorrence.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾ are part of the justification. The cause is the impurity of their nature, which cannot be purified, because they are among the people of the Fire. So blame only incites them and does not benefit them. The dog is at its most impure when it has bathed. Or it is a second justification, meaning: the Fire suffices them as reproach and rebuke, so do not burden yourselves with reproaching them.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿as recompense for what they used to earn﴾ may be a verbal noun (maṣdar) and may be a justification (ʿillah).

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[96] ﴿They swear to you, that you may be pleased with them. But if you should be pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people.﴾

﴿They swear to you﴾: this is connected to what preceded it. The omission of the one sworn by is due to its being evident, meaning: they swear by Him, exalted is He. ﴿That you may be pleased with them﴾: that is, by believing in the purity of their inner selves and their sincerity. ﴿But if you should be pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people﴾: in this there is a strong and most emphatic distancing from being pleased with them, for being pleased with those with whom Allah, exalted is He, is not pleased is something that hardly proceeds from a believer.

Then, exalted is He, pointed out that the hypocrites among the Bedouins are more abominable in filth, so one should not be deceived by their oaths, even though revelation does not expose them as liars. So He said:

The discussion of Qur'an 9:97

On His saying, exalted is He:

[97] ﴿The desert Arabs are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

﴿The desert Arabs﴾, namely the people of the badiya (desert, open country), ﴿are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾, i.e., than the people of the settled towns (hadar), because of their harshness, their roughness, and their wildness, and their upbringing far from witnessing the scholars and from knowing the Book and the Sunnah. ﴿And more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger﴾, i.e., and more deserving of ignorance of the limits of the religion and of what Allah has sent down of laws and rulings. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, i.e., He knows the state of every individual of the people of the wabar (tents) and the madar (towns). ﴿All-Wise﴾, i.e., in what He visits upon their evildoers and their good-doers, their erring and their correct, of His punishment and His reward.

Subtleties:

The first: Al-Shihab said: "al-'Arab" is this well-known people in general, and "al-A'rab" are the inhabitants of the desert among them; so the former is more general.

It has also been said: "al-'Arab" are the inhabitants of cities and villages, and "al-A'rab" are the inhabitants of the desert among the Arabs, or their clients; thus the two are distinct, and the singular and plural of each are distinguished by the ya' in both.

The second: What is mentioned in the verse about the likelihood of the desert Arabs' ignorance due to their distance from hearing the laws and their lack of contact with the people of truth, points to a reproach of the inhabitants of the desert. This agrees with what Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever dwells in the desert becomes coarse," and its completion: "Whoever follows game becomes heedless, and whoever goes to the ruler falls into temptation." And his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, coarseness and harshness are among the faddadin (those with loud voices)."

Tha'lab said: "al-Faddadun are the people of the wabar (tents), because of the harshness of their voices, and they are the people of the desert. It is said: Whoever keeps company with the faddadin, gains neither worldly benefit nor religion."

It is derived from al-Fadid, which is raising the voice or its intensity.

Ibn Kathir said: Since harshness and coarseness were among the people of the desert, Allah did not send a Messenger from among them; rather, the mission was from the people of the towns, as He said: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, from among the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109].

When that bedouin presented that gift to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he returned to him many times its value until he was pleased, and said: "I had resolved not to accept a gift except from a Qurashi, or a Thaqafi, or an Ansari, or a Dawsi," because these used to dwell in the towns: Makkah, al-Ta'if, al-Madinah and Yemen, and they are more refined in manners than the desert Arabs, due to the coarseness in the natures of the desert Arabs.

The third: Al-A'mash related from Ibrahim who said: A bedouin sat with Zayd ibn Suhan while he was narrating to his companions, and his hand had been struck on the day of Nahawand. The bedouin said: "By Allah! Your speech pleases me, but your hand troubles me!" Zayd said: "What troubles you about my hand? It is the left one." The bedouin said: "By Allah! I do not know whether they cut off the right or the left?" Zayd ibn Suhan said: "Allah has spoken truly: ﴿The desert Arabs are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger﴾."

Then Allah, exalted is He, pointed to another group of the hypocrites among the desert Arabs, with His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 98:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[98] ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who consider what they spend as a loss, and they await misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the misfortune of evil; and Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

﴿And among the Bedouins are those who consider what they spend as a loss﴾ meaning: they prepare what they expend in the cause of Allah and give it in charity outwardly, as a penalty (gharamah) and a loss, because they spend only out of fear (taqiyyah) of the Muslims and for show (riya'), not for the sake of the Face of Allah, mighty and majestic, nor seeking reward from Him.

Al-gharamah, al-maghram and al-ghurm (with a dammah on the ghayn) all refer to what a person spends of his wealth though it is not obligatory upon him: pure harm and loss.

Al-Raghib said: al-ghurm is what befalls a person in his wealth of harm not caused by any wrongdoing of his own.

﴿and they await misfortunes to befall you﴾ meaning: they wait for the turns of time (dawa'ir al-dahr) to strike you. (Dawa'ir is the plural of da'irah, which is the calamity and affliction that encompasses a person.) So "awaiting the misfortunes" means waiting for calamities, so that the affair of the Muslims may be overturned and changed, and they may be relieved of what they regard as a penalty. ﴿Upon them is the misfortune of evil﴾ is an interjected supplication against them, in the manner of what they await, or a report of the occurrence of what they await for themselves.

Al-Shihab said: al-da'irah is a name for a calamity; in its origin it is a verbal noun, like al-'afiyah and al-kadhibah, or it is an active participle meaning a turning reversal ('aqabah da'irah), and 'uqbah is originally the alternation and rotation of riders.

It is said: for time there are 'uqab, nuwab and duwal, meaning: one time for them and one time against them.

And (al-su') is read with a dammah on the sin, and it means harm, and it is in reality a verbal noun. It is said: sa'tuhu su'an, masa'ah and masa'iyyah. It is also read with a fathah on the sin, and it means corruption and badness, as said by Abu al-Baqa'.

﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ meaning: of what they say when spending that contains no good; ﴿Knowing﴾ meaning: of what they conceal of corrupt matters, among which is their awaiting of misfortunes. In this is a severity of warning that is not hidden.

Then the Exalted praised the sincere believing Bedouins, with His saying, glorified is He:

THE DISCOURSE ON THE INTERPRETATION OF HIS SAYING, EXALTED IS HE:

[99] ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in God and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness (qurubat) to God and as prayers of the Messenger. Unquestionably, it is a means of nearness for them. God will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in God and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to God﴾ — in compliance with His command, in preference to His love, and in severing love for anything other than Him.

﴿Qurubat﴾ is the second object of (yattakhidh, "takes"), and its plural form is considered with regard to its kinds or its individual instances.

Al-Shihab said: al-qurbah (with a dammah) is that by which one draws near to God, and the act of drawing near itself. According to the second meaning, taking it as a means to Him is a figurative attribution in the relation or by way of an implied supposition. (p-3241)

﴿ʿinda Allah﴾ is an attribute of ﴿qurubat﴾, i.e., a circumstantial adverb related to (yattakhidh). ﴿And the prayers of the Messenger﴾, i.e., the cause of his supplications for mercy, which complete his deficiency. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate for those who gave charity with goodness and blessing, and to ask forgiveness for them. From this is his saying (ﷺ): "O God, bless the family of Abu Awfa." ﴿Unquestionably, it is a means of nearness for them﴾ — the pronoun refers to what is spent, and the feminine form is according to the sense of goodness; the indefiniteness is for magnification, i.e., a great means of nearness comprising all kinds of nearness, which God completes through the supplication of the Messenger, and increases beyond its requirement by what He indicated with His saying: ﴿God will admit them into His mercy﴾, i.e., His Paradise.

﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving﴾, who conceals the fault of the one who falls short; ﴿Merciful﴾, who accepts the effort of the one of little means.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably (ala inna hā)﴾ is a testimony from God to the giver of charity regarding the correctness of what he believed, that his spending is means of nearness and prayers, and a confirmation of his hope, in a resumptive construction, together with the two particles of alerting and affirmation, which indicate the firmness and establishment of the matter.

Likewise: ﴿He will admit them﴾, and what the (sin) carries of affirmation of the promise.

How clearly this speech indicates God's pleasure with the charitable, and that charity has a high station with Him when the intention of its owner is purified. Ended.

In the Intisaf: the point in the (sin)'s indication of affirmation is that the meaning of the speech with it is: "I will do such-and-such, even if the matter is delayed," i.e., it must be done. Al-Shihab said: In this there is room for reflection.

When God, exalted is He, had explained the virtue of the believing Bedouins by what preceded, He followed it with an explanation of those who are above them in ranks of virtue and honor, with His saying, glorified is He:

(p-3242) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[100] ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in excellence—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they abide forever. That is the great achievement.﴾

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ means: those who preceded others in emigration (hijrah) and in support (nusrah). It has also been said that the first group refers to those who prayed toward both qiblahs, or those who witnessed Badr, or those who embraced Islam before the Hijrah; and the second group refers to the People of the First Pledge of al-'Aqabah, who were seven men, and the People of the Second Pledge of al-'Aqabah, who were seventy, and those who believed when Abu Zurarah Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr came to them and taught them the Qur'an.

Al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) preferred the first view and said: "The correct view in my opinion is that they are the foremost in emigration and in support. What indicates this is that He mentioned their being foremost, but did not specify in what they were foremost. So the wording remains general, except that He described them as Emigrants and Helpers, so it is necessary to restrict that wording to that by which they became Emigrants and Helpers, namely emigration and support. Therefore the meaning must be: the foremost, the first, in emigration and support, so as to remove the generality from the wording."

He also said: "Moreover, precedence in emigration is a great act of obedience, inasmuch as emigration is a deed that is hard on the self and contrary to natural inclination. Whoever undertakes it first becomes an example for others in this obedience. This strengthens the heart of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and removes loneliness from his mind. Likewise precedence in support: when the Messenger ﷺ came to Madinah, there is no doubt that those who were first to support and serve him attained a great rank."

It is also read as "al-Ansar" in the nominative case, as a conjunction with "the foremost."

﴿And those who followed them in excellence﴾ means: they trod their path in faith and obedience. ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ because emigration is a matter hard on the self, in leaving family and kin.

Support is a noble virtue, (p-3243) because it is the elevation of the Word of Allah and the support of His Messenger and his Companions. Excellence (ihsan) is among the states or stations of those brought near—so said al-Mahayimi.

﴿And they are pleased with Him﴾ for what He granted them of faith and excellence, and the reward and honour He gave them. ﴿And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: this is in exchange for what they left of their homes and families, and in exchange for what they gave the emigrants of their wealth; and for planting in their hearts the gardens of nearness, and making rivers of knowledge flow in their hearts and in the hearts of those who followed them in this emigration, support and excellence—so said al-Mahayimi.

Ibn Kathir read "min tahtiha al-anhar" as in all other places.

﴿Wherein they abide forever﴾ because of their perpetuating this religion by establishing its proofs and founding its principles until the Day of Resurrection, and acting according to its requirements, and choosing the enduring over the perishing. ﴿That is the great achievement﴾, i.e., beyond which there is no achievement.

Notes:

First: In al-Iklil it is said: this verse shows the preference of the one who precedes to Islam and to emigration, and that the foremost among the Companions are better than those who came after them.

Second: It has been said that the intended meaning of "the foremost, the first" is all the Emigrants and Helpers, so "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), indicating their precedence over all others.

It has also been said that it refers to some of them—the earliest Companions—and "min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah). Many have preferred the second view, and they differed in specifying them, as we mentioned earlier, while others held the first view.

It is narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad who said: "One day I said to Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: 'Will you not inform me about the Companions regarding what took place among them, and I will ward off the trials?' He said to me: 'Allah the Exalted has forgiven all of them and made Paradise obligatory for them in His Book, the good doers among them and the wrongdoers among them.'"

I said to him: "'And the foremost, the first...' the verse," so He made Paradise and good pleasure obligatory for all of them, and He stipulated for their followers that they should emulate them in their good deeds and not speak of them except in goodness, not evil.

(p-3244) That is, because of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith."﴾ [al-Hashr: 10]

Third: Al-Shihab said: The mention of the Emigrants before the Helpers is due to their superiority over the Helpers, as was mentioned in the account of the Saqifah. From this is known the excellence of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, over all others, because he was the first to emigrate with the Messenger ﷺ.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[101] ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾

﴿And among those around you﴾ means around your town, which is Madinah. ﴿Of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy﴾

That is: they became accustomed to it (marana) and skilled (mahara) in it. His words, Exalted is His majesty, ﴿You do not know them﴾ are evidence of their proficiency in it and their skill in it, meaning: they conceal themselves from you, despite your high standing in shrewdness and the truthfulness of your insight, because of the extreme care and pretense they show in observing taqiyyah (dissimulation) and in keeping away from positions of suspicion.

Al-Alusi (in al-Intisaf) said: It seems that His words, Exalted is He, ﴿have become adept at hypocrisy﴾ are a preparation for establishing that their state was hidden from him ﷺ, because of their experience in hypocrisy and their keenness for it. End quote.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We know them﴾ confirm what preceded regarding their skill in hypocrisy; that is: none knows them but Allah, and none other than Him is informed of their secret, because of their intense concern with concealing disbelief and displaying sincerity.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾: the exegetes have several views regarding "twice" (p-3245): the display of their hypocrisy and the burning of the Mosque of Harm; or disgrace and the punishment of the grave; or the taking of zakat, since they regard it as pure loss, and the wearing down of their bodies and their exhaustion through empty acts of worship that carry no reward.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: It is, as has reached me concerning them, what befalls them of the affairs of Islam, and what enters upon them of rage at that without any reward; then their punishment in the graves when they go to them; then the great punishment to which they are returned, the punishment of the Hereafter, in which they will abide forever.

Abu al-Su'ud said: Perhaps the repetition of their punishment is due to the disbelief accompanied by hypocrisy, or hypocrisy reinforced by obstinacy in it.

It is also permissible that what is meant by "twice" is merely multiplicity, as in His words: (Return the gaze twice) meaning: again and again, in accordance with His words: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 126].

Note:

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾ do not contradict His words: ﴿And had We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks; and you would surely know them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30], because this falls under the category of discerning them by attributes by which they are known, not that he knew all those around him from among the people of hypocrisy and doubt individually. He knew that among some of those who mixed with him from the people of Madinah there was hypocrisy, even though he saw them morning and evening. The evidence for this in soundness is what Imam Ahmad narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah! They claim that there is no reward for us in Makkah. He said: 'Your rewards will surely reach you, even if you were in the burrow of a fox.'"

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined his head toward me and said: "Indeed among my companions are hypocrites," meaning: they tremble and speak what has no soundness to it.

Ibn Asakir narrated from Abu al-Darda', that "a man called Handhalah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Faith is here, and he pointed with his hand to his tongue; and hypocrisy is here, and he pointed with his hand to his heart; and he did not mention Allah except a little. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O Allah, make for him a tongue that remembers, and a heart that is grateful, grant him my love and the love of those who love me, and turn his affair toward good.' He said: O Messenger of Allah! I had companions among the hypocrites, and I was their leader; shall I not bring them to you? He said: 'Whoever comes to us, we will ask forgiveness for him; and whoever persists in his religion, Allah is more entitled to him; and do not tear the veil over anyone.'" It was also narrated by al-Hakim.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar from Qatadah, concerning this verse, that he said: What is the matter with people who take it upon themselves to know the affairs of people: so-and-so is in Paradise and so-and-so is in Hell? When you ask one of them about himself, he says: "I do not know!" By my life, you know your own share better than you know the states of people, and you have taken upon yourself something that the prophets before you did not take upon themselves! The prophet of Allah Nuh, peace be upon him, said: ﴿He said: And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 112]. And the prophet of Allah Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said: ﴿The remainder from Allah is better for you, if you are believers; and I am not a watcher over you﴾ [Hud: 86]. And Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾.

A subtle point:

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and among the people of Madinah﴾ are conjoined to (among those around you) as a conjunction of a singular to a singular.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿have become adept at hypocrisy﴾ may be a fresh sentence with no place in terms of i'rab, brought to explain their high standing in hypocrisy after explaining their attribution of it; or it may be an attribute of the mentioned subject, separated from it by the conjoined predicate; or it may be an attribute of an omitted subject which takes its place, whose predicate is (from the people of Madinah), and the sentence is conjoined to the preceding sentence, meaning: and from the people of Madinah are a people who have become adept at hypocrisy. (Abu al-Su'ud conveyed this.)

(p-3247) When Exalted Allah explained the state of the hypocrites who stayed behind from the raiders, out of aversion to it, denial and doubt, He explained the state of the sinners who delayed from jihad out of laziness and inclination toward ease, despite their faith and their affirmation of the truth. So He, Exalted is His majesty, said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 102:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[102] ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾ — i.e., they confessed to them, and these sins were their staying behind from the military campaign, preferring ease over it, and being content with the bad company of the hypocrites. That is, they did not offer false excuses for their staying behind as others did. ﴿They had mixed a righteous deed﴾ — such as regret and their previous obedience — ﴿with another that was bad﴾ — such as staying behind from jihad. ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾ — i.e., will accept their repentance. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ — He overlooks the one who repents and bestows His favor upon him.

Notes:

The first: Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went on a campaign, and Abu Lubaba and five others with him stayed behind. Then Abu Lubaba and two men with him reflected, regretted, and were certain of ruin, and said: 'We are in shade and tranquility with the women, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers are in jihad! By Allah, we will tie ourselves to the pillars, and we will not release ourselves until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the one who releases us.' They did so, and three men remained who did not tie themselves. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from his campaign and said: 'Who are these tied to the pillars?' A man said: 'This is Abu Lubaba and companions of his who stayed behind; they pledged to Allah not to release themselves until you are the one who releases them.' He said: 'I will not release them until I am commanded to release them.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾. When it was revealed, he released them and excused them, (p-3248) while the three who had not tied themselves remained, not mentioned for anything; they are those about whom Allah said: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106] — the verse. Some people said: 'They are ruined, since their excuse was not revealed,' while others said: 'Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance,' until He revealed: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118]."

Ibn Jarir related through 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas something similar, and added: "Abu Lubaba and his companions came with their wealth when they were released, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! This is our wealth, so give it in charity on our behalf and seek forgiveness for us.' He said: 'I have not been commanded to take anything from your wealth.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] — the verse."

This portion alone was also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam and others. 'Abd related from Qatada that it was revealed concerning seven: four of them tied themselves to the pillars, namely Abu Lubaba, Mirdas, Aws ibn Khidham and Tha'laba ibn Wadi'a.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mandah in (al-Sahaba) related, through al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir, who said: "Among those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Tabuk were six: Abu Lubaba, Aws ibn Khidham, Tha'laba ibn Wadi'a, Murara ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayya.

Abu Lubaba and Aws ibn Tha'laba came and tied themselves to the pillars and brought their wealth, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah! Take this, which kept us from you.' He said: 'I will not release them until there is fighting,' and the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾ — the verse." Its chain is strong, as stated in (al-Lubab).

Ibn Kathir said: This verse, although it was revealed concerning specific people, is general in its application to all sinners who are wrongdoers yet sincere.

Mujahid said that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba when he told the Banu Qurayza that it was slaughter, and he gestured with his hand to his throat. Then he mentioned what preceded.

(p-3249) The second: al-Bukhari related in his Tafsir concerning this verse, from Samura ibn Jundab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "Two visitors came to me tonight, and they raised me up, and they reached a city built with bricks of gold and bricks of silver. A man met us, half of whom was as beautiful as what you have seen, and half as ugly as what you have seen. They said to them: 'Go and plunge into that river.' They plunged into it, then returned to us, the evil having departed from them, and they became in the most beautiful form. They said to me: 'This is the Garden of Eden, and this is your abode.' They said: 'As for the people who were half beautiful and half ugly, they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad, and Allah overlooked them.'"

The third: al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: each of them has been made mixed, so what is the thing it is mixed with? I say: each of them is mixed and is mixed with, because the meaning is that each of them was mixed with the other, as in your saying: "I mixed the water and the milk," meaning "I mixed each of them with its companion." This contains what is not in your saying "I mixed the water with the milk," because you made the water mixed and the milk mixed with it. And when you say it with the waw, you make the water and the milk both mixed and mixed with both, as if you said: "I mixed the water with the milk and the milk with the water."

Al-Nasir criticized him in (al-Intisaf) and said: The verification of this is that when you say "I mixed the water with the milk," the thing explicitly stated in this sentence is that the water is mixed and the milk is mixed with it; what is indicated by necessary implication, not explicitly, is that the water is mixed with it and the milk is mixed. And when you say "I mixed the water and the milk," the thing explicitly stated is making each of them mixed; as for what each was mixed with, it is not explicitly stated, but rather it is necessarily implied that each of them has something it is mixed with, which may be its companion or other.

So al-Zamakhshari's statement: (p-3250) that your saying "I mixed the water and the milk" conveys what "with the ba'" conveys, plus something more, is not so.

The apparent meaning of the verse — and God knows best — is that the departure from the ba' was only to include in "mixing" the sense of "doing": as if it were said, "they did a righteous deed and another that was bad," and then the sense of mixing was added to the doing, so they were both expressed together by it. End of quotation.

Al-Nihrir said: Al-Zamakhshari means that the waw is like an explicit statement of mixing each with the other, in the same position as when you say "I mixed the water with the milk" and "I mixed the milk with the water," unlike the ba', whose verbal indication is only the mixing of the water, for example, with the milk; as for the mixing of the milk with the water, if it were established, it would only be established by way of implication and rational indication. End of quotation.

This is sound, and there is no need for the aforementioned inclusion.

Then al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that it is from their saying: "I sold the sheep, a sheep and a dirham," meaning "a sheep for a dirham," i.e., the waw is in the sense of the ba'; and Sibawayh related this.

They said: It is a metaphor, because the ba' is for attachment and the waw is for joining, and both are of one valley. Ibn al-Hajib said regarding their saying mentioned: its origin is "a sheep for a dirham," i.e., each sheep for a dirham, and it is a substitute for the sheep, i.e., together with a dirham; then it became frequent, so they replaced the ba' of accompaniment with a waw, so its accusative and its inflection became according to what precedes it, as in their saying: "every man and his property."

Al-Shihab said: This is a strained interpretation, and therefore they said it is an explanation of meaning, not of grammatical inflection. End of quotation.

Al-Wahidi said: The Arabs say: "I mixed the water with the milk," and "I mixed the water and the milk," just as you say "I gathered Zayd and 'Amr." The waw in the verse is better than the ba', because the meaning intended is joining, not the literal mixing; do you not see that a righteous deed does not mix with a bad one as water mixes with milk, but they may be gathered together? End of quotation.

In the verse there is a type of rhetorical device called (al-Ihtibak), which is well known, because the meaning is: they mixed a righteous deed with a bad one, and another bad deed with a righteous one.

(p-3251) The fourth: al-Razi said: Here there is a question, which is that the word (asa, perhaps) expresses doubt, which is impossible with regard to Allah, exalted is He. Its answer comes in several aspects:

The first: the exegetes said: the word "asa" from Allah is binding, and the proof of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], and it was done. The true account of this is that the Qur'an was revealed in accordance with people's customary speech, and a great sovereign, when a needy person asks him for something, does not grant it except by way of hoping, with the word "asa" or "la'alla," to indicate that no one has the right to oblige me to anything or to impose anything upon me; rather, everything I do, I do by way of grace and kindness. So the mention of the word "asa" serves this meaning, along with the fact that it conveys certainty of response.

The second aspect: the intended purpose is to show that the one under obligation must be in a state of hope and apprehension, for that is further from complacency and negligence.

The fifth: al-Qashani said: Acknowledgment of sin is the preservation of the light of readiness, the softness of disposition, and the non-entrenchment of the habit of sin in it, for it possesses the ability to return and repent, and the evidence of seeing the ugliness of sin, which cannot exist except by the light of insight and the opening of the eye of the heart. For if darkness had settled and vice had become firmly rooted, he would not find it ugly nor see it as a sin, but would see it as a good deed, because of its suitability to his state. So when it is recognized that it is a sin, there is good in it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, to take from their wealth which they had brought to him, to give it in charity on their behalf as expiation for their sins, as was mentioned in the narrations earlier, with His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 9, verse 103:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[103] ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them growth, and invoke blessings upon them. Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Take from their wealth﴾, i.e., some of it, ﴿a charity﴾.

Al-Mahayimi said: So that their repentance may be sincere, since ﴿it purifies them﴾, i.e., from the defilements of staying behind with which they had been stained, and from the love of wealth because of which they had stayed behind. ﴿And causes them growth by it﴾, i.e., from all the blameworthy traits that arose from wealth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Tazkiyah (causing growth) is an intensification of purification and an addition to it, or it means growth and blessing in the wealth.

﴿And invoke blessings upon them﴾, i.e., show compassion to them by supplicating for them and having mercy upon them. ﴿Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them﴾, i.e., they calm their souls and reassure their hearts, and they are confident that He, glorified is He, has accepted their repentance.

Qatadah said: sakan means waqar (dignity/tranquility).

Ibn Abbas said: mercy for them. Imam Ahmad narrated from Hudhayfah that "when the Prophet ﷺ supplicated for a man, it would reach him, his child, and his grandchild." In another narration: "Indeed, the prayer of the Prophet ﷺ overtakes the man, his child, and his grandchild."

The clause is a justification for the command to invoke blessings upon them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾, i.e., He hears their acknowledgment of their sins and their supplication. ﴿All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of what is in their hearts of regret and grief for what they had neglected.

Remarks:

First: ﴿tuṭahhiruhum﴾ has been read in the jussive, as an answer to the command, while with the nominative it is read as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of address in ﴿Take﴾, or as an attribute of "charity (ṣadaqah)", and the tā' is for address or for the charity.

The return pronoun in the first case is elided, relying on what follows it, i.e., "by it".

It has been read tuṭhirahum, from aṭhara (as a variant meaning ṭahhara). And wa-tuzakkīhim was not read except with the affirmation of the yā'; it is a predicate of an elided subject, and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the command or in its answer, i.e., "while you purify them by it". This is according to the reading tuṭahhirhum with the jussive.

As for the reading with the nominative, then tuzakkīhim is coordinated with tuṭahhiruhum, as a circumstantial clause or an attribute.

Second: ﴿ṣalātaka﴾ has been read in the singular, and ṣalawātaka in the plural, in consideration of the multiplicity of those for whom the supplication is made.

Al-Shihab said: He made it plural because ṣalāh is a noun of genus, and the singular is for that reason; or because it is originally a verbal noun.

Third: Al-Shihab said: sakan is tranquility (al-sukūn), and that to which one finds rest, of family and homeland. If the intended meaning is the first, then making them themselves a source of rest and reassurance is an intensification, and this is the apparent meaning. If the intended meaning is the second, then it is a metaphor, by likening his supplication, in the seeking of refuge in it, to a dwelling-place. End.

Abu al-Baqa said: sakan here means masknun ilayha (that in which one finds rest), which is why it is not feminine, and it is like qabḍ in the sense of maqbūḍ.

Fourth: It has been said: the command in the verse concerns zakah. And "min" is partitive, and they had wished to give away all their wealth, so God commanded him to take a part of it for their repentance, because zakah was not accepted from some of the hypocrites; thus the verse is connected to what precedes it.

It has also been said: this is not the obligatory charity; rather, when they repented, they gave all their wealth as expiation for the sin they had committed, so God, exalted is He, commanded him to take a part of it, namely a third. This is what was narrated from al-Hasan, and it is the preferred view among them. Al-Razi reported that most jurists hold that this verse is an independent statement intended to make the taking of zakat from the wealthy obligatory, since it is their proof for the obligation of zakah. Then it was objected that taking it to mean what they mentioned requires that the verse not be coherent with what precedes and follows it.

I say: there is no doubt in the verse's connection to what precedes it, as the narration cited above makes clear. The specific occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of its wording, as is the rule in such cases. For this reason, al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, rejected the view of some Arabs who interpreted this verse as meaning that paying zakah is only to be made to the Messenger, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, since he is the one commanded to take it and to invoke blessings upon those who give charity; thus no one else can take his place. He commanded fighting against them, and the Companions agreed with him and fought them until they paid zakah to the Caliph, just as they used to pay it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

From this it is inferred that paying zakah to the Imam is obligatory, and his deputy is like him. These apostate interpreters overlooked that Allah ordained zakah only to fill the need of the destitute, to relieve the distress of the debtor, to free captives, to facilitate the wayfarer, and thereby to remove the resentment of the needy against those who were favored over them in provision, to instill in the hearts of the latter love for the former, and to direct mercy into the souls of these toward those wretched ones. Thus the Imam has no special status in itself; rather, it is because he gathers what comes to him from it and spends it in its stated channels.

Fifth: The words of the Most High ﴿and invoke blessings upon them﴾ have been used as evidence for the recommendation of supplicating for the one who gives charity.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Sunnah for the Imam, when he takes charity, is to supplicate for the giver and say: "May Allah reward you for what you have given, make it a purification for you, and bless for you what you have kept." Others said he should say: "O Allah, bless so-and-so." This is supported by what was narrated "from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who was among the companions of the tree, who said: When people came to the Prophet ﷺ with charity, he would say: 'O Allah, bless them.' Then my father came to him with his charity, and he said: 'O Allah, bless the family of Abi Awfa.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in the two Sahihs.

Ibn Kathir said: In another hadith, "a woman said: O Messenger of Allah! Bless me and my husband. He said: 'May Allah bless you and your husband.'"

I say: By these two hadiths is refuted the claim of one who asserted that the meaning of "invoke blessings upon them" is the prayer for the dead, as related by al-Suyuti in al-Iklil.

Sixth: The verse, like the two hadiths, indicates the permissibility of invoking blessings upon others than the Prophets independently.

Al-Razi said: Al-Ka'bi related in his Tafsir that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was covered: "Upon you be the prayer and peace." Some people denied this.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Invoking blessings is not fitting from anyone upon anyone, except in the case of the Prophet ﷺ."

Then al-Razi said: Indeed our companions prohibit mentioning the blessings of Allah upon anyone other than the Messenger, and the Shi'ah mention it for Ali and his descendants, and they argued that the text of the Qur'an indicates its permissibility regarding those who pay zakah, so how is it prohibited regarding Ali, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may the good pleasure of Allah be upon them? He said: I saw some of them say: Is it not the case that when a man says "Peace be upon you," it is said to him, "And upon you be peace"? This indicates that the use of this phrase is permissible regarding the general body of Muslims, so the family of the Prophet is more deserving. End.

I say: The prohibition of this is a matter of etiquette, not of Sharia law, because it has become, by custom, a special supplication for him ﷺ and his emblem, like a proper name by dominance, so others are not addressed with it except by following him, as a verbal courtesy.

Seventh: Al-Razi said, regarding the secret of his prayer, peace be upon him, being a comfort for them: The soul of Muhammad, peace be upon him, was a strong, radiant, pure, dazzling soul, so when he supplicated for them and mentioned them with goodness, effusions of the power of his spiritual strength overflowed onto their souls, and by this cause their souls were illuminated and their inner secrets were purified.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[104] ﴿Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity, and that it is Allah who is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful?﴾.

﴿Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity, and that it is Allah who is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful?﴾ This is an incitement to repentance and to charity, each of which erases sins, purifies them and annihilates them, and an informing that whoever repents to Him, He accepts his repentance, and whoever gives charity, He accepts it from him.

Remarks:

First: The pronoun in (yaʿlamū) ("they know") refers to those who are forgiven, so the mention of the acceptance of their repentance, although something indicating it has preceded, is for the confirmation of what came before concerning the acceptance of their repentance and the purification and purifying of their charity, for its affirmation, and for settling it in their hearts by explaining that the one who undertakes the acceptance of their repentance and the taking of their charities is Allah, glorified is He, even though the taking, purifying and purifying have been attributed to him, ﷺ.

Abu Muslim said: The purpose of the interrogative is the affirmation within the soul. And it is the habit of the Arabs, in order to make the addressee realize and to remove doubt from him, to say: "Do you not know that the one who taught you is owed your service? Do you not know that the one who did good to you is owed your gratitude?" Thus, Exalted is He, gave good news to these repentant ones of the acceptance of their repentance and their charities. End.

It is also permissible that the pronoun returns to others, namely the hypocrites, so the interrogative is a rebuke and reproach to them for not repenting, and an encouragement to it, and a removal of what they suppose of its non-acceptance. It was also read with the (tāʾ) (i.e., "Do they not know" in the second person).

According to the first reading this is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and according to the second it is with the implied (qul) ("say"). The pronoun may also refer to both the hypocrites and the repentant together, for comprehensiveness and specification.

Second: The pronoun, I mean (huwa), is either for emphasis, or for it together with specification, meaning that He definitely does that, because the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) conveys that, and the present-tense predicate is among its places.

It has been said: The meaning of specification in huwa is that this is not to the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ; rather Allah, glorified is He, is the One who accepts repentance and rejects it, so aim for Him and direct your repentance to Him, because the frequency of their returning to him, ﷺ, is a likely cause of the supposition of that.

Third: The transitive use of acceptance with (ʿan), because it includes the meaning of passing over and pardoning their sins from which they repented. It has been said: (ʿan) here means (min), as one says: "I took this from you and from you (ʿan-ka)."

Fourth: Taking here is a metaphor for acceptance and recompense, because the generous and the great, when they accept something, compensate for it. The attribution to Allah may also be taken as a metonymic (majāz mursal) usage.

It has been said: In the attribution of taking to the Messenger, ﷺ, in His saying: ﴿Take﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], and then to His own Essence, exalted is He, is an indication that the taking of the Messenger, ﷺ, stands in the place of the taking of Allah, in glorification of the status of His Prophet, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

Fifth: The clause: ﴿and that it is Allah who is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ is an emphasis of what it is joined to, and an increase in affirmation of what it affirms, along with an increase in meaning not present in it, as the intensive form conveys the repetition of that from Him, i.e.: "Did they not know that He is the One specified with accepting repentance, and that this is a continuous practice for Him and a constant matter?"

A subtle point:

Ibn Kathir reported from al-Hafiz Ibn ʿAsakir, from Hawshab, who said: The people campaigned in the time of Muʿawiya, and over them was ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and a man from the Muslims embezzled one hundred Roman dinars. When the army returned, he regretted it and came to the commander, but he refused to accept it from him, and said: "The people have dispersed, and I will not accept it from you until you bring it to Allah on the Day of Resurrection." So the man began going to the Companions, and they would say to him the like of that.

When he arrived at Damascus, he went to Muʿawiya to have him accept it, but he refused him. He left his presence weeping and reciting "Indeed we belong to Allah." He passed by ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Shaʿir al-Saksaki, who said to him: "What makes you weep?" So he told him his matter. He said to him: "Are you one of my followers?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Go to Muʿawiya and say to him: 'Accept from me your fifth, and give him twenty dinars, and look at the remaining eighty, and give them in charity on behalf of that army, for indeed Allah accepts repentance from His servants, and He knows best their names and their places.'" So the man did so.

Muʿawiya said: "That I had issued a legal ruling on it would be dearer to me than everything I own. The man has done well." End.

In this narration is the affirmation of a son for Khalid, and in my estimation the author of "Usd al-Ghaba" mentioned that he did not leave offspring, so let this be verified.

And His saying, exalted is He:

The discourse of Allah the Exalted:

[105] ﴿And say: "Work, for Allah will see your work, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

﴿And say﴾, i.e., to the people of repentance, purification and prayer: do not rest content with these alone, but rather ﴿work﴾ all that you are commanded to do. ﴿Allah will see your work﴾, i.e., He will increase you in nearness upon nearness. ﴿And His Messenger﴾ will increase you in prayers [for you]. ﴿And the believers﴾ will follow you, so their reward will accrue to you without any of their rewards being diminished in the least. This is what al-Mahayimi said, and it is strong in its connection.

Abu Muslim said: The believers are witnesses of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and the verse. Witnessing is not valid except after seeing. So Allah mentioned that the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers see their deeds, and it is an alert that they will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection, in the presence of the first and the last, that they are the people of truthfulness, rectitude, chastity and right guidance.

It is reported from Mujahid that the verse is a warning to those who oppose His commands, that their deeds will be presented to Him, blessed and exalted is He, and to the Messenger and the believers.

Ibn Kathir said: This is certainly going to happen on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On that Day you will be exposed; not a thing of yours will be concealed﴾ [al-Haqqah: 18], and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Day when the secrets will be examined﴾ [al-Tariq: 9], and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what is in the breasts will be made known﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 10]. Allah the Exalted has already shown this to people in this world, as Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If one of you were to work inside a solid rock that has no door and no window, Allah would bring forth his deed to the people, whoever he may be."

It is also reported that the deeds of the living are presented to the dead among their relatives and kinsfolk in the barzakh, as in the Musnad of Ahmad and al-Tayalisi.

﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, i.e., by death, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, i.e., by recompensing you for it.

Abu al-Su'ud said: Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun (since he did not say: "to Him") is, in terms of instilling awe and cultivating reverence, a matter that is not hidden. As for the reason for mentioning "the unseen" first, it is the vastness of His knowledge and the greater weight it carries over the witnessed, which needs no explanation.

From Ibn 'Abbas: "The unseen" is what they conceal of deeds, and "the witnessed" is what they display, like His saying: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 77]. So the precedence in that case is to establish that the relation of His all-encompassing knowledge to the secret and the public is one and the same; and it is the most eloquent and emphatic way. Or it is to announce that the rank of the secret precedes the rank of the public, for there is nothing that is made public except that it, or its near or distant beginnings, was previously latent in the heart. Thus the connection of His knowledge, exalted is He, to it in its first state precedes its connection to it in its second state.

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[106] ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command; either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness. And Allah is Knowing, Wise.﴾

﴿And others﴾ means: among those who stayed behind. ﴿Deferred until Allah's command﴾ means: their matter is postponed, awaiting His judgment concerning them, because their state is suspended between two outcomes. ﴿Either He will punish them﴾ for their staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk.

﴿Or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, that is, He will overlook them. ﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾, that is, of their conditions. ﴿Wise﴾, that is, in what He decides concerning them.

Points of note:

First: In the Seven Readings, it is read (mur'jawna) with a dammah on the hamza followed by a silent waw, and it is read (murjawna) without a hamza. Likewise (turji man tasha') is read with both forms, and they are two dialects: one says arja'tuhu and arjaytuhu, like a'taytuhu. It is possible that the ya' is a substitute for the hamza, as in their saying qara'tu and qaraytu, and tawaddha'tu and tawaddaytu, which is frequent in their speech.

On the basis that it is an original dialect form, it is from the ya' root. It has also been said that it is from the waw root, as stated in (al-'Inayah).

Second: It has been narrated from al-Hasan that this verse refers to a group of the hypocrites. Likewise al-Asamm said: they are hypocrites whom Allah deferred, and He did not inform about them what He knew of them, and He warned them with this verse, that if they did not repent, He would send down concerning them a Qur'an, so He said: ﴿either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and others besides them: they are the three who were left behind, that is, left behind from repentance, namely Murarah ibn al-Rabi', Ka'b ibn Malik and Hilal ibn Umayya. They sat out the expedition of Tabuk among those who sat out, out of laziness and inclination toward ease, pleasant fruits and shade, not from doubt or hypocrisy. Among them there was a group who tied themselves to the pillars, as Abu Lubaba and his companions did, and a group who did not do so, and these were the three. The repentance of those others was revealed before theirs, and these were deferred from repentance until the following verse was revealed, which is His words: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117] to His words: ﴿and to the three who were left behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118].

Al-'Inayah says: The anger against them was intensified despite their sincerity, while jihad is a collective obligation (fard kifayah), because it has been said that it was an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) specifically upon the Helpers, since they had given the pledge to the Prophet (ﷺ) for it.

Do you not see the words of their rajaz-poet at the Trench:

We are those who pledged to Muhammad, to strive while we remain forever.

These were among the most eminent of them, so their staying behind was a grave matter.

Third: The "either" (ʼimmā) in the verse is either for uncertainty with respect to the addressee, or for ambiguity with respect to Him as well, meaning that Exalted is He left their matter ambiguous to the addressees.

The meaning: let their matter be with you between hope and fear. The intent is to commit that matter to His will and His decree. Or it is for enumeration, meaning their matter revolves between these two outcomes.

And His words, exalted is He:

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[107] ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and to cause division among the believers and as a station of observation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before, and they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good." And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars.﴾

﴿And those who⁠﴾ means: and among the hypocrites are those who ﴿took﴾, i.e., built, ﴿a mosque for harm﴾, i.e., causing harm to the people of the Mosque of Quba' ﴿and disbelief﴾, i.e., strengthening the disbelief which they harbour ﴿and to cause division among the believers﴾, i.e., those who used to gather at the Mosque of Quba' in one assembly, performing the most noble of deeds, which is the prayer, intended to strengthen Islam by uniting the hearts of its people upon good works and removing discord among them. ﴿And as a station of observation⁠﴾ means: preparation, lying in wait, and expectation.

﴿for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before⁠﴾ means: those who had disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger previously, and he is Abu 'Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named "the Wicked." They had prepared it for him so that he might pray in it and gain ascendancy over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as we shall explain in detail.

﴿And they will surely swear⁠﴾ means: after the manifestation of their evil intentions and aims ﴿"We intended nothing but good"⁠﴾ means: we intended, by building the mosque, nothing but the good purpose, or the good aim, which is prayer, the remembrance of Allah, and providing space for those who pray. ﴿And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars⁠﴾ means: in their oath.

(p-3262) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[108] ﴿Never stand therein. A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand therein. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾

﴿Never stand therein﴾, i.e., do not pray in the mosque of discord, ﴿ever﴾, i.e., at any time, because it is a place of the wrath of Allah; for this reason he was commanded to demolish it and burn it, as will come. The application of the term "standing" (qa'im) to one who prays and one who performs the night vigil (mutahajjid) is well known, as in their saying: "So-and-so stands the night," and in the hadith: "Whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward..."

﴿A mosque founded on piety﴾, i.e., whose foundations were laid upon the obedience and remembrance of Allah, and the intention to guard oneself from the disobedience of Allah, by performing the prayer which forbids indecency and wrongdoing; and it is the Mosque of Quba. ﴿From the first day﴾, i.e., from the days of its existence, ﴿is more worthy that you stand﴾, i.e., that you pray, ﴿therein. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾, i.e., those who go to great lengths in outward and inward purity.

Then he pointed to the excellence of the Mosque of Piety over the Mosque of Harm with his saying:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[109] ﴿Is one who founded his building upon piety from Allah and approval better, or one who founded his building upon the edge of a crumbling embankment about to collapse, so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿Is one who founded his building upon piety from Allah﴾, i.e., fear of Him, ﴿and approval﴾, i.e., seeking His approval, ﴿better, or one who founded his building upon the edge﴾, i.e., the brink of ﴿a crumbling embankment﴾ — (jurf) with the ra vowelled with a damma or with a sukun — i.e., a precipice, ﴿about to collapse﴾, i.e., on the verge of falling, ﴿so that it collapsed with him﴾, i.e., fell along with him, ﴿into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[110] ﴿Their building which they built will never cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

﴿Their building which they built will never cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾: that is, the demolition of it will remain a cause of doubt and hypocrisy, increasing their existing doubt and hypocrisy. Its mark will not leave their hearts, and its effect will not vanish. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: that is, into fragments, and their parts are scattered. Then they will forget it.

As long as their hearts are whole and intact, the doubt remains lodged within them firmly. So the mention of "cutting" may be a figurative depiction of the state of the doubt's removal from them. It may also be intended literally: their hearts being torn apart and shredded by death or by the punishment of the Fire.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "unless they repent with a repentance by which their hearts are cut to pieces out of remorse and grief over their negligence." ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾: that is, of their intentions. ﴿All-Wise﴾: that is, in commanding the demolition of their building, to protect the Muslims from their wicked aims.

**Notes:**

**First:** al-Zamakhshari said: In the codices of the people of Madina and Syria, the reading is ﴿alladhina attakhadhu﴾ without a waw (و), because it is a separate story in itself. In the rest of the codices it is with the waw, joining it by conjunction to the story of the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-dirar), which the hypocrites founded, to the rest of their stories.

**Second:** The occasion of revelation of these verses: "There was in Madina, before the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there, a man from the Khazraj tribe called Abu 'Amir al-Rahib. He had become a Christian in the pre-Islamic period, had studied the knowledge of the People of the Book, and was known for worship in the pre-Islamic period. He had great honour among the Khazraj.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madina as an emigrant, the Muslims gathered around him, and the word of Islam became supreme, and Allah granted them victory on the day of Badr, the accursed Abu 'Amir choked on his saliva, openly declared enmity, and supported it. He fled to the disbelievers of Makka, conspiring with them against the Prophet (ﷺ). They gathered together with those who agreed with them from the tribes of the Arabs, and they came in the year of (Uhud). At the beginning of the battle, Abu 'Amir went to his people among the Ansar and addressed them, seeking to win them over to his support and agreement.

When they recognised his speech they said: "May Allah not grant you comfort, O sinner! O enemy of Allah!" They attacked him and abused him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had called him to Allah before his flight and recited the Qur'an to him, but he refused to accept Islam and was defiant.

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed against him that he would die far away, an outcast, and this supplication befell him. That is because when the people finished with (Uhud), and he saw the affair of the Messenger (ﷺ) rising and prevailing, he went to Heraclius, king of the Romans, seeking his help against the Messenger of Allah. Heraclius promised and encouraged him, and he stayed with him. He wrote to a group of his people among the Ansar, from the people of hypocrisy and doubt, promising and encouraging them that he would soon come with an army to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), defeat him, and turn him away from what he was upon. He had instructed them to take for him a stronghold and a place of observation for when he came to them afterwards. So they began building a mosque adjoining the Mosque of Quba. They built it, made it firm, and finished it, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was preparing for Tabuk.

They came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! We have built a mosque for the sick, the needy, the night of rain, and the cold night. We would love for you to come to us and pray for us in it.'

He said: 'I am on the point of a journey and in a state of preoccupation. If we return, God willing, we will come to you and pray for you in it.'

When he halted at Dhu Awan, a place an hour's distance from Madina, the news of the mosque reached him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Malik ibn al-Dukhshum and Ma'n ibn 'Adi, or his brother 'Amir, and said: 'Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it.'

They set out quickly until they reached Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, who were the kinsmen of Malik ibn al-Dukhshum. Malik said to Ma'n: 'Wait for me until I go out to you with a fire from my family.' He entered his household, took palm fronds, lit a fire in them, then they both set off running until they entered the mosque, while its people were in it. They burned it and demolished it, and the people dispersed from it, and what was revealed about them was revealed." This was mentioned by Ibn Kathir, who traced its parts back to Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Mardawayh.

(p-3265) It is also narrated that the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba, came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) during his caliphate, and asked him to permit Mujammi' ibn Jariya to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said: "No, and a delight to the eye! Is he not the imam of the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said: "O Commander of the Faithful! Do not hasten against me. By Allah, I prayed in it while I did not know what they had concealed in it. Had I known, I would not have prayed with them in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were elderly men who did not recite, so I led them in prayer, and I did not think except that they were seeking nearness to Allah, and I did not know what was in their souls." 'Umar accepted his excuse, believed him, and ordered him to pray in the Mosque of Quba.

**Third:** What we have mentioned, that the mosque in the verse is the Mosque of Quba, is because the context is about it, and the explanation of the rightfulness of praying in it comes from this, since it was founded upon obedience to Allah and obedience to His Messenger, and unifying the word of the believers.

Because the verse implies encouragement to maintain prayer in it, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to visit it on foot and on riding, and would pray two rak'at in it, as in the Sahih.

It is narrated from 'Uwaym ibn Sa'ida al-Ansari that "the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them at the Mosque of Quba and said: 'Allah, Exalted is He, has praised you well for purity in the story of your mosque. What is this purity by which you purify yourselves?' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah! No man or woman among us emerges from the toilet except that he washes his private part or his buttocks with water.'" Narrated by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tabarani, and the wording is his.

It is also narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the mosque founded upon piety, and he said: 'It is his mosque (the Prophet's mosque).'" Narrated by Imam Ahmad and Muslim.

(p-3266) Ibn Kathir said: There is no contradiction, for if the Mosque of Quba was founded upon piety from the first day, then the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is so by even greater and more fitting right. End of quote.

Its meaning returns to this: although this description applies to both of them, the more fitting of the two, afterwards, is the Prophet's Mosque. That is, the hadith is not given in the context of specifying what is in the verse, but in explaining which is most rightly described by this description now.

Al-Suhrawardi said: Each of them is intended, because each of them was founded upon piety from the first day of its founding.

The secret of the Prophet's (ﷺ) answering the question about that is to dispel what the questioner imagined, namely that it applied exclusively to the Mosque of Quba, and to draw attention to the distinction of this one over that one.

**Fourth:** al-Suhayli, may Allah illuminate his resting place, said: From the jurisprudence in the verse, meaning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from the first day﴾ [al-Tawba: 108], is the validity of what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, agreed upon along with 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he consulted them about the calendar. Their opinion agreed that it should be from the year of the Hijra, because that was the time when Islam became mighty, the period in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was secure, mosques were built, and Allah was worshipped as it is required. Their opinion agreed with the apparent meaning of the revelation, and we now understand from their action that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from the first day﴾ [al-Tawba: 108] means that day is the first day of the calendar by which dates are now recorded.

If the Companions derived it from this verse, then that is what is to be thought of them, since they were the most knowledgeable of people regarding the interpretation of the Book of Allah and the most perceptive of what is in the Qur'an of allusions. If it was by way of their opinion and effort, then Allah knew it and indicated its correctness before they acted, since it cannot be understood that someone says: "I did it on the first day" except with reference to a known year, or a known month, or a known date.

Here, in meaning, there is no reference except to this known date, since there are no indicators pointing to any other, neither a verbal nor a situational indicator. So reflect on it. In it is a lesson for whoever takes heed, and knowledge for whoever sees with the eye of the heart and perceives insight.

**Fifth:** (al-ta'sis, founding) is laying the foundation, which is the root of the building and its beginning, and by it it is made firm. So in (p-3267) the verse, piety and divine pleasure are likened, in an implicit metaphorical comparison (tashbih makni, hidden in the soul), to that upon which the root of a building relies.

As for ﴿he founded his building﴾ [al-Tawba: 109], it is an imaginative image (takhyil), used in its literal sense, or it is a figurative usage (majaz) based on its permissibility. So the founding of the building means the firming of the affairs of his religion, or it is an analogy (tamthil) for the state of one who is sincere to Allah and does righteous deeds, in the state of one who built a firm, established building in which he dwells and seeks shelter.
