Or, "the building" is an original metaphor (isti'ara asliyya), and "founding" is a nurturing metaphor (tarshih) or a subsidiary metaphor (tab'iyya). And "al-shafa" means the edge and the brink.

"Jurf al-wadi" is the side of the valley whose base is undermined by water, and which the torrents wash away, so it remains weakened.

"Al-har" is the crumbling, meaning the cracked thing that is on the verge of collapse and falling. It has been said: it is metathesized (maqlub), and its original form is (hawir) or (hayir). It has also been said: its middle letter was dropped arbitrarily, so its pattern is (fal). Its i'rab (grammatical inflection) follows its final letter, like (bab). It has also been said: there is neither metathesis nor deletion in it, and its original pattern is (fa'il) with a kasra on the middle letter, like (katif), and it is (hawira) or (hayira), meaning fallen or overlooking the fall.

The subject of (fa-nhara), either is the pronoun of the building, and the pronoun in (bihi) refers to what was founded, meaning the building of the builder fell with what was upon it. Or it refers to (al-shafa), and the pronoun in (bihi) refers to the building.

In terms of antithesis, the apparent sense would be: "Is he who founded his building upon error, falsehood, and anger from Allah better?" For this reason al-Kashshaf said: The meaning is: "Is he who founded the building of his religion upon a firm, strong foundation, which is the truth that is the piety of Allah and His pleasure, better, or he who founded it upon a foundation that is the weakest and most loosely held of foundations, and the least lasting, which is (falsehood and hypocrisy), whose parable is the parable of the brink of a crumbling precipice in its lack of stability and holding?"

(Shafa al-jurf) is placed in opposition to piety, because it is made a figurative usage for what contradicts (piety). That is, he likened falsehood to the brink of a crumbling precipice in lack of stability, so it is borrowed for falsehood by the indicator of its being set against piety, and piety is truth, and what contradicts truth is falsehood.

His saying ﴿fa-nhara﴾ [al-Tawba: 109] is a nurturing metaphor (tarshih). Its (ba') is for transitivity, or for accompaniment. ﴿So the brink of a crumbling precipice﴾ is an explicit, actual metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya tahqiqiyya), and the antithesis is in terms of the figurative meaning intended from it.

If you say: why did he vary between the two, giving the first in the manner of allusion (kinaya) and imagery (takhyil), and the second in the manner of metaphor (isti'ara) and analogy (tamthil)?

I say: Variety in the manner is observance of the right of eloquence, and a deviation from the apparent, for the sake of exaggeration at both extremes. He made those (the pious) founded upon piety and divine pleasure, which is greater than every reward, while the state of these (the hypocrites) is one of corruption that brought them to the most severe punishment and torment. Had he expressed it according to the apparent requirement, it would not have conveyed what it conveys of awe.

Our statement "(fa-nhara) is a nurturing metaphor" was clarified by al-Kashshaf with his saying: Why was the crumbling brink made a figurative expression of part of it for falsehood? It was said: ﴿so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawba: 109], meaning: falsehood fell with him into the fire of Hell. However, he nurtured the metaphor, so the word "collapse" was used, which belongs to the brink, and to depict that the one who acts in falsehood is as if he founded a building on the brink of a precipice of the valleys of Hell, and that precipice collapsed with it, so he plunged to its bottom.

**Sixth:** The verse indicates that every mosque built on the same basis as the Mosque of Harm has no legal standing and no sanctity, and it is not valid to make an endowment (waqf) for it.

Al-Radi billah burned many mosques of the Batiniyya, the Mushabbiha, and the Mujbira, and their minbars. Some of the commentators transmitted this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been said that every mosque built out of boasting, or showing off and seeking reputation, or for a purpose other than seeking the face of Allah, or with wealth that is not lawful, then it is attached to the Mosque of Harm.

And from Shaqiq: he did not catch the prayer in the mosque of Banu Amir. It was said to him, "The mosque of Banu Fulan has not yet been prayed in." He said, "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built on harm. Every mosque that was built on harm, or for show and reputation, its origin leads back to the mosque that was built for harm."

And from Ata': When Allah the Exalted opened the cities through the hand of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, he commanded the Muslims to build mosques, and not to take two mosques in one city, one of which would harm the other. End of quotation.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Zad al-Ma'ad*, on the lessons of the Battle of Tabuk:

Among them is burning the places of disobedience where Allah and His Messenger are disobeyed, and demolishing them, just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ burned the Mosque of Harm and commanded its demolition. It was a mosque in which prayer was performed and the name of Allah was mentioned, but because its construction was for harm, for dividing the believers, and as a refuge for the hypocrites, and every place of this kind, it is obligatory upon the imam to render it inoperative, either by demolishing it or burning it, or by changing its form and removing it from the purpose for which it was established. (p-3269)

If this is the status of the Mosque of Harm, then the shrines of polytheism, whose custodians call those within them to take rivals beside Allah, are more deserving of this and more obligatory to remove. Likewise are the places of sin and wickedness, such as taverns, the houses of wine-sellers, and the masters of evil deeds.

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, burned an entire village in which wine was sold. He burned the shop of Ruwayshid al-Thaqafi and named it "Fuwaysiq" (the little wicked one). He also burned the palace of Sa'd when he secluded himself from the subjects. End of quotation.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to burn the houses of those who abandoned attendance at the congregation and Friday prayer, but what prevented him was the presence in them of women and children, for whom these obligations do not apply, as he himself reported. End of quotation.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: Among them is that an endowment (waqf) is not valid for anything other than righteousness or devotion, just as the endowment of this mosque was not valid.

On this basis, the mosque is to be demolished if it was built over a grave, just as the deceased is exhumed if buried in a mosque. Imam Ahmad and others explicitly stated this. Thus, in the religion of Islam, a mosque and a grave cannot coexist. Rather, whichever of the two comes after the other is prohibited, and the ruling is for the earlier one. If both were placed together at the same time, it would not be permissible.

This endowment is not valid, nor permissible, and prayer in this mosque is not valid, because of the Prophet ﷺ's prohibition of that and his curse upon whoever takes graves as mosques or lights lamps over them.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: This is the religion of Islam with which His Messenger and Prophet was sent, and its strangeness among people is as you see. End of quotation.

Seventh: Some Yemeni exegetes said: The verse indicates the virtue of a mosque described with this attribute, meaning one founded upon righteousness. It also indicates that the intention of seeking closeness to Allah is a condition in building up the mosque, because (p-3270) intention is what distinguishes actions.

It also indicates that it is not permissible to increase the numbers of the disbelievers. This was mentioned by al-Hakim, because He the Exalted said: ﴿Never stand in it﴾ [At-Tawbah: 108], and by "standing" He meant prayer.

Eighth: Ibn Kathir said: The verse is evidence for the recommendation of praying in the ancient mosques founded from the first day of their construction on the worship of Allah alone, with no partner, and for the recommendation of praying in congregation with righteous people and devoted worshippers who are careful to perfect ablution and to keep themselves free from contact with filth.

Imam Ahmad narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ led them in the dawn prayer, and recited *ar-Rum* but became confused. When he finished, he said: "It confuses the Qur'an for us. Some of you pray with us but do not perform ablution well. Whoever attends the prayer with us, let him perform ablution well." This indicates that perfecting purity facilitates standing in worship, helps complete and perfect it, and carry out its prescribed acts.

Ninth: Abu al-Aliyah and al-A'mash held that what is meant by purity in the verse is purity from sins, repentance from them, and purification from polytheism.

Al-Razi said: This view is definite, because purification from sins and transgressions is what has an effect on nearness to Allah the Exalted, and on deserving His reward and praise. Also, He the Exalted described the people of the Mosque of Harm by harming the Muslims, disbelieving in Allah, and dividing the Muslims. Therefore, these people must be the opposite of those attributes, and that is nothing other than their being free of disbelief and sins. End of quotation.

Remarks: The claim that this view is definite is not accepted, for the word encompasses both the inner and outer purity. Rather, the second [meaning] is what was narrated by the authors of the Sunan, Imam Ahmad, and Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahih, that the Prophet ﷺ said to the people of Quba: "Allah has praised you for your purity; what do you do?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water."

Al-Bazzar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse concerns the people of Quba. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them, and they said: 'We follow the stones with water.'"

If this is authentic, then the meaning of the verse is that it urges the aforementioned purity and praises it. That the people of Harm have the opposite of those attributes can be inferred from the generality of this, and from His saying the Exalted: ﴿A mosque founded upon righteousness from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾ [At-Tawbah: 108].

Tenth: al-Qashani said: Since the world of dominion (*'alam al-mulk*) is under the subjugation and control of the world of the dominion of the unseen (*'alam al-malakut*), it follows that the intentions and states of souls have an effect on the actions they perform. Whatever is done with a sincere intention for Allah the Exalted, from a luminous state, is accompanied by blessing, goodness, unity, and clarity. Whatever is done with a corrupt, satanic intention, from a dark state, is accompanied by division, turbidity, loss of blessing, and misfortune.

Do you not see how the Ka'bah was honored, exalted, and made blessed because it was built by the hands of one of the prophets of Allah, with a sincere intention, a noble and pure soul, and complete sincerity to Allah the Exalted? We witness the effect of this in people's deeds, and we find the effect of clarity and unity in some places and regions, and turbidity and division in others.

This is nothing but that. For this reason He said: ﴿A mosque founded upon righteousness from the first day﴾ [At-Tawbah: 108], because bodily states influence souls, just as psychic states influence bodies. When the place of standing is built upon righteousness and purity of soul, the soul is affected by the gathering of resolve, the purity of time, the goodness of state, and the taste of spiritual experience. When it is built upon show and harm, it is affected by turbidity, division, and constriction.

It also indicates that the purity of the builder's soul and the sincerity of his intention have an effect on the building, and that the blessing of a place, and its being built upon goodness, requires that people of goodness and righteousness be in it, those whose state is fitting to the state of its builder. It also indicates that Allah's love is due to the people of purity, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ [At-Tawbah: 108].

Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth, in return for which they shall have Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. (That is) a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an. And who fulfils his covenant better than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made, and that is the great triumph.

When Allah the Exalted guided the believers to faith, while souls are tempted by love of wealth and of their own selves, He, out of His abundant care for them, lifted them from the station of loving wealth and selves through a profitable trade and a desirable transaction. He made Paradise the price of their wealth and their selves, and so offered them something better than what had been taken from them.

The verse is therefore an exhortation to jihad, by explaining its excellence, following the explanation of the state of those who stayed behind from it.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The matter has been emphasised in a manner that admits no further increase, in that He expressed His acceptance from the believers of their selves and their wealth which they expended in His cause, and His rewarding them with Paradise in exchange for them, by means of purchase, through the method of the subsequent metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya). Then He made the object sold, which is the essential and the aim in the contract, the selves and wealth of the believers. The price, which is the means in the transaction, is Paradise. He did not reverse the matter by saying that Allah sold Paradise to the believers in exchange for their selves and wealth, so as to show that the aim of the contract is Paradise, and that what the believers expended in return for it, of selves and wealth, is a means to it, signifying the perfection of care bestowed upon them and their wealth.

Then He did not say "for Paradise," but rather ﴿that for them is Paradise﴾, as an emphasis on the certainty of the price reaching them and its being exclusively theirs. It is as if it had been said: "for Paradise which is established for them and specific to them."

(In al-Kashshaf and al-Inaya) it is said: You will not see an exhortation to jihad more excellent or more eloquent than this verse, because it presents it in the form of a contract whose contracting party is the Lord of Might, whose price is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to a human heart. He did not make the object of the contract merely their being killed, but also their fighting, for the elevation of His word and the victory of His religion. He also made it recorded in the heavenly books, and what a document that is. He made His promise true, and none is more faithful in promise than Him, so His deferred payment is stronger than the immediate payment of others. He indicated the profit and the great triumph in it. This is an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), depicting the jihad of the believers and their expending of their wealth and selves in it, and Allah's rewarding them for that with Paradise, through buying and selling. He then introduced His words ﴿they fight﴾ and so on, as an explanation of the place of delivery, which is the battlefield. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this when he said: "Paradise is under the shade of the swords," and then He confirmed it with His words: ﴿And that is the great triumph﴾.

Because of the eloquence and subtle appropriateness to the context in this, the commentators did not turn to making the word "purchased" alone a metaphor for "exchange," although they mention it in other places, because His words ﴿so rejoice in your bargain﴾ require that there be a purchase and a sale, and this can only be by way of imagery.

Among them is one who permitted that the meaning of ﴿He has purchased from the believers their selves﴾ is by spending them in righteous deeds, and "their wealth" by expending it in them. His words ﴿they fight﴾ were made a new (independent) clause to mention some of what the statement encompasses, out of concern for it. End of quotation.

His words ﴿a promise binding upon Him﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar) emphasising what is indicated by the price being deferred. Mentioning that it is in the Torah and what is conjoined to it is an affirmation of it, and an information that it was revealed to the messengers in the great books.

In this is the indication that the legislation of jihad and its reward is established in the law of those before us. What remains in the existing Torah and Gospel, despite their distortion, contains what points to jihad and urges it, and whoever refuted the People of the Book who claim that jihad is a distinctive feature of Islam has transmitted it from them. Consult the books circulated on that subject.

Then Allah the Exalted described the believers from whom He purchased their selves and wealth, with His words:

(p-٣٢٧٤) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
[112] ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the wanderers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and those who keep the limits of God. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾

﴿The repentant﴾: that is, those who repent from sins. It is in the nominative as a form of praise, meaning: they are the repentant. This is shown by the reading "al-tā'ibīna" (the repentant, in the accusative/genitive form) with the yā', down to His words, and "al-ḥāfiẓīna" (those who keep) in the accusative as a form of praise, or in the genitive as an attribute of "the believers."

It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is what follows it, meaning: the repentant from sins in truth, who combine these qualities. ﴿The worshippers﴾: that is, those who worship God alone, sincerely devote worship to Him, and are eager for it. ﴿The praisers﴾ of God for His blessings, or for what befalls them of ease and hardship. ﴿The wanderers﴾: that is, the fasting ones, or those who travel the earth in contemplation and reflection. We shall draw attention to this. ﴿The bowers, the prostrators﴾: that is, those who pray. ﴿Those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and those who keep the limits of God﴾: that is, in what He has made lawful and unlawful. ﴿So give good tidings to the believers﴾ who are described by the aforementioned attributes.

The word "the believers" has been placed in the position of their pronoun, to draw attention to the fact that the essence of the matter is faith, and that the complete believer is one who is like this. The object of the good tidings has been omitted, either for glorification or because it is known, due to His words in the verse of al-Aḥzāb: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them from God is great bounty﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 47].

Remarks:
The first: what we have previously stated concerning the interpretation of "the wanderers" as "the fasting ones."
Al-Zajjāj said: this is the statement of the people of tafsir and language, all of them. Al-Ḥākim narrated it as a marfū' report, and so did Ibn Jarīr.
Ibn Kathīr said: its being a statement of a Companion (mawqūf) is more authentic.
(p-٣٢٧٥) And from Ibn ʿAbbās: everything God mentions in the Qur'an of "siyāḥah" (wandering), it is fasting.
And from al-Ḥasan: "the wanderers are the ones who fast the month of Ramadan."
Al-Shihāb said: "siyāḥah" has been borrowed for fasting because it restrains from desires, just as wandering mostly restrains from them.
Al-Rāzī transmitted from Abū Muslim that "al-sā'iḥīn" are those who travel in the earth, derived from "al-sayḥ," the flowing of water, and that what is meant is one who goes out striving (jihād) as an emigrant (muhājir).
Its explanation: God urged the believers in the first verse toward jihad, then mentioned this verse in describing the attributes of the strivers, so they should be described by all these attributes.
Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated something similar from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: they are the emigrants (muhājirūn).
And from ʿIkrimah: they are those who move about to seek knowledge.
Ibn Kathīr said: there has come what indicates that siyāḥah is jihad. Abū Dāwūd narrated from the hadith of Abū Umāmah that "a man said: O Messenger of God! Permit me to wander (siyāḥah). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The wandering of my nation is jihad in the way of God.'"
I say: if this hadith were taken as the tafsir of the verse, it would agree with everything that has been reported from the predecessors concerning it, because jihad in the way of God, as it is applied to fighting the polytheists, is also applied to everything that involves striving against the self in worshipping Him, including emigration and fasting, and travel for seeking understanding of the religion or for reflection. Rather, that is the greater jihad.
This is if the aim is to reconcile the transmitted reports. But if the word is meant in its original linguistic reality, namely traveling in the earth specifically, which ʿIkrimah expressed as "those who move about to seek knowledge," then it alone would suffice in meaning, pointing to a great attribute, and this is what led Abū Muslim to restrict himself to it; it is the truth in the interpretation of the verse.
(p-٣٢٧٦) I have seen a statement of some of the investigators supporting it, which the investigator should look at, and here is its summary: He said: The Wise Book often commands a person to devote a part of his life to wandering and traveling, for the sake of discovering traces and learning the news of the perished nations, so that this becomes an example of admonition and reflection, striking the heads of the rigid with an iron hand.
I do not wish to burden the reader of those verses, for that would lead to lengthiness; rather, I want to take from them what establishes the claim, and that is in His words: ﴿the wanderers﴾ in this verse. The word "sā'iḥūn" does not occur in the Noble Qur'an except this single unique time.
Despite that, the people of tafsir have overridden it, so some said they are the fasting ones, and some said other than that.
The correct view is that ﴿al-sā'iḥūn﴾ means the travelers, derived from "al-sayḥ," which is running over the surface of the earth and going about in it, and this root conveys the sense of spreading.
It is said: "sāḥa al-mā'" meaning it flowed and spread, and "al-sayḥ" is also flowing water going over the surface of the earth.
"Al-sā'iḥ" is also used with a meaning opposed to the solid, namely spilled water, because by its liquidity it spreads in its container.
We know of the words of the Qur'an that they must be taken according to their apparent meanings and their true meanings, except where an intellectual impediment prevents it; and there is no impediment here to intending the reality. Accordingly, the word ﴿al-sā'iḥūn﴾ must be taken according to its apparent, true meaning, namely those who travel and go about the lands in order to see the traces, to connect with admonition and reflection through them, and for other benefits that history has known.
Likewise, we know that a figurative meaning may not be intended except when there is an indication preventing the literal meaning; but here the matter is the reverse, due to the abundance of indications demanding that the literal meaning be intended rather than the figurative, such as the verses: ﴿Travel﴾ [al-An'ām: 11] (p-٣٢٧٧) ﴿Have they not traveled?﴾ [Ghāfir: 21] ﴿Have they not traveled?﴾ [Yūsuf: 109] ﴿So travel﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 137] ﴿And others travel in the earth﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of God﴾ [al-Nisā': 100], and the verse.
These verses are clear indications that "sayḥ" means travel. Although they are from a different root, their meaning meets the meaning of "sayḥ." Moreover, we do not lack an indication of this from the same root itself, such as the verse: ﴿So travel freely in the earth for four months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2]. The word "sīḥū" here explains "al-sā'iḥūn" in this verse, and they say: the best interpretation is that which is explained by what is received.
In sum, diverting this word from its apparent meaning is a limitation upon the nation, a management that dulls its resolve and weakens its activity, and a barrier between it and the happiness of encompassing the traces of the perished nations and seeing the civilization of the inhabited world, the matter which is now the sought-after lost thing among the Westerners; and in it is a veiling of the light of the Book, which is the first guide for the scholar not to spare effort in traveling and wandering, and to go about in the lands, that is, to investigate.
A continuation of this will come in the interpretation of the verse: ﴿wandering women﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 5] in Surah al-Taḥrīm, God willing.
Al-Rāzī said: wandering has a great effect in perfecting the soul, because one meets various kinds of harm and hardship, (p-٣٢٧٨) so he must endure patiently; and he may meet distinguished people of differing kinds, so he benefits from what the other does not have.
He may meet the great men of the people, so he belittles himself in their presence; he may attain many desires and benefit from them; and he may observe the differing conditions of the world due to what God has created in each region of particular circumstances belonging to its people, so his knowledge grows.
In sum, wandering has strong effects on religion. End.
Some said: O intelligent one, it is not hidden from you that God urged the children of Adam to travel in His mighty Book, and rebuked those among them who put on the garment of laziness, and cast themselves into the pit of inactivity, and took pleasure in sitting idle instead of crossing the lands and traversing the valleys. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Have they not traveled in the earth, so that they would have hearts by which to understand or ears by which to hear?﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 46]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Travel and you will be healthy; fight and you will be rich."
Many scholars, wise men, and men of letters have spoken on the merits of travel, in verse and in prose.
Among its greatest benefits is the increase of one's knowledge, and others benefiting from what he knows and acquires; and among them, and it is the greatest of them, is the pleasure of his Lord and increased reward for benefiting His servants; and the dearest of God's servants to God are those most beneficial to His servants.
Likewise, by taking admonition from the conditions of people, reflecting on their affairs, and gaining insight in His domain into the hidden secrets and the wisdoms by which God manages the affairs of creatures and perfects the making of existing things.
Whoever comprehends the secret of the Creator increases in magnifying Him and draws near to Him through obedience and compliance with His commands and prohibitions. And it is not hidden what befell the prophets and messengers, the Companions and the Successors, the saints and the righteous, of journeys and travels through villages and cities, for observation and reflection.
(p-٣٢٧٩) The second: al-Qāḍī said: the mention of bowing and prostration was made a metonymy for prayer, because the other forms of the one praying conform to custom: standing and sitting. What departs from custom in this is bowing and prostration, and by it the distinction between one who prays and another becomes clear.
It may be said: standing is the first degree of humility before God, bowing is its middle, and prostration is its ultimate. So bowing and prostration were singled out for mention, because they indicate the utmost humility and servitude, and as an alert that the purpose of prayer is the utmost submission and glorification. Al-Rāzī mentioned this.
The third: They mentioned, regarding the secret of the conjunction in two places among these attributes, several opinions:
As for the first, namely His words: ﴿and those who forbid what is wrong﴾, they said: the secret of the conjunction there is either to indicate that the item conjoined with what precedes it is in the ruling of one quality and one attribute, because between them there is mutual implication in the mind and in external reality, since commands entail prohibitions, and there is opposition apparently, since one is a demand for an act and the other a demand for abstention; so they were between complete connection and disconnection, which calls for the conjunction. Unlike what precedes them. Or because when He enumerated their attributes, He conjoined these two to indicate that they are one thing and one quality, and the counted item is their combination, as if it were said: those who combine the two descriptions. Or the conjunction is due to the opposition between them. Or to remove ambiguity. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Mughnī: "The apparent view is that the conjunction in this attribute was because commanding and forbidding, insofar as one is commanded and forbidden, are opposites, unlike the rest of the attributes; or because the one who enjoins what is right is also one who forbids what is wrong, and what is wrong is leaving what is right, and the one who forbids what is wrong is one who enjoins what is right. So attention is drawn to the importance of each of the two attributes, and that what is obtained in the course of the other is not sufficient for it."

As for the second, namely His words: ﴿and those who keep the limits of God﴾, it was said: the secret of the conjunction there is the notification that the enumeration has been completed with seven, since seven is the complete number, and the eighth begins another enumeration conjoined to it; for this reason it is called "the waw of eight." It was objected to this that what indicates completion is the word "seven," because it is used for multiplicity, not for what it counts.

The view of the "waw of eight" was mentioned regarding His words: ﴿They will be seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and al-Mughnī weakened it.

It was said: the secret of the conjunction is to indicate that what precedes it details the virtues, and this summarizes them, because it encompasses what precedes it and other things; and the like of this is brought conjoined, as in: "Zayd and ʿAmr and the rest of their tribe are generous." So because it differs from what precedes it in summary and detail, and in generality and specificity, it was conjoined to it.

It was said: by the strength of the comprehensive attribute through implication, because whoever attains the preceding attributes has guarded the limits of God.

It was said: what is meant by guarding the limits is its apparent sense, namely establishing the prescribed punishments, such as retaliation against one who deserves it.

The first attributes up to His words ﴿those who enjoin﴾ are praiseworthy attributes of the person in himself, while these are for him in relation to others; therefore the expression of the two categories changed: the conjunction particle was left out in the first category and was used in the second.

Since the first attributes must necessarily be combined in one thing, the conjunction (ʿatf) was omitted here because of the strength of their connection. This is unlike the following attributes, for it is permissible for their doers and those to whom they relate to differ.

This is what prompts the parsing of "at-tā'ibūna" (the repentant) as a subject (mubtada') described by what follows it, with "al-āmirūna" (those who enjoin) as its predicate (khabar).

It is as if it were said: they are the perfect in themselves, the ones who perfect others. The first was placed first because the one who perfects others cannot perfect them until he is perfect in himself. By this the arrangement (naẓm) has come together in the finest order without strain, and God knows best what He intends. Thus [it is stated] in al-ʿInāya and Ḥawāshī al-Mughnī.

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[113–114] ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114].

﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114]

Since Allah, the Exalted, made clear at the beginning of the surah and after it that disavowal (al-bara'ah) from the polytheists and the hypocrites is obligatory, He, glorified is He, here clarifies what further strengthens this, by forbidding seeking forgiveness for them after their polytheism and disbelief have become clear, because their manifest state necessitates severing allegiance (al-muwalah), even with relatives. For their kinship, though it may produce a bond with them and mercy toward them, does not benefit them in receiving the light of forgiveness: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be set up with Him﴾ [an-Nisa: 48]. So seeking forgiveness for them is in the category of opposing the promise and threat of Allah.

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that the reason for Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father was that it was due to a promise he had previously made to him, in His words: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 47] and His words: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4], and that this was before his persistence in polytheism was confirmed. ﴿But when it became clear to him﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114] that ﴿he disassociated himself from him﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114], meaning from his father entirely, let alone seeking forgiveness for him.

Allah, the Exalted, clarified what moved Abraham to seek forgiveness, namely his excessive compassion and patience, by His words: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was ʾawwah﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114], meaning one who often sighs (ta'awwuh) from excess of mercy and tenderness of heart, ﴿forbearing﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114], meaning patient with what afflicts him of harm. For this reason he was forbearing toward his father, despite his threat to him in His words: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾ [Maryam: 46], and he asked forgiveness for him by his words: ﴿Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. That was before the distinction was made clear, so it is not permissible for anyone else to take him as an example in this.

In the verse there is an emphasis on the obligation of avoidance after the distinction has been made clear, since the Prophet ﷺ disavowed his father after the distinction was made clear, while he was in perfect tenderness of heart and forbearance. So it must be that others are even more inclined than he to avoidance and disavowal.

(Notes)

First: The exegetes cited here numerous narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. Since some of them found these to be contradictory, they attempted to reconcile them by multiplicity of occasions of revelation. There is no contradiction, because of what we have already mentioned: that the statement "it was revealed concerning such-and-such" may mean that the ruling of the verse encompasses what occurred regarding such-and-such, in the sense that its revelation applies to it. And it may mean that such-and-such was the cause of its revelation. What is here is of the first type, and its parallels in the revelation are many, and we have drawn attention to this repeatedly, especially in the introduction. So memorize it.

Second: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: "I would not abandon the prayer over anyone of the People of the Qiblah, even if she were an Abyssinian woman pregnant from fornication, because I have not heard that Allah prohibited the prayer except for the polytheists," and then he recited the verse. This is sound jurisprudence.

Third: Some of the Yemenis said: "The verse has been used as evidence that one who sighs during the prayer does not invalidate it." This is reported from Abu Ja'far: if he says "āh," his prayer is not invalidated, because Allah, the Exalted, praised Abraham, peace be upon him, for that. The position of the Imams, however, is that it is invalidated, whether he says "āh" or "awwah," because that is among the speech of people, and Allah, the Exalted, did not mention that Abraham's sighing was during the prayer. End.

Fourth: In "al-ʿInayah" it is said: "Awwah" is an intensive form (faʿʿal) of "al-taʾawwuh," and the measure of its verb would be triliteral, since the patterns of intensity are regularly derived from it. Qutrub related a triliteral verb for it, namely "āha yaʾūhu, awhan," like qāma yaqūmu. Others denied this, saying that it is only said "awwaha" and "ta'awwaha." He said:

"When I rise to saddle her at night, she sighs the sigh of a grieving man."

Taʾawwuh is the saying of "āh" and the like, of what a grieving person says, and so it is used as a metonym for grief and tenderness of heart. End.

"Awwaha," with the second letter doubled and the h sukun, and "awwah," and "awh" with sukun on the w; all three vowel patterns are attested. He said:

"So alas, over visiting Umm ʿAmr, how much more with enemies and slanderers?"

Sometimes they change the waw to alif, saying "āh min kadhā," as he said:

"Āh from your ʿayyāk ... you left my heart distracted."

"Āh" with a kasrah on the h and tanwin is also reported, as are "āhan" and "wāhan." There are other dialects, which the Taj (al-Taj) brought to twenty-two. All of them are words said at complaint, pain, and sorrow, indeclinable on whatever final sound they are bound to, except "āhan," whose accusative is because it is treated as a verbal noun, as if it were said: "I lament with a lament."
